Notes of the Week

The terror in Eretz Israel continues; the 43rd Jewish victim has already been recorded.
—o—
In Pińsk 12 chadarim and the "Moshav Zkenim" (old-age home) were burned down; the damage amounts to 80 thousand złoty.
—o—
The well-known lawyer Hofmokl-Ostrowski has been sentenced to 3 months and to the loss of the right to practise for 10 years.
—o—
In England it came to a bloody clash between English fascists and communists.
—o—
In America the severe heat caused enormous damage; the number of victims reaches 1800.
—o—
Behind Hielon[?] a railway disaster occurred. 2 people were killed and 3 wounded.
—o—
In Madrid the leader of the monarchists in Spain was murdered.
—o—
In South America a terrible earthquake occurred; the damage is very great.
Almost a "Blood Libel" in Olkusz

A certain Król was employed by Mr. Gliksman in Olkusz. Suddenly Król vanished. This was a juicy morsel for the dark elements, who spread a rumour that Król — who is, by the way, a grown-up[?] gentile — had been carried off by the Jews to Kraków in order to draw blood from him for matzot (well, it is almost Tisha b'Av, after all, so the Jews must have blood for the kinot [lamentations]...).
The story was also exploited by the "Kurier Zagłębia", which ran the report of Król's disappearance under the heading: "Jews have abducted a Pole!"
Fortunately the "treasure" was found. It turned out that he had gone to Myślenice to work for the Słomnicki firm.
Appeal to All Merchants in the Buying-up Trade in Będzin and Vicinity

Thousands of Jewish families in Poland draw their livelihood from the buying-up trade (skup wtórny[?]). This form of trade has lately been heavily burdened both by the tax authorities and by the administrative authorities. Out of understanding for the difficulties of this kind of trade and its minimal profits, various allowances had until now been granted in assessing the turnover tax, and especially in the tax rate. The latest changes in the turnover-tax law have put an end to the allowances, and from 1936 the turnover of the buying-up trade is calculated together with the others at the rate of 1.7 per cent. The changes introduced thus raise the previous tax rate from 0.5 to 1.7 per cent. The high taxation may completely ruin the trade, which relies on very small profits and large turnovers.
The Będzin Association of Retailers and Small Traders, watching over the interests of those engaged in "skup" — who in Poland number in the tens of thousands — has undertaken a broad campaign aimed at securing the possibility of continued trade and existence.
So that the campaign may be crowned with due success, the executive of the Central Association of Retailers and Small Traders has decided to convene an all-Polish congress of buying-up traders, to take place in the course of August of this year in Warsaw. The congress is to be attended by buying-up traders of all branches, such as: grain, dairy (nabiał), hides, scrap iron, rags, etc.
We point out that, owing to the specific character of the congress, those directly concerned must take part. All buying-up traders of Będzin and vicinity must register immediately at the Będzin Small Traders' Association, Małachowskiego 2, so that a meeting of those concerned can be called to elect delegates to the congress.
We therefore call on all buying-up traders who hold licences (patents) for "skup" to register immediately at our association.
The Board of the Będzin Small Traders' Association.
Memorial Services for Dr. Herzl and H. N. Bialik

On Sabbath memorial services were held in the synagogues of Zagłębie in honour of the yahrzeits of Dr. Herzl and Chaim Nachman Bialik, of blessed memory.
In the Będzin synagogue a memorial service organised by the New Zionist Organisation took place on Sunday. Speeches were made by Messrs. Chmielnicki (Zawiercie[?]) and Jasny (Sosnowiec).
On the same day in the evening a second memorial service was held by the Zionist Organisation. The cantor with the choir recited El Male Rachamim[?] for Herzl, for Bialik, for the martyrs in Eretz Israel, and the new Yizkor. [It] made a shattering impression. Messrs. Chigarzki[?] and Manela[?] spoke on current affairs.
— In Sławków, under the chairmanship of the president of the local Zionist Organisation, Mr. L. Testiler, a mourning academy was held in the fire-brigade hall.
Speeches were delivered by Messrs. Sztern and Szulc.
The second part of the academy was performed by the members of "Hanoar Hazioni".
Dąbrowa

A Bloc between the Kromołów Hasidim and the Artisans.
On Sunday negotiations took place in the artisans' premises on concluding a technical bloc for the kehilla elections between the Kromołów hasidim and the artisans.
On this question Messrs. Ch. Landner, Frejlich and T. Mit-Dawnik[?] express their views; [it is] decided[?] to form the bloc.
—o—
The Zionists on the Kehilla Elections.
Under the chairmanship of the president of Keren Hayesod, Mr. Aharon Nachman Gutman, a members' meeting devoted to the kehilla elections in our town took place on Sunday evening.
Mr. G. Gutman discusses the activity of the kehilla at the present moment and stresses that only the Zionists, as the majority, are called upon to lead the principal Jewish bodies, such as kehillot, town councils and other institutions, which have lately been so neglected by the uninvited guardians.
An election committee is chosen of Messrs. G. Gutman (president), Nejer[?] Bornsztajn (vice-president), Gurfinkel (treasurer), Nusbaum, Kaszuk (secretariat).
It was decided to call, on this coming Saturday night, a consultation of all national groupings going to the Zionist Congress and to create a united national Zionist bloc.
—o—
Summer Colonies of "Hashomer Hadati".
As every year, this year too "Hashomer Hadati" is organising 2 colonies in Jeleśnia. Up to 40 people take part in the colonies, who will go through the instructors' course.
The management of the colony consists of M. Krage (Warsaw), Orlean (Eretz Israel) and the Andrychów rabbi Yechiel Rausz[?].
—o—
From the Tailors' Guild.
On Monday, under the chairmanship of Mr. Cukrowski, a meeting of the tailors' guild took place, attended by 120 members.
The meeting dealt with the question of the forthcoming kehilla elections.
During the discussion it emerged that the report about the merger of the Dąbrowa Artisans' Association with all the guilds does not accord with reality.
Finally an election committee was chosen of Messrs. Cukrowski, J. Jakubowicz, Welgrin, Szenhof, Filc, M. Plachte and J. Krauz.
—o—
"He" Gave One — Reb Yaakov Gave Back One and Another..
Elchanan Kwaśniewski of Będzin, walking on Saturday night along Będzińska Street in Dąbrowa, was accosted by 3 hooligans; one of them struck Kwaśniewski and shouted:
— "Żydziu, daj złotego!" [Jew-boy, give me a złoty!]
Kwaśniewski took stock of the situation and instead of money gave the fellow back one and another, at which the hooligans took fright and ran away from the Jew.
What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — short news items.]
Hitler Will Not Come, but His Hasid Will Sit in "Yoshev be-Seter" [i.e. in prison].
Teodor Baranowski of Rybnik "preached" publicly that "in a few months Hitler will come and with an iron broom he will sweep the Poles out to Russia".
For this "prophecy" Baranowski was sentenced to 6 months' unconditional imprisonment.
—o—
Paid 300 zł. to Have Her Husband Murdered.
In the Lubliniec district [powiat] a certain Wakszewski[?] was found murdered. The investigation established that Wakszewski had been murdered by a certain Kensy[?], who had received 300 zł. from Wakszewski's wife to murder him.
—o—
A Terrible Storm.
On Saturday afternoon a storm accompanied by heavy thunder[?] passed over the Upper Silesian area, causing considerable damage.
In Katowice the tunnel on Mikołajowska Street was flooded to a height of one metre.
Besides that, the water flooded a number of cellars.
—o—
Punishment for Violating the Foreign-Currency Ban.
Before the Chorzów district court stood a certain Józef Bartak of Będzin, who was accused of wanting to smuggle a certain sum of money from Poland to Germany.
Bartak was sentenced to 6 months' imprisonment.
—o—
A Petard Thrown into a Stationery Shop.
On Tuesday morning, when Mr. R. opened his stationery shop in Katowice, he smelled kerosene. Looking around, he saw a petard lying there, which had been thrown in through the window and luckily had not exploded.
It is presumed that the petard-thrower, seeing that the petard had not exploded, poured kerosene into the shop with the aim of starting a fire.
—o—
An Expensive Dream...
At the station in Szopienice, in the third-class "poczekalnia" [waiting room], a certain Pitawarczyk[?] of Będzin dozed off.
This was exploited by "the pickpocket" Szmul Michalek, who pulled a wallet with money and documents from the sleeping man.
—o—
A Railway-Ticket Racket Uncovered.
The investigating authorities are on the trail of a well-organised gang [szajka] of railway-ticket forgers.
Warsaw railway officials are also said to be involved in the racket.
Zawiercie.

[Zawiercie — community, antisemitism, trade, municipal; followed by an item from Cieszyn.]
An Informer's Denunciation of the Kehilla Board.
The local magnate Mr. R. Rozenberg, whose assessment ["etat" — communal tax] the kehilla board had raised, sent the voivode a denunciation ("mesirah") against the kehilla board and against the secretary, Mr. Lewkowicz[?].
—o—
Beaten on the Train.
This week R' Pinchas Lewenberg of Zawiercie travelled to Ząbkowice. In the carriage sat 2 more Jews and Miss Lehman of Łódź[?]. Into the same carriage came also a hooligan, who began to pick on Mr. Lewenberg because he wears a Jewish cap, at which the girl reacted. For this the hooligan attacked the girl, beat her and tore her dress on her.
—o—
The Concession for Butchers Revoked.
As we have already written, the starosta [district head] had permitted the butcher shops ("yatkes") to open on Sunday morning instead of Saturday night.
A delegation of Christians approached the starosta with the request to revoke the decision on trading on Sunday. The starosta granted their request, and this week a ban was issued on opening the butcher shops on Sunday.
Yehezkel.
—o—
Zawiercie Receives Credit of Half a Million zł.
At the conference held recently in Kielce under the chairmanship of Vice-Voivode Bieniewski, the question of distributing the promised credits for the towns of Zagłębie was discussed.
It was decided that of the 9 million zł. which the Fundusz Pracy [Labour Fund] lends out for public works, half a million zł. is allotted to the Zawiercie district.
—o—
Suffered a Heart Attack While Bathing.
The 24-year-old student Manka, who had gone to a summer residence in Cieszyn, was bathing in the municipal pool, where he suffered a heart attack and died.
An Open Letter to President Mr. Rubinlicht.

[Będzin — post office; open letter to the kehilla president.]
In connection with the article in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" No. 26, "The Będzin Post Office and Its Branches", I intervened with the naczelnik [head] of the Będzin post office about opening a branch on the western side of the town (Czeladzka — Guszycowska[?] Streets), and the naczelnik answered me that the question is no longer topical, or more correctly, that no post-office branch will be opened, and he cited you, Mr. President, saying that you had declared to him in the name of all the institutions of which you are president that a post-office branch in that part of town is entirely superfluous.
I therefore ask: what and who convinced you, Mr. President, to give the naczelnik such a declaration and thereby harm the interests of Będzin's merchant community?
With due respect,
J. Gelbart.
Dawid Priwer, of blessed memory

[Sosnowiec — mourning; obituary.]
After a lengthy illness there died at the age of 39 the well-known Sosnowiec communal activist Dawid Priwer, may he rest in Eden.
Dawid Priwer was a man of the people in the full sense of the word. Quiet and modest, he took an active part in a number of societies, was one of the founders and loyal workers of "Maccabi" and later of the "Lira".
Dawid, or as "the street" called him — Dudek[?], held the post of director of the "Moshav Zkenim" [old-age home]. But for the old people he was not merely a director but a veritable father. He simply sacrificed himself for the old people and also for the institution.
Thousands of friends, with "Maccabi" at their head, accompanied the noble man to his eternal rest. At the open grave moving speeches were delivered: Dr. Hercman[?] on behalf of "Dobroczynność" [the charity society] and the Moshav Zkenim, for "Maccabi" — Józef Goldberg, and for the "Lira" — Szymek.
Peace to his dust! May his soul be bound up in the bond of life.

Should We Respond

[Zagłębie and Upper Silesia — the economic boycott; opinion.]
Boycott for Boycott?
(On the boycott campaign in Zagłębie and Upper Silesia).
In normal times this question would not even have occurred to us. But now, when the boycott against the Jews has been turned by the Endecja [the National Democrats] into an economic war, the question comes to our minds unbidden — as a means of defence, of counterweight [?], of counter-attack, as a protective measure, as a necessity of self-defence.
Since the boycott is given official approval through the "owszem" [Premier Sławoj-Składkowski's "economic struggle — owszem (by all means)"], since it is fixed as a weapon against Jewish livelihoods, then this question arises instinctively, just as it arises in a person who stands before an abyss and sees before him a danger, a disaster — the instinct to guard oneself, to save oneself.
For it is surely clear: if the economic boycott becomes a system, a task, an idée fixe for a part of society — to push the Jews out of their livelihoods of hitherto — then the question must arise before us: what are we Jews to live on, after all [?]?
We have never thought, God forbid, of paying measure for measure, evil for evil, bad for bad; that is not the point, and that is not what is at issue now either. Fortunately we are still quite far from that sort of chauvinism.
But what is at issue is a very serious problem: must we let them spit in our porridge? Must we let them climb onto our heads? Simple and elementary: every human being has the right to exist, to work, to earn his bread, to wage a struggle for subsistence for himself and his family, to fight for his existence. And now they come to a part of the population and tell them: because you are Jews, you do not have this right which we non-Jews [?] have. We need not compete with your economic positions — but simply take them away from you, tear them out, even by force. If you will not let go — we will beat you out of your skin [?], knock the ground from under your feet.
Then indeed we have no choice left but to answer: if you behave thus towards us — we too shall have to act thus towards you. For we are not, on your account, simply going to lie down and die.
And another thing: one can exist economically, sustain oneself materially, only when people have economic relations among themselves, when they exchange trade, craftsmanship, products, tools, etc. That is what animates society economically. If you do not want to have any economic relations with us Jews, it means you want to crowd us out, to bring us to ruin both economically and physically. Then we shall have to repay you in the same coin. And we shall see who is stronger in this field.
For economic struggle — in that we Jews already have thousands of years of practice. For a few thousand years we have been waging a struggle not only for our spiritual and physical existence — but also for our economic existence, and you can see: they have not defeated us, we have held out.
So on that score we have nothing to fear. We have endured worse. But the point is that a rupture in the economic sphere estranges one part of society from the other, provokes quarrels, strife, hatred, and that is not normal for a country. That is why we do not want it. We want to avoid it. We want to live in peace. We want calm and order to prevail.
Therefore we say to you, boycott-callers! We shall not answer you with boycott for boycott until you see for yourselves that you have made a bitter mistake, that you have made a bad calculation, that you have been misled by malicious leaders who did not have your good in mind, but their own [?] egoistic interests and narrow-minded intentions.
We shall not answer you with boycott — until your eyes open and you look around to see who are your "friends" and who are your "enemies". Until you come to your senses and understand that it is a sin to boycott fellow citizens merely because we are of another nation; until you grasp that one cannot live in "domestic peace" while living, after all, together with millions of Jews, that there can be no normal economy, no healthy business climate, when one shuns living limbs of the body — having nothing to do with them, keeping no economic contact with them.
A. Y. G—ski.
An Oath for the Annulment of Overdue Taxes

[Poland — taxes; law.]
The tax offices have now begun checking the books and establishing from which of the tax debtors the overdue taxes cannot by any means be collected, in order to annul these debts. Before the overdue taxes are annulled, however, every tax debtor will be required, through the court, to take an oath that he does not possess any property unknown to the tax office.
The annulment of the overdue taxes will apply only to those who have been thoroughly ruined, where all distraints [zajęcia] have produced no result, and where in the opinion and according to the investigation of the tax office there are no prospects of collecting the overdue taxes in the near future.
The tax authority will now gradually summon, through the court, the persons who owe old taxes, so that they submit to the court a list of all their property and, on an appointed date, take an oath in court that they own no more than is stated in the list.
If the tax authority decides to demand an oath and a disclosure of property from someone, it must do so through the local municipal court. The tax authority has no right to do this itself. The tax authority forwards the files to the court with the request that the tax debtor be ordered to disclose his property under oath.
The order to disclose the property and take an oath is issued by the court on the basis of Art. 621 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
This article states that at the creditor's request the court orders the disclosure of the property and the taking [?] of an oath that nothing of the property has been concealed and that the list of property is correct and complete.
In the list of property the tax debtor must write out all things that have any value and are his property, such as goods, furniture, household; one must state the places and addresses where the things are located; one must also enumerate all sums of money one has lying with other people, and their addresses.
Only one's own things, which are the property of the debtor, need be entered in the list. One need not enter things belonging to a close relative. For example, if the tax debtor is a man and the household of the apartment is the property of his wife on the basis of a marriage settlement [intercyza] or the like [?], such things need not be entered in the property list.
The court and the representative of the tax office may question the tax debtor about his property and may ask all kinds of questions aimed at discovering the debtor's property.
Article 625 states that if the tax debtor refuses to submit a list of his property, or refuses to take the oath, or does not respond to the court's summons and does not appear in court on the appointed day, the court may, at the request of the creditor — the tax office — punish the tax debtor with arrest of up to two weeks.
This can go on until the arrest amounts in total to 6 months. Each time one can be punished for no longer than 2 weeks, and in total the arrest may amount to 6 months.
Once one has submitted a list of property under oath, one is exempt from swearing for 5 years. That is, for [lit. "and"] 5 years no creditor may demand an oath again. Neither the tax office for other taxes nor any other creditor can demand an oath. The tax office may, however, continue to claim its debt, even after the oath. Now, however, on the basis of a ministerial circular, the overdue taxes will be annulled after the oath.
A debtor summoned to court to disclose his property may demand that no oath be taken from him only if he can declare that the tax office can collect his tax debt from his shop with its goods or from his property, and that the tax office has not yet exhausted all means of execution to collect its debt. The defence can be sent to the court in writing, but on the day of the summons one must appear specially; the defence can also be presented orally, in person, on the day one is summoned to court.
The "Morawiec" and the "Beautiful Blonde"!...

[Humorous feuilleton — summer holiday.] Almost a true story.
Told by Y. Aberzhanek [Oberżanek?]

As you know, I am already an old "letnik" [summer holidaymaker]; every year I send my household to a letnisko [summer resort]. There is no river where my wife ["mayn yurene"] has not dipped herself, no plaża [beach] where she has not roasted herself, no forest where she has not "gemazhet" [?] in the evening hours. I am an old letnik, son of a letnik.
Every summer I decked out ["oysgestroyet", from Polish stroić] the letniczka [the lady holidaymaker, i.e. my wife][?] like a princess, clothed the little ones, and spent my holiday together with my household.
Well, that was a holiday — I wouldn't wish it on my enemies.
First of all she dismissed the maid. If I am on holiday, then what the devil does she need a maid for? And so, right on the first day, she began to "make use" ["skorzhishtshen", from Polish skorzystać] of my holiday.
At 6 in the morning she woke me:
— Motele, what, are you forgetting?[?] It's already 6 o'clock!
— Motl, are you getting up or not? Climb down from the "gniazdo" [nest], wash out a pot and go to the cowshed for half a litre of milk, do you hear?
Well, I saw that I would get nowhere, so I went out to the cowshed to bring milk.
When I came back with the milk, she said to me:
— Well, now, Motele, you'll go out to the butcher's for meat,
I didn't answer a word and went to the butcher's.
The butcher asks me:
— For soup, or for a stew?
— How should I know! Where would I know that from? You know what, give me half this and half that — that is, a bit for soup and a bit for a stew.
When I came home with the portion, my wife raised a hue and cry:
— Shlimazl, what have you brought me? Nothing but "khabes" [?] — there are more bones here than meat! How can you let them palm off such a "tsulog" [make-weight of bones] on you? A grown man, and you can't send him for a piece of meat!...
And so it went on all the time: I went for milk, to the butcher's for meat, brought buckets ["viardes", Polish wiadra][?] of water, chopped wood, made the fire, washed the dishes ["sgefes"][?], scrubbed the floor ["parloge", i.e. podłoga], fed the children, pushed the pram ["vozek", wózek] into the forest. That's how it went the whole holiday.
That's how it was every summer. After every "holiday" I felt that if I had another two or three such "holidays", my little wife would soon become a widow, and since I don't grudge her that "przyjemność" [pleasure], I decided: I'm not renting any more letnisko, and that's that!
This year my wife asks me:
— Well, Motele, what about a letnisko?
— I don't hold with it — I answered.
— What do you mean?
— That's what I mean! This year I'm not renting a letnisko. We'll behave the way all modern people behave.
— How do modern people behave?
— I'll go to a pension, you'll go to a pension too, the children we'll send off to a colony [kolonia, summer camp] — and the deal is done!
Kakh hava. That is just how it was. The children went to a school colony, my wife went to a pension, and I thanked and praised God that I was rid of the letnisko, of the Friday "banaushn" [?], of roasting myself in the Erev-Shabbes "tsugn" [?], and above all — that I would no longer have to "zastępować" [stand in for] the maid. This year I go "solo" to a pension, I'll be a "wolny ptaszek" [a free bird], and for the first time I'll "skorzystać" [make use] of my holiday.
Well, so I got ready for my holiday. I ordered myself elegant silk pyjamas, a modern "veln" [woollen?][?] suit, elegant sport[?] shirts, bathing trunks, white tennis shoes[?], white slippers — a whole "front"!
What else did I do? I shaved myself "na gładko" [smooth], dyed my greyish hair coal-black, trimmed my little moustache "à la française" ["a-la frantsoyski"] — fit to be led to the wedding canopy...
Now I set about inquiring where to go, to which pension. I picked a pension among "blorshesh" [?] — and, of all places, "nad morze" [by the sea].
When I arrived there and [they] saw[?] the "lord", there was joy and gladness. The "gentle sex" surrounded me on all sides. I introduced myself as an "eligible bachelor" ["kavalir tsum hobn"]. Every one of them wanted to "win my heart"; I "amused" ["gebaziet", Polish bawić] the company with "tłuste dowcipy" [fat jokes] from old almanacs. They offered me matches with fat dowries. I went about like at Daddy's in the vineyard. I felt fine, and I thanked God that I don't have to go to the butcher's for meat, to the cowshed for milk, that I am a "wolny ptaszek" and will enjoy a holiday by the book.
But when you are destined to get trouble, it finds you even in a pension — hear a story:
At the very best moment my pension-keeper tells me that a beautiful blonde has come to the pension, a young rich widow, and when she heard that there is a "przystojny" [handsome] cavalier here, she wants to get acquainted with the "Morawiec" ["morowiec", Polish slang: a splendid fellow][?] — with me, that is.
"Bardzo proszę" [with great pleasure] — I answered. A young rich widow, a beautiful blonde — what could be better? The pension-keeper arranged with me to meet in the evening in the dance hall. I got ready for the "spotkanie" [rendezvous]: dyed my hair, spruced up the French moustache, put on the new "veln" [?] suit, a white silk sport shirt, shaved "na gładko", combed myself with despair, sprayed myself with perfume, a rose in the lapel,
and waited for the young rich widow, for the beautiful blonde.
My heart was pounding; I was already curious to see the beautiful blonde who wants to get acquainted with me, the "Morawiec" — and he who waits, gets what he waits for.
As I sat a while lost in thought, the pension-keeper comes up to me and whispers in my ear:
— The young widow is already here. She is waiting for you in the next room.
I needn't tell you, of course, that the "young rich widow" was none other than my own wife. When she caught sight of me, the "Morawiec", she raised a hue and cry:
— Motl!.. and fell down in a faint.
And I myself? I lost my tongue, my teeth chattered tooth against tooth, and when we both came to, I asked her:
— Yentl, since when did you become a widow? The deceased is still alive.
— Well, and you? Since when did you become an "eligible bachelor"? You already have children to marry off!
You want to know the end? The end was that I fled the pension; she did the very same, the "young rich widow" — she too packed her baggage and left without a goodbye.
Well, and what now?
Now we are both getting ready to go back to the letnisko to finish my holiday. She assures me that she won't send me to the butcher's for meat.
Now I ask you, gentlemen, for advice:
— Should I believe her?
Notes of the Times / The Gmina Elections at the Present Moment

[Editorial — Sosnowiec, kehilla elections.]
The election fair and tumult in Sosnowiec, as in several towns and shtetls in Poland, have already begun.
Here in Sosnowiec the election clamour is accompanied by a rabbinate question.
One can already foresee, unfortunately — and this is a well-founded fear — that the election clamour will shout down the terrible plight of the Jews and drown out the cry of woe and the groaning of the Jewish masses and their call for help.
It must therefore be stated in good time, as a warning and an admonition, to the address of the leaders of all parties and institutions — whom the election tumult is already beginning to tear out of the criminal passivity in which they have long been sinking [?] — that the Jewish masses will not deliver themselves into their hands as electoral cannon fodder, to be ground up in the fight for their party ambitions or personal manipulations.
In such a terrible time, when the antisemitic mafia has thrown itself with such wild impetus upon the Jewish people and with its beastly hands tears [?] and mutilates [?] the Jewish body and the Jewish soul — at such a time the Jewish gmina must become the institution where all the forces of the people gather and concentrate; the institution that will organise and cement all the constructive, honest and capable elements into a great work of rescue.
In view of the danger of annihilation and ruin that threatens the entire Jewish community, the party people must now push aside everything that divides them, and set at the top, as the guiding line of their work, the gathering of all creative forces for constructive, practical and moral self-help. Upon all parties there also lies the task of driving out and chasing away, with joint forces, from the surface of Jewish public life all sorts of careerists and corrupt souls who have settled on our people's body, gnawing and devouring it, teeming and swarming like bees, and poisoning the atmosphere of our public life, murderously exploiting the despair and dejection of the masses for their narrow-hearted, self-serving and ambitious ends.
This plague and affliction, which unfortunately has sprouted and blossomed out in recent years in our public life, carries within it seeds that may poison our national existence.
Only the awareness that the grave, dangerous situation and fate are shared equally by all Jews as such, without distinction of occupation or conviction, from the Jewish intellectual with a diploma to the Jewish lumpen-proletarian; that only a united people's front can provide any real help to the masses in their hard and bitter struggle for a human and Jewish existence; and that only with united forces will it be possible to root out the bacilli of demoralisation and corruption that have crept into our life —
only this awareness gives meaning to, and justifies, the anticipated tumult around the elections to the Jewish kehillas.
We are not so naive or blind as not to see that, unfortunately, the psychological ground for such a united Jewish people's front does not yet exist, and that the parties active in the Jewish street do not do the least thing to create such ground.
But a duty lies upon the voting masses to compel the parties and their leaders to fit the election campaign to the gravity of the hour, and to steer it in the direction of competing not in petty party ambitions or demagogy, but in a maximum of sincere will for constructive, help-bearing work carried out by honest and creative forces.
This the masses must do, and this they will do.
Are We Already Living More Cheaply Now?

[Economy — cost of living worldwide.]
In the first five months of the current year a fall in the prices of the most important foodstuffs set in in many countries throughout the world. One cannot even deny that precisely in these months things get cheaper every year: plants begin to grow, and the population feeds on the produce of the soil, which lowers the costs of our daily life.
But this year, it turns out, other articles that we use in life have also become cheaper, so that one may calmly say: we already live a little more cheaply today than a year ago. — True, it is not yet so much cheaper that we actually feel with our senses that we need less money than a year ago at the same time. In some countries individual articles have even become a little dearer. But all this was not so strong that it could anywhere raise the budget of our daily expenses.
According to statistics published by the Leipzig Fair, foodstuffs have become cheaper to a great extent in England, Holland, Finland and Turkey. The reason for the cheapness is that in these countries the grain harvest last year was so large that it could not all be sold, and so competition has now begun within the country itself.
In Poland, Hungary and Yugoslavia, too, grain and cattle have become cheaper. The countries to which cattle or grain used to be sold at cheap prices have fallen away.
In most countries of the whole world consumption has declined. The workers have nothing to do; the need is great, and people have nothing to buy with. So the cattle remaining in one's own stock must be sold, because fodder for the cattle is too dear. The same is true of grain, which is beginning to spoil.
Thus today in Poland, for example, one lives five to eight percent more cheaply than a year ago, and in Hungary and Austria about fifteen percent more cheaply.
Clothing and footwear, too, have recently become cheaper, especially in America, where the prices of clothing articles have dropped by about thirty percent. In Czechoslovakia, too, one can today get clothes and shoes 25 percent cheaper than a year ago.
Only in Poland and Hungary is the customs duty on clothing articles still so high that prices have remained as they were a year ago; almost everywhere else they have become cheaper.
The only country where the cost of foodstuffs has recently risen is Japan. That country exports not only all kinds of goods that industry makes, but also everything the soil yields. Therefore there is dearness within the country itself, which grows higher from day to day.
Hopefully everything will soon become cheaper still in the world.
Z. Haber, Vienna.

Heard and Seen.

By Ben Amotz.

New Yizkors...
— "If you will it, it is no legend"... We saw it on 22 Tammuz 5696. On that day no fewer than [?] two memorial services were held in the Będzin synagogue in honour of Herzl's yahrzeit: in the morning by the New Zionist Organisation (N.Z.O., in the foreign tongue) and in the evening by the old Zionist Organisation.
And the ordinary Jew of all the year round, the man of the people, who does not renounce [?] any of the Zionist obligations, stands gaping and asks: "Is the Herzl of the morning not the same as the Herzl of the evening?" Well, if Jewish parties argue over whom grandfather Mendele Mocher Sforim belongs to — everyone looks in "Grandfather" for what suits him — but the Basel Programme, which was laid down by Herzl, is also the ABC of the New Zionists; so must one "keep a Sabbath of one's own"?
And perhaps the New Zionist Organisation was out to pay compliments to the Agudah youth, or rather to the yeshiva boys whom Sokolow bade leave the beit midrash and enter the Zionist camp — and what reward do they get for it? And the N.Z.O. speaker launches into a description of the heavy sufferings of the Agudah pioneers, who nowadays burn all their bridges behind them and go up to the Land of Israel, where they must pass the examination of the Third International right up to... communism"...
— "If you will it, it is no legend" but a true fact that "when Sokolow of blessed memory cried out at the last Congress: 'King of the people of Israel, the people lives!' he meant not Weizmann but Jabotinsky"... — so said the speaker at the morning memorial in the Będzin synagogue. And the "masses" literally swallowed the pearly words: they saw the splendour of the future Jewish kingdom and also learned who the destroyers of the movement for the Kingdom of Israel are.
The audience of the evening memorial too heard of new victims, of destroyed settlements, of thousands of uprooted trees, of ruined orange groves and vineyards, and of a new Yizkor:
— Remember, O people of Israel!
For a people so wretchedly [?] fragmented and splintered, a people that fights itself so mutually — is enriched with
— new Yizkors...

"I cannot make kiddush"...
We receive a delegation of children. We have come — they say — to the editorial office to unburden ourselves.
— What do you want, children? — we ask.
— We do not ask for things that can satisfy our bodies, but our souls..
And the children relate:
We are staying at the summer colony in Sławków. It is not the first time we are there, and precisely for that reason we cannot bear the great wrong being done to us Jewish children, or rather
— to the Sabbath...
Always, when the Sabbath came, we children — despite being torn away from our home surroundings, from the Sabbath atmosphere that reigns in every Jewish home — were nevertheless enveloped in a Sabbath mood. The candles on the tables, the supervisor's kiddush, which made us forget for a while the daily weekday drabness, and we became
— Sabbath-like...
But today there is no trace of it left; modernism [?] has taken from us both the Sabbath candles and the kiddush.
— We were even bold enough — say the little children — to ask Mr. Kierownik [the director] to make kiddush. But unfortunately we did not find the right address, and he told us openly and honestly:
— I can't do it...
Afterwards we regretted the intervention — a question about a deed — Mr. Kierownik might even be offended that we come to him with such superstitions [zabobony] — to make kiddush, of all things! But we certainly did not mean, God forbid, to offend him. On the contrary, we thought Mr. Kierownik would gladly accept our proposal and would indeed make kiddush...
— But what do you want from us? — we asked.
— We ask that the holiness of the Sabbath not be taken from us — [just?] two little candles and kiddush.
And hearing out the children's small request, we wanted to say to them:
— Children, how naive you still are. When you grow older you will have the opportunity to get to know many such "modern" types; you will find out later that there are very many women whose entire modernism consists in not lighting Sabbath candles, and that there are also many such "intelligentsia" for whom it is a disgrace [?] to say
— "I can't make kiddush"...

Jewish strokes of luck...
It is not as bad as people think; as the saying goes: "The devil is not as terrible as he is painted." Never mind — even in the present time we are living through, Jews also have many strokes of luck.
For instance, how many misfortunes would we have suffered if all the libels hurled at us had not burst like soap bubbles?
And the "luck" that happened just like that on Sunday evening in Małobądzka [?] Street can be dismissed with a wave of the hand: luck it was that the petard explosion occurred during a downpour, Jews were out strolling little, and in all no more than one single Jew was wounded...
Therefore we say that things are still not so bad with us; even in the present bitter time we have to record
— Jewish strokes of luck...

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Matot-Masei)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Matot-Masei
—o—
a) "He shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth" (Num. 30:3)
"According to all that proceeds out of his mouth" — with the same measure with which you bring the word out of your mouth — "he shall do", so must you also carry it out; do not be cooler in carrying it out than in promising... Imrei Chen.
* * *
"And you shall do as you have vowed[?] to the Lord your God, a freewill offering" — at the moment of vowing it is for a person a freewill offering, a thing of good will[?]; when promising, a person is in general a volunteer, ready with his whole heart to do it. What is needed is only that the same generosity of heart should be present also at the "you shall do", when the promise is carried out... Leket Amarim.
* * *
"The wise in heart will take commandments, but a prating fool shall fall" —
The wise man carries out [—][?] the commandment he takes upon himself; whereas the "fool" — "of prating lips" — gets tangled up only in promises, always puts it off till tomorrow and remains stuck in putting it off... The Vilna Gaon.
—o—
b) — "And behold, you are risen up in your fathers' stead, a brood of sinful men" (Num. 32:14)
There are sinners even after death... These are parents who brought up their children badly; and when the children sin, it is after all the parents' fault — so it turns out that even after their death the parents sin. "Our fathers sinned and are no more" — our parents sin even when they are no longer here, when they are no longer alive... — so the Frankfurt Gaon interpreted it.
And this is also what the verse says here: "And behold, you are risen up in your fathers' stead" — if you continue the sins of your parents, if you walk in their ways, you make them sin even after their death... Imrei Shefer.
—o—
c) — "Your servants have taken the sum... And we have brought the Lord's offering, to make atonement for our souls..." (Num. 31:49–50)
It turns out that heading the count, leadership, causes sins for which one must bring an offering. If they had to do with leadership, then [though] they had much Torah and many good deeds, they had to bring an offering "to make atonement for our souls"... R. Shlomo Kluger.
—o—
d) "And you shall be guiltless before the Lord and before Israel" (Num. 32:22)
The commandment to be clean before God and men does not come in the imperative — "cleanse yourselves" — but in the passive form: "you shall be guiltless". For making oneself clean before people — that is not the commandment. One need not make oneself clean, but be clean... not with the intention of justifying oneself[?] before people, but simply to do good[?], and thereby be clean before people as a matter of course... Divrei David.
—o—
e) "We will build sheepfolds here for our cattle" (ibid. 32:16)
The Midrash rebukes the tribes of Reuben and Gad for wanting first to build pens for cattle before houses for children. But in the desert the Jews lived by miracles: they ate manna, drank from Miriam's well and dwelt[?] beneath the pillar of cloud. So the tribes of Reuben and Gad set about building pens for the cattle first, because whoever can, lives by miracles — but cattle cannot live by any miracles. Kohelet Yitzchak.
—o—
f) "Until the death of the high priest, who was anointed" (Num. 35:25)
"Who was anointed by him" — whom the murderer anointed; for a high priest in whose time murders take place has been chosen only by murderers... R. Yitzchak Tartshiner[?].
—o—
Avot, Chapter Two.
g) "Be careful with those in authority" (Mishnah 3)
Having spoken before about those who occupy themselves with communal needs, he says to them: "Be careful with authority" — do not think that if you have authority, power, you may lord it over the public and trample with your feet, sure that the power will support you; "they do not stand by a man in his hour of need" — then, when the community turns against you, the power will not help you at all... R"M Yitzchari[?].
—o—
g) [sic] "More charity, more peace."
He who increases charity, who causes others to give charity — he increases peace. Most quarrels come from misers. Siftei Avot.
A festive welcome in honour of Kiepura

[Sosnowiec — culture.] At the Sosnowiec railway station.
On Monday evening our editorial office received a telegraphic invitation to take part in a welcome in honour of Jan Kiepura, who was arriving in Sosnowiec at 11.30.
The telegram reads:
"Zaglembier Tsaytung", Będzin — Warsaw, 13/7, 17.30. Travelling abroad by Torpeda outside the timetable, I shall stop today at the Sosnowiec railway station, and ask the esteemed editors to share the impressions.
With greetings, Jan Kiepura.
Because Kiepura was held up by his admirers at the larger stations, the special Torpeda train in which Kiepura was travelling arrived at the station in Sosnowiec late.
When Kiepura appears at the window, he is greeted with stormy ovations. As a child of Sosnowiec he steps out of the carriage and takes his place on the platform. Around him gathers a large crowd of friends and admirers, with whom he chats cosily, asking after his teachers and schoolmates.
Jan Kiepura, who, as is well known, is the son of a Sosnowiec baker (his mother is of Jewish descent), asks whether the bakery still exists, whether the bakery's pastries are tasty, etc.
Kiepura, a very cheerful man, looks at the present situation optimistically. The crisis — he says — is already coming to an end, but the main thing is that "one mustn't worry, but just[?] live; mankind must know that one lives only once"...
Moved by the festive welcome, he fulfils the wish of the gathering and sings: "I sing for you", "I love all women", "Nina" and "Salamia".
After every "number" the air trembles with stormy applause, whereupon the crowd starts singing "Sto lat", and a group of admirers lift him onto their shoulders and want to carry him into town. At the "cries for help" a policeman runs in, rescues Kiepura and leads him into the train.
On taking leave, Kiepura gave us a greeting for the readers of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" and especially for his Jewish friends and acquaintances in Zagłębie with [—]
At 1 o'clock Kiepura left Sosnowiec for Katowice, where he was awaited by a large crowd of friends and admirers.
In Katowice, too, he had to sing in front of the "Hotel Monopol".
From the World of Film.

[Cinema — Hollywood and actors.] America snaps up the best directors.

It is by now a well-known rule: if a director or a star distinguishes himself in Europe, Hollywood immediately tries to snatch him up for itself. Money then plays no role, of course, and this "snatching" goes on constantly. Recently America "snatched up" the director An-ton[?] Litzak[?] [i.e. Anatole Litvak] (a Jew), who is known in Europe mainly in the film world of France and England. He is a director with an artistic imagination and European taste. Now this director has already signed a contract with Hollywood, and he is already preparing there an exotic film, "The Sahara Desert," with the well-known star Charles Boyer in the lead role.

The actor Herbert Marshall.

In the course of the last few years a young, interesting actor with a serious, intelligent face has begun to push forward into the front ranks. We have seen him as the partner of Greta Garbo, Joan Crawford, Sylvia Sidney, Marlene Dietrich, Norma Shearer and others.

Herbert Marshall comes from England; his parents were actors, and from childhood on he absorbed the actor's craft. Two years before the World War he appears in English provincial theatres; when the war breaks out he is mobilized and sent off to the French front. In 1917 he is seriously wounded, and until the peace is concluded he remains in hospital.

Then he begins acting in the theatre in London, but he is drawn to film.

In 1928 he travels with his wife, the actress Edna Best, to Hollywood, to try his luck in the international film metropolis. He succeeds, and within a short time he becomes a respected star. One of his most important partners was Gloria Swanson.

Now Herbert Marshall is busy with two new motion pictures, one of which is a spy picture (Marshall already played in a spy film some time ago), and the second is called "Forgotten Faces." In both films his partner is the young actress Gertrude Michael, who appeared on the film horizon only recently.

[Feuilleton — humoresques.] By S. Rubinshteyn [Sz. Rubinsztejn].
(Two humoresques).

A.
When the Devil Gets Scared for Once.

A mother of seven daughters, with whom she had gone off to a summer residence (no harm in trying — maybe a suitable match will turn up after all), sat reading a humoresque in which the writer pokes fun at old girls left on the shelf; and since she had a forty-year-old spinster, she felt a stab, as if the writer had meant precisely her daughter.
There he goes, the rascal [łobuz], pouring salt on her wounds and teasing her:
— Rather than one forty-year-old maid, better two girls of twenty...
It can only be that neighbours and enemies put him up to it...
In great vexation the woman cried out: "Oh, devil!"
In our life it often happens that when you mention the devil he pops up at once.
And sure enough, no sooner had the woman cried out "Oh, devil!" than the devil was standing before her and saying:
— Here I am, gracious lady, what do you desire? How may I serve you!
— Are you really the devil? — the woman could not believe her own eyes — but you look just like a real gentleman [?]. One can't even see any horns under your top hat, nor any chicken feet in your patent-leather shoes.. Not for nothing do we have a saying: "The devil is not nearly as terrible as he is painted"...
Politely and elegantly the devil bowed and said:
— Thank you very much, gracious madam, for your compliments, for whose sake it is worth being a devil; and I assure you that writers commit a great injustice against us brother-devils, inventing slanders about us: the devil roasts people on red-hot spits, the devil whips the dead man with iron rods... Lies and falsehood, never happened, nothing of the sort; I assure you, gracious lady, that the devil is never as terrible as the newspaper writers and the "Reshit Chochmah" paint him.
The woman smiled:
— It is very pleasant to spend time with you, Mr. Devil, and in general it is very good to have a good friend like you. Especially [?] since you are a sensitive and likeable devil, since you know how to please women.
— Certainly, madam — said the devil — at any time. Whenever women have needed my help, I have never refused them.
— You know what, dear devil — said the woman — I have seven daughters...
— Seven daughters are no laughing matter — said the devil.
— And among the seven daughters — the woman went on — I have one daughter who is not married, and since I like you as a devil, I would like you to become my son-in-law.
The devil was frightened to death and vanished in the blink of an eye.

B.
Trousers.

It would seem — what could be simpler than a pair of trousers? And yet one can learn a lot from them, even about love.

1.
He was a young man in love; he used to come to her room, and he would come all dressed up, with a red bow tie and white socks [?].
He was a sportsman and went in for such things. But above all he paid attention to his trousers.
His trousers always had to have the finest crease, and she loved him all the more for it...
So they would sit in her room, sitting and talking about side matters, but their heads were dizzy with love.
Suddenly he would grab her and sit her down on his knees, saying:
— Come to me a little!...
She would let herself be sat down, but remark: what a pity about the trousers, you've only just pressed them...
But at that minute he was in love, deeply in love, and he would gaze at her devotedly and laugh good-naturedly: who cares about the trousers now?
She would see in his words a great sign of his strong love for her, and remain content.
And when the sun had set in the west and the twilight shadows began to creep out of all the corners, our sportsman's trousers would already be entirely like [—][?], not a trace of the fine crease..

2.
Some time later they got married.
He became a husband and she — a wife.
Time ran on, and now it is already three months after their wedding. Sunday, 6 o'clock in the evening.
Our sportsman lies on the sofa, reads a newspaper and is bored...
But his trousers are still creased — not with the crease of old, but with wrinkles...
Flustered, she bustles about the room.
And suddenly she goes over to the sofa, sits down beside her husband, forgets herself and leans on his knee.
He growls angrily:
— Don't lean on me! You know I pressed the trousers only eight days ago.
She gives a start:
— Truly a pity about the trousers!
She gets up and goes off to the kitchen, to the Primus stove.
He stays lying on the sofa, bored.
— — — — — — — — —
Moral: before the wedding, love is dearer even than the finest crease of freshly pressed trousers...
After the wedding, even an eight-day-old crease is dearer...

All this time both of them, Dovidl and Malkale, kept thinking and thinking about what they could do to prevent the wedding. The thought of running away was even born in them. But where to? And with what?

So the half year went by and the wedding drew near. On the Sabbath morning before the wedding Dovidl was called up to the Torah. In the afternoon Dovidl came to Malkale again, but this time, when they saw each other, they both burst into pitiful weeping.

Her father and mother heard the weeping and ran into the room where the two were.

The mother wrung her hands.
"But I told you, Yosef, that the children love each other. There [?]! You have broken two hearts. I told you not to match Dovidl with another girl. You lusted after matchmaking money? Now you have it!"
"What kind of talk is this about love, God preserve us? Among Jews one makes a match!" the dayan answered.
"A match! A match! Well, couldn't you have carried out that match for your own child?"
"I didn't think that far ahead at all," he answered in embarrassment. "Well, go home, Dovidl," he said hesitantly, "everything will heal."
"Nothing will heal!" Malkale screamed. "I can't live any more! I can't!! I can't!!!"
And she threw herself on the bed and broke into violent weeping again.

The wedding took place with great pomp. Dovidl saw the bride for the first time only under the wedding canopy. But even then he saw her only so-so [?], for how could he have seen her, when the canopy stood in a dark courtyard and the bride was veiled? Dovidl did not know whom he was marrying. Before the wedding he had not been allowed to see the bride. "It isn't proper for a beys-medresh boy to go and look at a girl," and he himself had no interest in seeing her either, and certainly not under the canopy. Only after the ceremony, when the bride and groom were led in to the "golden soup", only then did he see his wife, Nechama, and Nechama saw Dovidl.

A whole evening his heart wept within him. He did not know what was happening to him. The next morning he began to look around him, and nothing pleased him. The young wife was even more educated than Malkale; besides Polish she also knew French, but he would not have exchanged a single word of Malkale's for all the languages Nechama spoke.

Nechama was clever and, on top of that, very proud. She worked out what she had to do. At first, when the match was proposed to her, she tried to protest, but she soon became convinced that with her fanatical father she would achieve nothing, so she thought that she must pay the price for freeing herself from her father's house. The price was — to marry blind [?]; if she found a young man who was to her liking, then even if he were pious and fanatical, she would teach him and make a person of him; if not — the moment she was out of her father's house she would already be a free person, she would get a divorce and only later begin a new life.

Nechama took a good look at Dovidl in the first days after the wedding and decided that she could make a decent man of him.

After the wedding, when they began to grow closer, she said to him:
"Dovidl, you already know how to study Torah! But it is good to know secular things too, and languages as well. I want to teach you — are you willing?"
"I have long wanted to know secular things, but I never had the opportunity; I will be very grateful to you for it."

And so it was. Dovidl became a diligent pupil of his wife, who taught him everything she knew. He had a good head and a gift for languages too, so he quickly acquired considerable knowledge of Russian and Polish; a little German he already knew from before, and he went on studying.

Within a year a little girl was born to them, but since he was boarding at his father-in-law's table and had no worries about a livelihood, he went on studying and studying.

Coming to the conference is the chairman of the Palestine Office, chairman of the main organising committee for the World Congress in Poland, Eng. A. Reiss.
The conference opens punctually at 10 a.m. in Będzin, in the new premises of Poale Zion, Kołłątaja 45.
The conference, which promises to be a large one, has aroused enormous interest.
12 localities are taking part in it.
Commissarial Kehilla Administration Demands, Through the Tax Office, 10 zł. “Etat” from Rabbi Hager

[Sosnowiec — kehilla, taxes.]
As is known, rabbis are exempt from paying the kehilla tax. The commissarial [government-appointed] kehilla administration, however, does not hold with this exemption, and has assessed Rabbi Hager at 10 zł.
And as if that were not enough, the administration handed the debt over to the tax office for collection.
On Tuesday a sequestrator [bailiff] indeed affixed a “vignette” [?] [seizure label] in the minyan room [prayer room] of the above-mentioned rabbi
The Committee of 12 Has Elected a Committee of 5

[Sosnowiec — kehilla elections.]
As we have already written, at the “Peace” conference, which took place at the premises of the House-Owners' Association, a committee of 12 men was elected, who are to work out the peace programme for the kehilla elections.
On Sunday the committee held a meeting, at which a narrower committee of 5 persons was elected.
The committee of 5 will decide on “peace” or “war”.
The Activity of the Out-Patient Clinic at “Linat Holim” Is Being Expanded

[Sosnowiec — health, institutions.]
Under the chairmanship of the president, Mr. Goldkorn, a meeting of the board of “Linat Holim” took place together with the doctors' committee.
On the agenda was the expansion of the out-patient clinic's activity with regard to the doctors' duty shifts. It was decided that women's diseases shall be received 2 times a week, and that help shall be given to ear and throat patients.
Regarding the night emergency service [pogotowie], the doctors' committee was charged with working out the relevant regulations for the night duty shifts.
With a Knife in the Head...

[Sosnowiec — crime.]
Pesach Czubatka, a member of “Brit HaHayal” [the Jewish ex-servicemen's league], while walking on Sunday night along Dekerta Street, was attacked by a hooligan, who struck him with a knife in the head.
Czubatka was immediately taken to the Jewish hospital, where he received first aid.
As rumour has it, this was an act of revenge, because a few months ago Czubatka had helped to get the same hooligan arrested by the police.
Jewish Porters Are Going Separately to the Kehilla Elections

[Sosnowiec — kehilla elections, workers' organisations.]
At a meeting held by the Jewish transport workers, a resolution was adopted that in the coming kehilla elections, too, the porters will put forward a separate list.
—o—
Investigation of the Incident During the Parade.
These days the representatives of the sports clubs “Maccabi” and “Nordia” were questioned on the matter of the well-known incident which occurred at the time during the defilade [parade].
As can be seen, the authorities have taken an interest in the matter.
—o—
A Cashier, Too, May Not Lose His Temper..
Before the local municipal court the trial took place against the bank cashier Pająk, who had made an “awantura” [a row] in the apartment of the court bailiff [komornik] Jakimczyk.
Pająk was fined 10 zł.
—o—
A Lesson for Others.
Mr. S. Hibszer hired a “malarz” [house-painter], one Kzits [?], to paint the apartment.
Kzits, however, prefers the bitter drop to painting, so he got from Hibszer an advance for paints, with which he bought himself brandy, and never came back to work.
General Meeting of “Maccabi”

[Sosnowiec — sport, associations.]
Next Monday at 8 in the evening a general meeting of the “Maccabi” members will take place in “Maccabi's” own premises.
It is worth noting that the further existence of “Maccabi” depends on the general meeting. We are sure, however, that the meeting will be well attended by the members who want this important sports club to go on existing.
He Is Curious to Know Who Has Gone on Holiday?...

[Sosnowiec — crime.]
The police arrested a certain Daniel Neidgires [?], a Lithuanian, while he was gathering information on who from Sosnowiec had gone away on holiday and which apartments were “free” of their occupants.
120 Eligible Voters Wronged in Strzemieszyce?

[Strzemieszyce — kehilla elections.]
In connection with the kehilla elections an election committee has been formed in Strzemieszyce.
It goes without saying that it ought to include all groupings. But the Strzemieszyce communal workers act otherwise, and the “recalcitrant” — [?] the rabbi and also the opponents [?] of the board of the G[emilut] Ch[esed] [free-loan] fund — were completely disregarded. Incidentally, 120 voters have been wronged.
— What will the committee answer to this?
The unemployed will be employed 4 days a week

[Sosnowiec (?) — unemployed and public works.] A conference took place at the local magistrate [city hall] last Monday, at which it was decided to increase the number of working days, i.e. instead of 3, the workers will be employed 4 days a week.

Gruesome robbery-murder of a Jewish merchant

He split the body into 4 parts with an axe and hid it in a sack in the forest.
Jewish Kielce was shaken this Wednesday by the terrible news of the gruesome and cruel robbery-murder committed in the village of Belno[?] (Kielce district) on the Jewish merchant Baruch Mangersen[?] from the little town of Łagów.
The story of the bestial murder is as follows:
On Monday before dawn the Kielce resident Yitskhok Organek[?] set out together with his brother-in-law Baruch Mangersen to the villages to buy feathers. On Tuesday morning they arrived in the village of Samsonów, and from there they went on together to the village of Belno. There Baruch Mangersen went in to a certain peasant, Czeplak[?], to buy a little merchandise. His brother-in-law Yitskhok Organek waited for him for several hours at another peasant's, and he did not come back.
Towards evening, seeing that his brother-in-law was still missing, Organek found the matter highly suspicious. He began searching for him all over the village and could not find him by any means. Organek reported this to the Samsonów police post (posterunek), which immediately sent a policeman over to Belno and began searching for the vanished merchant.
The policeman first went into the dwelling of the peasant Czeplak, where Mangersen was supposed to be, and began an investigation. Czeplak declared that the Jewish merchant had indeed been at his place but had left right away. The policeman began to search, and in a side room he noticed traces of blood. He then put Czeplak in chains, left him under the watch of the local sołtys [village head] and ran to the telephone to inform the investigative authorities in Kielce.
Early in the morning several investigating officers arrived in Belno from Kielce and, together with the local police, began a vigorous investigation.
The traces led into the nearby forest, where, after a lengthy search, a gruesome sight was discovered.
Under a large heap of bushes ("krzaki") a blood-soaked sack was found lying, containing the dead body of the tragically murdered Baruch Mangersen. The head, the feet and the hands had been chopped off, the body had been split into 4 parts, and everything together, as already mentioned, lay in the sack. The sight of the gruesome murder is simply indescribable.
The police then went back to the peasant Czeplak and took him for interrogation. Czeplak confessed to the bestial murder and showed the place where he had hidden the 30 zł. 50 gr. that he had robbed from the murdered Jew. Czeplak, shackled in chains, was taken under strict guard to Kielce.
The funeral of the tragically murdered Baruch Mangersen will probably take place in Kielce today, Friday.
Mangersen was 43 years old and leaves a widow with 7 small orphaned children.
The cruel murder of the Jewish merchant made an extraordinarily depressing impression in Jewish circles in Kielce and the surrounding area.
"My wife is at the dacha"...

Mr. Z. (Bodzentyńska Street) had been waiting impatiently for this year's dacha season. He rented a dacha for his wife, and he himself of course stayed in town.
"At last I'll be rid of her jealousy," he consoled himself before his friends, "I'll remind myself of the 'good old years'."
Recently[?] he came home accompanied by 2 other petty householders[?] and 2 women. They brought drinks and snacks along, and there was a "zabawa" [party].
The merriment, however, was broken off quite unexpectedly and in a brutal manner.
The culprit was Z.'s jealous wife.
Sitting at the dacha she had grown very uneasy about how her husband was making use of the "dacha separation".
Without thinking long, she suddenly came into town to carry out an inspection.
When she entered the house she found her husband with the whole company drunk, and they did not even notice that she had come in.
Only when the half-drunk women caught sight of the wife standing there with a raised umbrella were they struck dumb.
The merry atmosphere that reigned in the room was torn apart by a woman's scream:
"Scoundrel, I'll show you right now!"
And she could be relied upon — she showed him.
Knives, forks and plates flew at the guests' heads. The ladies, who were sitting at the table at the time, quickly pulled their clothes on.
We shall confine ourselves merely to noting that the uproar was "immortalised" in a [police] report.
Constituent meeting of the organising committee of the World Jewish Congress

On Wednesday evening the constituent meeting of the organising committee of the World Jewish Congress took place in the premises of the Jewish community (kehilla).
A presidium of 7 persons was elected: Messrs. editor Ch. Wilani[?], G. Górski, Sz. Strawszyński[?], D. Knobel, A. A. Rozenblum and A. J. Szejnfeld.
Mr. G. Górski was elected chairman of the committee; vice-chairmen — editor Wilani[?] and Sz. Strawszyński; secretary — A. Szejnfeld; and treasurer — D. Knobel.
The presidium held a meeting at which it was decided to issue an appeal to the Jewish population about the significance of the World Congress. It was also decided to organise a large election rally and to set up four election bureaus on election day (the 26th of this month).
A "blue bird" from Stanisławów locked up in the Kielce "Chad Gadya"...

A "blue bird" [con-man] from Stanisławów came to Kielce, who, poor fellow, had no luck at all: on his very first "job" he was caught and put into the local prison.
The unsuccessful performance went as follows:
An elegant person walked into the shop of Brajndl[?] Kaminer, introduced himself as the authorised agent of a Jewish charitable institution and asked for a proper donation. But on receiving a refusal, he snatched 10 zł from the open cash-box. At the alarm raised by the clerk, Miss Tenenbaum, a policeman came running and detained the thief.
Deadline for submitting candidate lists for kehilla board members
The period for submitting candidate lists to the election commission, for councillors and kehilla board members (parnasim), begins on 9 September and will last 5 days.
The Herzl and Bialik memorial service in the synagogue

In memory of the late Zionist leaders Dr. Herzl and Ch. N. Bialik, of blessed memory, a solemn memorial service was held in the town synagogue on the occasion of their yahrzeit.
Mr. Y. M. Rajzman[?] spoke with a sermon on the life and work of Dr. Herzl and Ch. N. Bialik, of blessed memory, and afterwards Cantor Górnicki recited "El male rachamim" prayers.
Several hundred Jews from all strata of the Jewish population attended the memorial.
Damage running into millions from storms in the Kielce region

Damage running into millions from storms in the Kielce region.
The damage caused by the raging[?] storm and cloudburst in the Końskie, Opatów, Stopnica and Kielce districts is being assessed; the losses run into the millions. The Kielce voivode, Dr. Dziadosz, interrupted his leave and came to Kielce to organise help for the population that suffered from the disaster.
On examination concessions and the right to keep apprentices

On examination concessions and the right to keep apprentices.
In order to specify the circular of the Ministry of Industry and Commerce of 15 May 1936, the Kielce Chamber of Crafts announces: 1) The right to keep apprentices has been recognised also for those craftsmen who prove that before 16 December 1927 they employed in their workshops young or under-age workers as apprentices or as qualified workers. The certificates establishing the right to keep apprentices are issued by the Chamber of Crafts for a fee of 3 zł.
2) One may be admitted to the master's examination after presenting the following documents: a) a craft card; b) a certificate from the Industry Office that one has already run an independent workshop for 6 years without interruption — this period may already include the working time after receiving the craft card; c) a certificate that before 16 December 1927 the candidate employed young workers as apprentices or qualified workers.
3) Until 30 June 1937 one may be admitted to the journeyman's examination on the generally binding terms, regardless of whether one completed the apprenticeship with a master or [with] a craftsman who has no master's diploma; the condition is that the candidate must have reached 18 years of age.
After 30 June 1937 one may enjoy this[?] right if the apprenticeship contract was registered before 1 January 1937.
Tax distraints on farmers suspended

Tax distraints on farmers suspended.
The Ministry of Finance has already sent a circular to all tax offices that the enforced collection (distraint) of all taxes from farmers is to be suspended in the period from 15 July to 15 October.
The purpose of this order is to ease the financial situation of the farmers, so that they are not forced to sell grain too cheaply.
How to guard against typhus / His parents would not consent to the match — so he shot himself

How to guard against typhus.
The health authorities fear that because of the great heat typhus may begin to spread.
In this connection a series of instructions will be published on how to protect oneself from this serious disease.
Everyone must remember to wash fruit before eating. Carefully sort through the vegetables bought, and eat foodstuffs as little as possible in a raw state; nor may one drink any unboiled water.
It would also be advisable to avoid greeting by shaking hands. Also [to act] in such a way[?] that it is easier to isolate an infected person, if there already is one, from the others, his[?] relatives and acquaintances.
Special attention must be paid to the fight against flies, because they are the chief spreaders of epidemic diseases.
—o—
His parents would not consent to the match — so he shot himself.
In Wolbrom, 21-year-old Nowakowski[?] committed suicide by shooting himself.
The reason is that his parents would not let him marry the girl with whom he was deeply in love.

Great Demonstration in Sosnowiec over the Danzig Affair

Through the initiative of the Legionnaires' Union, a great demonstration took place on Wednesday evening in front of the town hall against those who want to take away Poland's rights to Danzig.
Up to 10 thousand people took part in the demonstration, among them various delegations with their banners at their head, to whom the [city] president Kaczkowski[?] made a speech, which ended with cheers in honour of the President of the State Mościcki and the General Inspector of the Army Rydz-Śmigły. The orchestra played the Polish anthem.
There also spoke the chairman of the Legionnaires' Union Mr Taba, Dr Malicki, and appropriate resolutions were adopted.
—o—
Conference of Zagłębie Artisans.
Next Sunday, the 26th of this month, at 4 in the afternoon, a conference of all the Zagłębie artisans' associations will take place in Będzin, in the premises of the Central Artisans' Union (Kołłątaja 45), at which a position will be adopted on the project to reform the purchase of patents [trade licences] for artisans' workshops for the year 1937, on the possibility of employing[?] a larger number of workers on an already purchased patent, the World Jewish Congress, kehilla elections, loans for artisans, and many more topical questions.
—o—
Wife Tried to Murder Her Husband in His Sleep.
An unusual incident took place this week in the flat of a certain Czubała[?] in Sosnowiec on Słowacka[?] Street.
When Czubała was sunk in a deep sleep, his „woman of valour“ struck him with an axe over the head.
At Czubała's cries for help the neighbours came running, broke open the door and disarmed the would-be murderess.
In a serious condition Czubała was taken to hospital.
—o—
One Rescued, the Other Drowned.
In the Brynica, 2 boys who were bathing began to drown. By chance Mr Niskind was passing by, and he succeeded in rescuing one of them. The second was already taken out dead.
—o—
12-Year-Old Boy Murders His Own Father.
In the flat of the Grajczak family on Mariacka Street in Sosnowiec a shocking[?] tragedy took place.
Grajczak came home at dawn in a drunken state, began to make rows and also started beating his wife.
The 12-year-old Grajczak could not bear the injustice and, in order to protect his mother, grabbed a kitchen knife and stabbed his father in the chest.
A few hours later Grajczak died.
—o—
The „Upper Silesian Wanderer“ Dissolved.
The police directorate in Katowice has dissolved the German youth organisation called „Der Oberschlesische Wanderer“.
—o—
Tragic Death of a Young Child.
Mrs Marja Klehnia[?] of Tarnowskie Góry[?] went out for a walk with her two-year-old only son. While walking on the stairs the child slipped and fell. The child was killed on the spot.
—o—
Festive Distribution of the Prizes for the Best Sportsmen of „Hakoach“.
On Saturday night the distribution of the prizes for the sportsmen who distinguished themselves at the competition in Bielsko took place in the premises of „Hakoach“ in Będzin.
In the presence of many activists[?] and guests, also from Bielsko, the chairman of „Hakoach“ Mr Michał Gutman gave a short speech on the occasion and called out each of the prize-winners individually; the assembled public received the „lucky ones“ with stormy ovations.
In conclusion Mr M. Plesner spoke, expressing thanks to Mr Bauszykowski[?] („senior“[?]) for his services to the club, and as a token of gratitude presented him with a valuable gift.
At the „material“ part [the refreshments] the public spent the time until late at night.
—o—
A Storm over Zagłębie.
On Sunday evening a violent thunderstorm with thunder and lightning passed over Zagłębie. The low-lying streets were flooded. During the storm the electric light went out several times.

Next Week a Session of the Będzin Kehilla Council Is to Take Place.
Yesterday the chairman of the Będzin kehilla council Mr Langner wanted to call a session of the council.
Because for that date the kehilla president had called a session of the board, the council session will probably take place next Wednesday.

What a Madman Can Do.
In the village of Burki beyond Sławków a mentally ill man threw himself with an axe upon his sister, dealt her several blows over the head, and then with the axe murdered the sister's child of one and a half years.

An Open Appeal to “Agudat Yisrael” in Dąbrowa

[Dąbrowa — yeshiva; open letter.] (Devoted to the state of the yeshiva ketana “Netzach Yisrael”.)
Three months ago, on the initiative of “Agudat Yisrael”, a yeshiva k[etana] named “Netzach Yisrael” was founded in our town for the young boys who leave the cheder and, for various reasons, have no means of going away to yeshivas.
The very distinguished scholar and fine expounder Rabbi Sh. Z. Rozenblum of Łomża was invited as instructor and head of the yeshiva. His “pension” was set at 10 złoty a week. We do not wish to comment on this “wonder”, and certainly not on the attitude and “respect” shown to the esteemed head of the yeshiva, for understandable reasons: so as not to fire bullets[?] at open gates[?]...
How astonished we were to learn — and from some of the initiators themselves — that even this bare minimum has for some time now not been paid. The town promised its support and has delivered it, whereas you are not fulfilling your obligations. (We do not yet wish to make the reasons public.)
In this connection we warn you, in the name of the entire Jewish population of our town: if within the next few days you do not settle the above-mentioned debt, which you took upon your own responsibility, we shall be compelled to publish your names and to fight you, and all the actions you undertake, without mercy.
The Culture Commission of the independent “Poalei Agudat Yisrael” in Dąbrowa.
Local Tax on Flats in New Buildings

[Taxes — local tax.] The Minister of Finance explains that the legal position regarding the exemption of tenants of flats in new buildings from the local tax is now as follows:
Tenants of flats in new buildings, or in buildings raised by additional storeys or extended, are exempt from local tax if the buildings were completed after 1 January 1919 or will be completed by the end of the year 1940.
The relief is valid for 10 years for buildings into which people began to move before 1 January 1929, and for 15 years for buildings into which people began to move only after 1 January 1929.
As for rebuilt buildings, the tenants were exempt from local tax only until 1 January 1932, so that at present they are subject to the obligation to pay local tax.
Several Thousand Złoty Found in a River. But They Were Counterfeit

[Ząbkowice — crime; counterfeiting.] As we have already written, a small factory of counterfeit 10- and 5-złoty coins was discovered at the home of a certain Sołtanik in Ząbkowice.
Last Thursday Mrs. Sołtanik, searching in the storeroom, found 4 thousand counterfeit złoty, packed in rolls of 25 pieces. When she saw this, she grabbed the “treasure” and carried it to Mr. B. Mirovnik[?], so that he would hide it. M. took the money and later threw it into the river. By chance this was noticed by the owner of the river, who with the help of firemen fished out the “find” and handed it over to the police.
In this connection Mirovnik and his son-in-law were arrested; only on Saturday were they released.

Dear Mr. Editor!
Your esteemed "Zaglembier Tsaytung" (No. 29) printed a letter from Mr. J.
