The Tolerated, Lawless Beggary.

The subject we want to touch on here is in fact an old and rather painful one. Therefore, like all old matters, it is of no interest to the Jewish reader, who wants the newspaper to serve him at all times something fresh and wriggling — otherwise somehow it does not read well, and it is banal.
Yes, the subject is banal already in that more than once we have expressed the deepest sorrow in the columns of our newspaper. It concerns the Jewish plague that has settled like leprosy on our aching shoulders. That is beggary.
Beggary! What an honoured place does it occupy today in our little Jewish world? To say that it occupies the head of the table would be too modest, too primitive, for de facto beggary is the actual ruler, the one who sets the tone over our entire society. Whatever we approach, whatever one should [?] speak about and establish [?], we at once see the outstretched hands, which put on an expression of pity and plead: "Have God in your heart, throw something in, don't let a respectable man fall, who has sunk [?] into his great misfortune."
Such an opinion about Polish Jewry can be formed [?] by anyone who watches from afar how the thread of life drags on.
Formerly we knew that there are professional beggars, for whom we are obliged to care. But this "caring" was arranged so strangely, so lawlessly, that one did not know what should be supported and in what way, and everything was mixed up in one round dance [?] until it could not be recognized, until it could not be distinguished. A man fallen on hard times, for whom it was not easy to stretch out his hand for alms, whose blood rushed to his face when carrying out such an experiment, was systematically pushed in with the professional, generations-old beggar, and in this way the contingent of professional beggars was enlarged by ourselves.
No account was taken of the seriousness of the plight of those fallen on hard times, whom one left to swim in the water where they were threatened with drowning, so that some were rescued and passed the examination of becoming professional beggars, while many lost their balance and went down into the abyss...
That is the way in which society cared for the masses in a time of trouble.
We are a people — as the world says — of merciful ones, sons of merciful ones, and yet no people in the world is as indifferent to its children as we Jews. True, we are soaked through with pity, we give alms when a hand is stretched out to us, but it goes no further, and the trouble lies in the fact that we do not consider whether we sometimes make the person unhappy when we throw the grosz into his hand? Do we not thereby make him a cripple forever — an eternal wanderer from door to door?
1. We, the people of lineage.
The groszy are given by the middle class, which has no means and no possibility for something better [?] with which people could be rescued in a time of trouble. But the question arises: what are our patrons doing, the notables in this field? Have they lifted a hand or a finger so that the whole people should not fall into poverty? Indeed one sees the whole middle class, on which the mass of the people weighs most heavily, with almost no way out [?] any more. If it goes on like this, if our rich Jews remain cold and apathetic towards the oppressed, the middle class will surely mix with poverty as in a storm, and it will be impossible to distinguish the first from the last.
Thanks to the lawlessness, beggary has reached the stage where everyone begs. Stretching out one's hand for alms is no longer a disgrace. What more do you need — there are local cheders to which one gives the name "yeshiva", and then, as if it were really something, one tells the children: go around the town collecting money. What more do you need — even private newspapers are sent into your home without your asking, and afterwards one comes to you for the donation.
Our whole sphere, both the public and the private, is entirely caught in a net of beggary, whether in this form or another. In the given case it makes no difference, as long as one begs on the widest scale. Unfortunately, the approach to and the concepts of philanthropy are wrapped in a tangle of beggary. Apparently it is too little for us that poverty and want reign everywhere, thanks to which we are struck down [?] and humiliated at every step, both inwardly and outwardly — one strives in addition that everything be marked with the stamp of beggary.
Why is this so? What has led to it? Very simply: the boundary between charity and obligation, between duty and commitment to the community, has been removed; people have stopped distinguishing between a voluntary gift and the fulfilment of a sacred duty to society.
R. Let.
On Sending Used Clothes from Abroad as a Gift to Relatives in Poland

[Poland — Emigration and relief.]

1) Every addressee must sign an undertaking that the articles will be used exclusively for himself and for his family. The articles may not be handed over to anyone else within a period of 2 years.
2) From now on used articles of artificial silk may be sent; in addition, it is now permitted to send used tablecloths, bed sheets and bedding covers, which until now it was not allowed to send.
3) Since the "CEKABE" society receives many inquiries about how long it takes for a parcel to arrive, we draw the attention of all persons to the fact that receiving a parcel must take a fairly long time. Firstly, the shipments are dispatched only once a month (especially in the winter months).
Besides that, the customs inspection in Gdynia takes a certain time, and afterwards the forwarding of the parcel by post from Gdynia to the addressee's locality.
Therefore "CEKABE" draws the attention of all persons who need winter clothing that they should already write now to their relatives in America to send the parcels with used clothing now, so that the parcel with winter clothing arrives at the beginning of winter and not, as used to happen before, only at the end of winter.

Tisha B'Av Thoughts

[Essay — Tisha B'Av.] By Avraham Shoyer [Abraham Szojer].

For two and a half thousand years we have been waiting [?] and lamenting the destruction of the Temple.
Troubles, sufferings, the torments of exile and expulsions we have lived through from Jeremiah's time until today, of every kind and variety, more bitter and sharper and more ruinous along our long road of exile — and no other "Eichahs" have we for Tisha B'Av, although we created them. We read and sing and recite the same Eichah.
New hopes we had, and new disappointments; they rose [?] and sank — and only the same day and just [?] the same scroll.
And when the dark night broke and the east [misprinted "morekh"] lit up, hopes began to crystallise and, more or less, to be fulfilled — hopes that had begun twenty-four hundred years ago, on the first day of exile, on the banks of the rivers of Babylon.
And a question, a new question comes to mind, a problem that had to be decided: must one still lament the destruction? After all, the destruction is already ceasing to be a destruction; the hopes are, after all, already about to be realised?
And the prophet of the reviving generation, the prophet Zechariah, answers: what you lamented and wept — did you do it for My sake? And when you eat and when you drink — are you not the eaters, are you not the drinkers? [cf. Zechariah 7:5–6.]
What a person does to sustain his existence is a wholly natural process of life; instinct makes him do it.
And if we fast and if we weep on Tisha B'Av generation after generation, it is a sign that mourning and weeping are very natural for us, that they are part of our existence, they are "our bone and flesh", they are our life; and as long as there is mourning and as long as there is weeping over the destruction of the Temple, it is a sign that we are healthy, viable and lastingly alive, just as a person's appetite shows that the body is healthy and normal.
* * *
The Jewish people has not created a second Scroll of Lamentations since [we] went into exile for the second time, for the last nearly two thousand years.
The same melody, the same "I am the man that hath seen affliction", the same "How doth the city sit solitary", the same "How hath [the Lord] covered with a cloud", the same "How is the gold become dim", and even the same "Remember, O Lord, what is come upon us".
We recite the same kinot [dirges], because our lamenting prophets, from Jeremiah to the very last, had nothing to add. In the new "Eichahs" lie the same causes as in the old.
A people dwelling [?] in the desert, in a waste land, in a thirsty land, where the fire burns and dries and devours all its branches, all its fruits — cannot have a "strong rod", a "spirit and steadfastness" [?] and self-control [?]; it is a lament, a weeping [?], an eternal lament...
We have no strong branches, because we are not planted but transplanted. We have no fruit, we have no sceptre of a ruling people — we have no leader and cannot have one — because a fire burns and dries up the "vine of Israel", burns and scorches the growing [?] vine in the desert.
We are a "How doth she sit solitary" people: a people in which each of us is "alone unto himself"; for himself he thinks, for himself he plans, for himself he [?] — each of us is "a world unto himself" — there is no unity.
Unity among the "sitting-solitary" cannot exist, and therefore we always arrive at "How hath He covered with a cloud". Darkening, clouding over — that is the result of "sitting solitary": clouded, sulky, glowering and discontented he goes about, always angry, always criticising: that is not how it is done, that is not what is said, that is not how one acts.
And if someone does act — they come at him with the broad Eichah, with "How is the gold become dim".
They dim the gold, they darken "the most fine gold", they look [?] for faults, they suspect the earnest, they belittle the greatest achievements, they lay stones on the road that is hard enough already. If the one who works for the people stumbles, they laugh to themselves with a venomous, petty feeling of revenge; if he falls — they go and push him further so that he cannot get up...
And the people stands bewildered, in despair he stands in the desert, transplanted in the dry land, and the fire burns in all his branches and devours all his fruits, and there is no strong rod, and there is not a single sceptre of rulers.
The people cries out: Remember, O Lord, what is come upon us!..
It is a child and has remained a child — our old lament, our great shame!
* * *
And yet we live, and yet we exist, we feel — we fast, we weep — it is a good sign for us that this eternal lament is a sign of our revival.
It is a token of our normality: a people that weeps over its destruction is not destroyed.
Our young, strong lads, trampled by [?] the wrath of the street and broken, are coming to us.
Do not lament and do not weep if you see some of them limping; do not cry out and do not tear the hair from your heads if you see some of them blind — the lame will become straight, the blind will begin to see.
For "one generation passeth away and another generation cometh" — as the generation that has gone, such a one must come; it is the period of transition. As one went away, so one comes.
The main thing is the return.
And when one comes — the bent backs straighten, the half-short legs will straighten out, will stretch. The dark ideas will become bright, the short-sighted will become far-sighted, the squint-eyed will become straight-eyed, the blind will become seeing, the deaf — hearing.
Do not lament and do not weep over our trampled and broken children.
Rejoice in every invalid of ours, rejoice in every cripple of ours — our land is a land of the resurrection of the dead: all the weak-chested will become strong-chested, all the sick will become healthy, all the atrophied will come back to life.
It is the time of the resurrection of the dead. The dead are rising. The dead rise in the same form in which they died. Exile crippled them, made them invalids — invalids have risen; but they will become healthy, because the air of the Land of Israel will make them healthy.
One does not become straight in one minute after having been crooked for a long time; one does not suddenly become seeing [?] after having been blind for years and years. Not "in an instant" did we become an exile people, and not all at once, suddenly, will we become an out-of-exile people; little by little our crippled children will become healthy, little by little our blinded children will come to see — if only they come!
Rejoice in every cripple, exult over every invalid — they will become healthy!
———
Tisha B'Av is the symbol of our existence. As long as we fast on Tisha B'Av and weep and mourn, it is a sign that we will rejoice on that day.
On Tisha B'Av the eternal light that the priests used to kindle was extinguished; but on Tisha B'Av the eternal light that the people kindled was lit — the Messiah, the hope of the people. The constant shining fire that went before us in the long, dark exile and gave light — it is that same light which our broken and trampled lads kindle on the mountains of Zion!

From Dreyfus to Blum

[History — France; the Dreyfus Affair.]
Dr. M. Immerglück
(On the 30th anniversary of the rehabilitation of Captain Dreyfus)
A historical survey.
It was in the last decade of the last century. The Third Republic was still in its puberty, in that stage of development in which the body stands in constant contradiction to the soul, and a hard struggle goes on until it reaches a measure of consolidation.
The French Revolution had not merely opened the gates of the Bastille, but had also flung wide open the gates of the ghetto. The famous Declaration of the Rights of Man also contained, ipso facto, the equality of all citizens. All people, the Declaration said, without distinction of race or religious affiliation, are born equal and must also be citizens with equal rights; and as such the Jews too indeed had the possibility of developing their abilities without restriction in all fields of political, social and economic life.
In the economic field, in the first years of the Third Republic, "Saint-Simonism" predominated at the time. After the great landowners had been dispossessed following the Revolution, the centre of gravity in political-social life shifted to the middle bourgeoisie, i.e. mobile capital took over the initiative. Various companies arose with the aim of exploiting all kinds of industries and other enterprises. At the same time 2 works by the famous economist Saint-Simon appeared, in which he claimed[?] all political power for industry, arguing that industry is the main nerve, the pulse of social life. In Saint-Simon's camp there were, naturally, also the Jews, whose interests he represented in any case; and in the opposition against it, the discontented fanatical Catholics and plain antisemites — they too tried to found, [kesem — unclear word], for the sake of competition, companies, but unfortunately they suffered a defeat.
So it was also with the then famous crash of the "Union Générale". Thus in the hostile camp the thirst for revenge against the "Jewish" Saint-Simon trust kept growing, and they impatiently awaited a favourable moment to take vengeance; and if one wants to find, one finds: suitable accomplices they found in the camp of a part[?] [derveler — unclear word] of those discontented militarists who could by no means digest the defeat of 1871 and sought a scapegoat at any price — and so the Dreyfus Affair arose.
For some time various secrets about the artillery and the railway mobilisation had been sold to the German military attaché von Schwartzkoppen. At the instigation of the antisemitic newspaper "La Libre Parole", Captain Dreyfus was arrested and brought before a court-martial, which, on the basis of the testimony of Major Esterhazy and Captain Henry, sentenced him to degradation and lifelong deportation to Devil's Island. The reaction had triumphed, and with the triumph in its hand it went on to play out its game.
Fortunately, however, there still lived in France grandchildren of the great Revolution who were immune to the antisemitic poison: Scheurer-Kestner, Zola, Senior Lieutenant Picquart, Clemenceau, Labori, Briand and others took up the fight for truth and justice. Zola then wrote, addressed to the President of the Republic, his famous "J'accuse", in which he drew his attention to the judicial murder and demanded a revision of the trial. Soon afterwards the country was divided into two camps: Dreyfusards and anti-Dreyfusards. Meanwhile the defence succeeded in proving the untenability[?] of the testimony of Captain Henry, who was also arrested and later hanged himself in his prison cell.
It also had to come to a cassation, which annulled the lifelong deportation and sentenced Dreyfus to 10 years' imprisonment; and although the President of the Republic soon pardoned Dreyfus, the Dreyfusards did not desist from their tireless pursuit of justice. In the month of July 1905 (Clemenceau was then Minister of the Interior) the revision of the trial took place for the second time, which proved Dreyfus's innocence. Dreyfus was rehabilitated, promoted to major and decorated with the order of "Knight of the Legion of Honour". 25 years later one could read in the memoirs of von Schwartzkoppen that Esterhazy had been a German spy and Captain Henry his accomplice.
Justice finally triumphed in France, and after the black [mahshe — unclear word] camarilla had suffered such a defeat, France's political and economic rise knew no bounds.
In a short time France won the sympathy of almost the whole world, which also helped her to emerge victorious from the World War. The French people, the noble sons of the great Revolution, did not let themselves be caught by the liquorice-sweet talk and promises of the antisemitic camarilla, but fought courageously and heroically for justice. The testamentary executors empowered to put the Declaration of the Rights of Man into practice did not waver the whole time, despite all disturbances on the part of irresponsible muddlers of minds. So it is indeed no wonder that there it could come to a front of genuine democracy and pacifist spirit, at whose head stand 2 Jews: Victor Basch and Léon Blum.
But will the young child, with its sentimental-romantic world-view, be able to fend off the strong attack of the united international black camarilla?
People Have Been Playing Chess for 1000 Years

[Article — chess; Vienna.] In Semmering, not far from Vienna, twelve women, the best women chess players of the whole world, are now gathering in order to win the women's championship in chess. Until now the champion has been the Russian woman Menchik, who is not coming this time because she already feels too old for it. She writes that she regards the Polish woman Gerlecka as the greatest woman chess player, who almost "checkmated" her the last time in Moscow. Besides Gerlecka, four more very great women chess players will be represented, who now hope to receive the champion's title, namely: the second Polish woman, Hermanowa, the Englishwoman Michell, the Austrian Graf and the Swede Beskow. It looks as if a wild war will be waged, for hundreds of guests from all over the world have registered who want to watch the battle of twelve female heroes on the chessboard.

It is worth mentioning that, as the researchers record, it is now a thousand years since people began playing chess in Europe. At the court of the Austrian Babenberg emperor, in the year 936, someone who had returned from the distant lands brought some kind of game with sixty squares, on which whole armies marched.

That was the game of chess, which soon took hold not only of the imperial court with all its counsellors, but also of all the higher Austrian officials. The whole work of the Austrian government almost came to a standstill; almost nothing at all was done anywhere, people only played chess.

Soon the game spread to all the royal courts, and in the fourteenth century, when the first university was founded in Vienna, professors and men of learning travelled around the world and spread chess-playing.

Even among the priests in the monasteries, people played nothing but chess day and night.

In the year 1760 a Hungarian baron by the name of Wolfgang von Kempelen brought to the Leipzig fair a kind of apparatus with little buttons and little sticks, with which one could play chess. This "machine-man", as it was called, won all its chess games and afterwards toured all of Europe. The greatest chess players lost their games against the automaton. Empress Catherine, too, played against the apparatus and lost a lot. But in Russia he was persecuted, because people said he was a black magician and a swindler. Some said that inside the apparatus sat a small person, a skilled [?] chess player, who constantly helped [?] in the playing.

Several years later the baron died in poverty. It was said at the time that he had been murdered because he was a black magician...

Napoleon, too, was a great chess player. When he took Vienna, he immediately sat down to play chess with the great chess master of the day, Allgaier, who was then living in Vienna. Napoleon lost that game of chess; nevertheless Allgaier received a great fortune from him.

Today Vienna is also famous for its chess clubs. There are more than 20 thousand chess players in Vienna, united in about 50 clubs and associations. The president of the Austrian federation of chess players is Baron Rothschild.

In the whole world there are today more than 3 million chess players, organized in thousands of associations.

Z. Haber, Vienna.
On the Olkusz Line.

By Ben-Amotz.

Everybody's going...
"And yet the earth does turn" — Copernicus cried out in the last minute of his life, and we, his "followers," confirm it with full certainty: it is indeed a wheel that turns in the world; the earth spins like a carousel, and the "travellers" move up and down. The proof?
— The Beskids: the Beskids were always the preserve of the "morigim" [?]; not just anybody allowed himself to travel to the Beskids.
— "I go to the Beskids" [in Polish] — a modern woman used to boast, "and the riffraff goes" [in Polish] — and the riffraff goes to Olkusz, with difficulty [?], and all the more so — to Krshnitse [?]... What did the Holy One, blessed be He, do? What does the Master of the Universe do? He puts thoughts into the hearts of the Zagłębie dacha-ladies that this year they should take a fancy to... Olkusz.
And "when the rebbe travels, all the little Hasidim travel along" — so indeed the Olkusz line has become thoroughly Jewish: "Germans" [assimilated Jews] are travelling, half- and full-fledged intelligentsia, Hasidim, kest-sons-in-law and candidates for bridegrooms; in short, the line has "popularity" [Polish] — everybody's going.

The four winds...
Olkusz is divided into 4 sides, corresponding to the four winds of the world. Simply to say "I'm at a dacha in Olkusz" — is to say nothing. The summer-resort area around Olkusz has certain landmarks. "Czarna Góra" [?] first and second; the difference between the "first" and the "second" is, to this day [printed "er hayom"], to this very day not yet established by the scientific world. But in the opinion of outside travellers the difference between the "first" and the "second" is as follows: the "better" society, for example (of course, mainly Sosnowiec people come into consideration here..), lives in the villas opposite the railway station. On the first "Czarna Góra" live "coloured" Jews, i.e. half Agudah and half Mizrachi people, whereas on the "second" — there, in the "capital" of Jewishness, live rabbis, "fine" Jews, haemorrhoid sufferers [misprinted], coughers and the like.
There is also a special corner, up toward the "east," the one at "Mazaniec" [?], where a "mixed" population lives: year-round Jews and "free" Jews, that is, Jews who, God forbid, would not eat bareheaded, but secretly smoke a cigarette or snatch a little dance to the sounds of the gramophone — and why not? What's wrong with it... After all, one is on "holiday" [Polish].

The forests.
The cream of Olkusz is — the forests. Without them Olkusz would look like a Jewish cantor without a beard... But just as forests share the same fate as people — as the verse says, "For man is a tree of the field," man is likened to a tree — so the forests really do share the fate of people. For example, there are clever, educated people who perish for lack of bread and livelihood, poor things, may it not befall us; while on the other hand there are (unfortunately the majority...) idiots, illiterates who own huge estates, and they pronounce opinions on questions of the highest importance. But forgive me, dear readers, for climbing onto a "philosophical line"; yes, where were we? At the forests: there are "free" forests and "disciplined" forests.
The "free" ones belong to private persons and the "disciplined" ones to the state. When you take the first step into a "free" forest, it seems to you at first that there is a paper factory on the site. A million heaps of dirty papers and scraps of newspaper, exactly like at the cemetery on Zawale [?] Street in Będzin; but when you go on a bit further you no longer ask questions: "it can't be otherwise" — what do you want, that where Jewish holidaymakers sit it should be clean?..
The situation is different in the state forests: there is a warden who looks after order, and moreover sees to it that none of the holidaymakers, God forbid, enjoys the forest without a "spa tax."
The sun bakes and we trudge [?] through the sandy soil that lies spread over the road leading to the second "Czarna Góra." The forests are, no evil eye, "populated" with our brethren the children of Israel; people sit in whole camps, "wagon" [?]-style, children in the hundreds (may they multiply). Hammocks, push-chairs, women in dressing-gowns and the men in their tallit-katans (the modern men go about half naked). At first we don't know where the "first" ends and where the "second Czarna Góra" begins, but when on a "veranda" a 5-pood Jewish woman appears, her face painted red, and calls out [?]:
— Moshe, what d'you want? D'you want that you should eat the lunch, or the flies?.. — then we know for certain that we are on the "second"...
On the way we meet a group of modern young ladies, "modestly dressed," who urge us to raise an alarm in the press against the Olkusz magistrate and the town council [Rada Miejska] in particular, which is so barbaric and does not provide any pool, beach, etc. "One can simply — complains a girl — 'dry up' [?] in this Olkusz; there is — she says — some little stream, but the stream is so 'shallow' [Polish] that for the water to go over your ears, whoever 'bathes' [Polish] has to stand on his head..."

The guest-houses.
A chapter of their own are the guest-houses, of which there is a sufficient [?] number. And since we have sentimental feelings for the Land of Israel, we paid our first visit to "Tel Aviv." Already a kilometre before the guest-house we "sensed" that we were approaching "Tel Aviv"; and when we stepped onto the "spot," our "enthusiasm" grew from minute to minute; our eyes could not get enough of the great colourfulness and aesthetics that had sprouted on every plate, and of the "international" population one meets in "Tel Aviv."
There are also many original features there: the "eating-house" [jadłodajnia], the "price list" for the dishes, and the difference whether one eats at the common table or "separately." The prices of the dishes, in proportion to the fine building, are not expensive; it is also to be welcomed that in "Tel Aviv" all dishes have equal rights — it is not lineage that plays the role but the calories, and thanks to that the "mizeria" [cucumber salad] appears on the price list together with the "cutlets"...
The real fair takes place when the crowd comes for lunch. Men sit down separately and women separately. In the Hasidic room the table is "laid" for our own kind, and where the radio "plays," the "better society" eats. Each dining room has its own "waiter," recognisable by his clothing: the "better people" are served by a waiter in a white coat, and the Hasidim — by a waiter in just a shirt. When the crowd, and the radio too, fall into ecstasy, one gets the impression of being at the new port in Tel Aviv.
About the other guest-houses — another time.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Devarim)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Devarim
—o—
a) "These are the words which Moses spoke unto all the children of Israel" (1:1)
The expounders of allusions say that "ELeH" (these) is by gematria: A-vak L-ashon H-ara (a trace of evil speech) — that is, it was chiefly for this that Moses rebuked the Jews: for evil speech; and that is why it says "which Moses spoke unto all Israel", because for this sin, the sin of evil speech, he had to rebuke all the Jews. "Most of them [sin] in robbery, a minority in sexual transgressions, and all in evil speech." It is a sin in which there is, unfortunately, no person who does not stumble..
Ḥeirut Shimshon.
—o—
b) "And, behold, ye are this day as the stars of heaven" (ibid., 10)
A Masoretic note: "And behold ye are this day as the stars of heaven", "And behold ye walk after the stubbornness of his heart".
Because those who are great "as the stars of heaven", those who look only up into the sky, those who walk after the stubbornness of their heart — they do not care about anybody...
Melo ha-Omer.
—o—
c) "Wise men and understanding" (ibid., 13)
"Would it enter your mind [that they were] women? What does 'men' teach us? — Righteous men." Rashi.
On this R' Eizel Ḥarif said jokingly:
Would it enter your mind women? Why should such [?] a supposition have arisen at all? Is it possible to think of women? Are there then wise and understanding women?.. So there is no need to say "wise men", for if they are wise — I shall know by myself that they are not women..
•
The author of the "Ktav Sofer" was once a guest of a friend of his, a well-known gaon, and saw how the latter consulted his wife on all community matters. So he said to him: Now I understand why it is stressed [?] precisely regarding leadership that it be only men — because the verse means that not only may women not be leaders, but they may not be leaders indirectly either: they may not run the male leaders...
—o—
c) [sic; should be d)] "And I made them heads over you" (ibid., 15)
"Judges must possess seven qualities: wise, and understanding, and known.. and if [men with] seven are not found, one brings [men] with three [?]; and if not — one brings [men] with one, as it is written: A woman of valour who can find." Midrash Rabbah, chapter 1, §62 [?].
The question arises: what proof does the Midrash bring from "a woman of valour"?
But by this the Midrash means to show that "men of valour" (anshei ḥayil) does not mean, as is commonly understood, men of strength or of money, since about "a woman of valour" the verse explains right away: "She doeth him good and not evil" — and that is also the meaning of "men of valour": people who will do good, who will help in spirit.
Dvash ve-Ḥalav.
•
The Midrash says: and if not — if no candidates have been found possessing the other qualities, "one brings with one": one should elect a new one [?] who possesses at least one quality — the quality of "a man of valour".
Why does the Midrash seize precisely on this quality?
Because those who are merely wise, merely understanding — it may happen that they will never become heads; whereas mere men of valour — which according to Rashi means rich men — with such [?] it cannot possibly happen that they will not become leaders...
Imrei Ḥen.
—o—
d) "For the Lord thy God hath blessed thee in all the work of thy hand" (2:7)
"In all the work of thy hand": God blesses only when a person acts. A dice player, one who lives from card-playing, is disqualified as a witness, because he is not engaged in "the settlement of the world".
(Whereas those who devote themselves to Torah — of them it is said "and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper": "whatsoever he doeth" — everything he has to do, "shall prosper" — he attains it through success.)
Panim Yafot.
—o—
e) "And it came to pass in the fortieth year" (1:3)
Rashi says on this that one should rebuke only near death, and after one has already done the other person some favour.
And this is what the Masorah means: "The number of thy days I will fulfil", "and their treasures I will fill", "and my heart I will fill with arguments".
After "the number of thy days I will fulfil" — when one is already at one's last days, near death, and no longer has any ulterior motives; and after "their treasures I will fill" — when one has already done the other person good — only then may one allow oneself "and my heart I will fill with arguments": to reprove the other, to rebuke him.
Binyan Ariel.
Little Feuilleton. The boom in the "eating trade"..

[Satirical feuilleton — resort boarding houses; elections to the World Jewish Congress and the kehilla.] The boom in the "eating trade"..
These last days one notices that the boarding houses (pensionaty) are full; in many boarding houses there is no room.. In the "eating trade" there is a strong boom.
So one asks a question: where does this come from? What's the big deal? What does one need boarding houses for nowadays? Getting fat is forbidden, one must keep one's figure, doctors order eating as little as possible — so what does one need the boarding houses for? Not eating one can do at home too!.. What is the reason for the sudden boom in the "eating trade"?
Chatting about it, one Jew spoke up:
— Gentlemen, I do know where it comes from.
— Well, by all means! Let's hear it!
— Listen then: we are now on the eve of elections; we Jews are going to have elections twice — elections to the World Jewish Congress and elections to the kehilla.
— So what has one got to do with the other [lit. how does a slap come to a "good Shabbos"]? What connection do elections have with boarding houses?
— Of course there is a connection, and a very strong one at that. Just imagine, gentlemen: how many candidates do we have for a World Congress? And which Jew does not want to become a dozór [kehilla board member] in the kehilla? Take all the candidates together with the speakers, the "kettle-bangers" [windbags], the "spodik-twirlers" [?] and plain schlemiels — they are all going off on holiday now, so that they will have the strength to "win over the masses".
That is why the boarding houses are so packed now.
From the World of Film

[Cinema — film news.] When everything goes under.
When the whole edifice collapses, when everything goes under, then one misfortune follows another. The wheel of fate spins lightning-fast and the end comes. That is the leitmotif of the film "Forgotten Faces", in which everyone slips and falls.
A man shoots his wife's lover dead, gives his only little daughter away into strangers' hands and himself gives himself up to the police; he sits in prison, is later released for a certain time, and meets his former wife, who is now lonely and forsaken. The mother wants to blackmail her daughter, the father does not allow it, and then comes the catastrophe: the woman shoots her husband dead and herself jumps out of the window, dying on the spot. In this way the path is cleared for the daughter, who does not know who her parents are — to her they are unknown, forgotten faces. Playing in this film: Herbert Marshall, Jane [?] Rhodes and Gertrude Michael.
—o—
Red Roses.
That is what the new film with the famous Hollywood actress Marlene Dietrich will be called. It is possible that her partner in this film will be Gary Cooper, who lately is one (if not the only one) of the most popular male stars in Hollywood.
The Sick Man

[Fiction — sketch.] (A Sketch)

— Now, don't talk, it will harm you! There, like that... lie quietly, don't move, and now a few more little pieces of ice... Now, do it for my sake, I won't torment you any more... There, there, now you'll fall asleep.

For the tenth day now she has been sitting at her husband's bedside. With the coming of the windy days, when winter clings with its wild tricks to its power, Mordechai grew worse; he began to cough hollowly and to spit a kind of "vartn" [?] like "opgeveyblevetn leykhekh" [?].

For ten days now he has been lying in bed, and the cough tears his lungs apart, which he spits out into the spittoon.

She sits by him, wipes the sweat from his high, pale forehead, smooths his black, wet hair, and quietly "snatches" a cry [?].

She sits hunched and broken, dozes and wakes with fear in her eyes at every sound: lest Mordechai again sit bent over the spittoon and spit out pieces of his young life.

* * *

Sitting like this, half asleep, the last two years of her life float up before her like a tale of long ago.

She had met him then at a health resort. Both were standing in the queue for the water. He, slender, elegant and smiling, says:
— There are many spa guests here today; one waits up to 15 minutes. He says it half in earnest, and meanwhile shows his big white teeth.
She does not mind that he has chosen such a pretext to make her acquaintance, and answers to the point:
— Really a lot. I have spa card number 44801.
— But few beautiful women — he moves on to the main thing.
— Oh, you are insulting me!
— No, no, God forbid! I consider you the most interesting and the most beautiful.
— One mustn't believe it!
— Słowo honoru! [Polish: word of honour!]
— But for the how-manyth time have you already repeated the same thing today? Tell the truth!
— Heaven forbid, I am saying it for the first time and only to you. I would not have said it to anyone else, because on principle I tell no lies. Well, what do you say now?

And so it began. They isolated themselves from the company, strolled, went on excursions, frolicked, and always just the two of them. Every afternoon they went off from the "dep-tak" [deptak, the promenade] and for hours [?] crawled over shady paths, wandered along distant roads, and they felt royally good. They did not care that below [?] them the orchestra was playing and thousands of people were making noise and laughing — laughing even when they had no wish to...

* * *

All this lasted only one year.
Soon after the wedding the lung disease began to torment him: he caught a chill on an excursion, and pieces of his solidly built body began to vanish before her eyes. His slenderness turned into a skeleton, his face became drawn, pale, his hands translucent, blue.
She sensed her catastrophe, knew how dangerous his illness was for her, and nevertheless did not keep him away from herself.
But the disease galloped ahead. His lungs began to tear like a rotted thread, and in their life together a change took place.
He himself avoided physical closeness with her, but on the other hand he clung to her, to her 26 years, which beckoned towards life.
He would call her to the bed, take her hand in his sweaty, translucent hand, look at her as if wishing to get at the concealed truth, and always say the same thing with a sickly bitter smile:
— As you see, you won't have to suffer long. It's going at a fast tempo...
— Now, don't talk nonsense — she broke in with girlish nimbleness and motherly warmth — we'll yet go sledging down the mountains together.
— You think one can live without lungs as without an appendix [lit. "blind gut"]. You will surely climb the mountains, but someone else will smile at you.
— He's got carried away talking again [?]: we will jump over the mountains together, and you'll turn out a liar [?]...
— You see — he points at the spittoon — blood is a symbol of birth and death, of rising and setting. My redness, which I spit out every day, is a sign of sunset, of decline, which I am approaching with quick steps.
— Maybe you'll stop talking nonsense — Dina scolds every time, good-naturedly, and does not let him talk any more.
She shouts at him, comforts him, and does not herself believe her own words.
He feels it, and sometimes looks at her as if he suspected her of already wanting all this to end herself...

* * *

The same day, towards evening. The rain had stopped pouring; on the window panes single drops like unshed [?] tears; in the west a piece of red sky had broken through a crack; a clamour [?] from a flock of birds burst into the room; one little bird settled on the window with a beakful of "food", took a "snatch", a look into the room, and fled to its little ones. A gang of children were singing a little song that their grandmothers had played with, and shouting at the tops of their voices.
Dina went over to the window and, as if suddenly, saw that the acacia tree was covered with blossom. Spring — and she knows nothing of it! Two little birds chased each other from one branch to the other, until the "he" won. A rooster ran eagerly [?] after a hen and, seizing her by the head, coupled with her. The "lebeler man" [?] saw it, and before he had thought it over, the hen had shaken herself off to the side [?] and, as if nothing had happened, rummaged in the sand.
Dina watched all this as if with a conscious, sudden attentiveness. She combed her hair, tossed back her blond hair and felt a kind of gnawing in her heart. She pressed her face to the pane and looked outside with longing eyes, like a harem wife through the bars. She noticed another pair of birds appear on the acacia tree, chase each other teasingly and vanish into a hole in the attic.
She stood at the window and her 26 years seemed to wake up and demand something. The gnawing began to grow.
But at that moment she hastily tears her face away from the pane — a hollow sound rouses her. Mordechai, sitting up, is bending over the spittoon so as not to stain the bedclothes with the red-pink fluid streaming from his mouth. Drops of sweat run down his face and his pale lips tremble like a child's when it is about to cry.
Dina quickly runs over to him, lays his head down low, nervously [?] cracks a piece of ice and puts [?] it into his mouth:
— Mordechai, don't force yourself to cough! Have pity on my young years, take a piece of ice.
— Now, stop — she whispered — perhaps it will be enough now. And with hands trembling with pity, and at the same time, for the first time, with anger [?] at her broken life, she wiped the sweat from his pale, high forehead and felt her eyes growing moist.
— What, you're crying? — Mordechai whispered tremblingly — you're crying too now? And who will convince me that my end is still far off, if you no longer believe it either?
— I'm not crying. My eyes are watering from lack of sleep. Lie quietly, everything will be fine. Hush, not a word!
The children were shouting:
"Sycamore, sycamore, sycamore people,
What are you doing here?
We are building bridges
For the Lord Starost" — — —
[Polish children's song, printed in Yiddish transliteration.]
— — — — — — — —
P. Blumenkranz, Częstochowa.
Der Kokh-Lefl [The Cooking Spoon] — Monologue of a Summer-Resort Butcher.

[Humour and satire — "Der Kokh-Lefl"; poem.]
Humour and Satire
Compiled by Amutsli.
—o—
Monologue
of a Dacha Butcher.
As soon as the dacha season comes,
I straightaway hire me a mare,
pack up wife and children, a block
with an axe,
and set out for the dacha.
Since I'm a butcher known to everyone.
"A vektsr[?]" p'n doypra[?] tradu[?] atke [line not deciphered],
and I take my axe in hand —
the women besiege the meat stall.
"Reb Moshe, give me this! Reb Moshe, give me
that one!"
And I just chop and porge,
with bones, without bones, this way and that,
and... can't satisfy the women.
One shouts[?]: I want to roast, the second —
to fry,
a third — to chop a meatloaf.
The fourth wants to make a little broth,
so she needs "something fat and something thick".
And so I must toil, sweating
and panting,
and on top of that swallowed up by the women...
I spit out my liver, my gall
bursts,
as if they were eating my lungs...
And yet among the "beasts", be they
the very worst,
one also finds a better piece —
oh, with the women, the various ones,
there are also better... gluttons.
Yes, one, a dark one with burning
eyes,
that tease and call to life —
wants precisely a cut of the better sort,
well, can one refuse such a one?
The second, a blonde, with heavenly
glances,
keeps swaying and humming,
that I should give her a portion without
bones,
if not, she won't come any more!
And so a third. A fourth, a fifth,
each has different demands!
I chop and I cut and I
porge
and am held captive by the women..
And yet it would be a lovely world,
if only the business succeeded..
so that I would not be left with the dry
spit,
and the women — with the fatty roast.
The summer runs away, and the luck
waits to melt away[?]...
Oh, what above heavens and worlds!
I have empty pockets, an empty stomach,
and my wife keeps scolding me
— "A stroke, a cholera, you villain!" —
she gives me a glare with her peepers...
— "Serves you right, Moshe the thief, you're left
in the end
by the dry, bare block!"
Hastily Snatched Dacha Letters.

[Humour and satire — "Der Kokh-Lefl"; letter.]
Best friend, don't hold it against me that I'm making it short. I'm waiting for the train and writing in a hurry at the station. I'm already, with luck, at the dacha, and in general I'm constantly travelling: at half past 7 in the morning I go into town, at 1 in the afternoon I go out of town, at half past 2 I go into town, at 10 in the evening I go out of town again, and so on. I rush to the train, then[?] I rush from the train, and when I get home I'm worn out as after the longest journey, and I fall asleep like a dead fly on a window, and I don't even have time to "eat" a little fresh air. Still, it's a miracle that I have so much travelling about, and when it occasionally gets roomier in the carriages (which almost never happens) and I can snuggle up to a window, I also catch a bit of sky with a little smoke. Meanwhile, with luck, I've already lost the first 3 kilos in the first week, and if you have time and are good at sums, would you be so kind as to work out what may be left of me in roughly two months, and for heaven's sake send me the reckoning right away. But when you [see] how I already jump up onto the steps of the carriage like a real chief conductor, you'd say yourself that I've become a thoroughly practised traveller. I must cut it short, the train is already moving.
From me, Khatskl Datshnik.

In the Tangle of Life (3)

[Serialized novel — Kraków, Vienna; installment 3.]
(A novel with dramatic events in Kraków, Zawiercie and New York)

His studies were now no longer merely a matter of knowing languages. They had opened his eyes altogether, and he became quite a different person. He now read a great deal in Hebrew as well, and became a maskil, and on top of that an ardent Zionist.

His father-in-law — his wife's father — at first looked askance [?] at the whole business, but he did not want [?] to interfere between the couple and let them live in their own way, until it came to a serious clash.

Dudl was a man who could not bear lies. When he had opened his eyes and seen the world, the first thing he did was to start criticizing the Hasidim and the rebbes, whom he called "false prophets". Well, this was promptly carried to the Hasidic shtibl, and a fight against him began. People started calling him names like "apikoyres" [heretic] and "meshumed" [apostate], and when he once tried to convince others that Zionism was a kosher thing, the fanatical Hasidim of those days became thoroughly incensed against him. They, the pious fanatics, decided not to keep silent, and they raised a furious [?] storm against him.

His father-in-law, Reb Yona Piątkowski, himself a great fanatic, began to admonish him. A quarrel broke out. The father-in-law travelled to his rebbe to ask his advice, and when he came back he began to shout:

"A divorce! A divorce! Nothing but a divorce! Such an apostate I may not keep under my roof! The rebbe has ordered it so!"

Dudl and Nechama wept. Her mother wept along with them. She tried to "shout down" the divorce, for the sake of the grandchild, who was by then already over two years old. It did not help either that Nechama begged her father, nor that Nechama's two other sisters did not want to allow a divorce. Reb Yona was obstinate. The rebbe had said so, and the rebbe was for him above everything in the world, more important than wife and children. He did not rest until he had had Nechama and Dudl divorced, gave him his things and simply drove him out of the house.

Nechama became hysterical after the divorce; even the rabbi and the scribe wept along.

And Dudl went off home, to Kraków.

In Kraków Dudl spent only a short time. His father gave him a cold reception. Even at Reb Yosef the dayan's, his former teacher, he no longer found the warmth of old. Malkele, the dayan's daughter, he learned, had already married and was living in the town of Drohobycz. The world there felt too narrow for him, and he decided to go away to Vienna to study.

In Vienna he soon entered the university, in the philosophy faculty. Moreover Professor Jerusalem, who was a "white Jew" [a fine Jew], received him very well. He threw himself into his studies with zest.

By the university there was a café where the students used to eat. In recent days he had begun counting his groschen, and he did not allow himself more than two rolls with a cup of coffee. Once he noticed that a woman student from his class was watching him closely to see what he was eating. He knew her; her name was Selma — a slender, blonde young Christian, a Catholic. Soon she came up to him and slipped something into his hand. He did not want to take it and protested, but she would not let him be and argued with him:

"It's no disgrace! You'll give it back later. But meanwhile you mustn't go hungry!"

Dudl took the money from her, but he was ashamed to look her in the eyes.

So several days went by. She kept watching over him at lunch and gave him [money] for [—?]. Dudl finally decided not to go into the café any more. He really did go hungry for several days. But some days later he came in to see a friend. Selma at once rushed over to him:

"Where have you been? I've been looking for you everywhere! Why are you avoiding me? I'm not giving you my money. It is part of my task to watch which of the new students are not eating and to help them. Don't be ashamed."

This gave him fresh courage, and he began to look more at Selma. He liked her energy. He now began to feel drawn to her. He talked with her a few times. She had [?] heard a good opinion of him from the professor. They began to be together. Dudl now also got a few Hebrew lessons with Jewish families. Selma began to draw even closer to Dudl, and they often used to spend time together. They fell in love.

Selma had a widowed mother and a rich brother, who spied [?] on both of them — the mother and Selma. Selma knew nothing of subtleties: if you love a person, you must do everything in the world for him. Dudl was now as if drunk. This was for him the first truly strong love of a grown man.

But soon Dudl's sky clouded over. Selma confided to him one day that she was pregnant. Dovid trembled.

"What are you going to do?" he asked her.

"Nothing."

"What do you mean? I can't marry you!"

"Who says not?"

"But I am a Jew."

"And I am a Catholic. Well, so what, one becomes a Catholic too, and we'll both get married."

Dudl shuddered at these words.

"Convert?"

"So what?" she asked.

Several months passed in great agitation between him and Selma. Suddenly Selma vanished. Weeks and weeks went by and he did not see her. He reasoned that since she was in the late months, she was ashamed to come to the university. But one day a man came to him, at the university, and introduced himself as Selma's brother. Selma had given birth to a child, a boy, and she wanted to see him, Dudl, the father of her child.

He Sold One Sister Honey 'from Rajcza' and Another 'from Zakopane'. A Trick by a Wily Swindler

Into the flat of the S. family on Kołłątaja[?] Street came a young Christian, who told Mrs. S. that he had been recommended by her mother, who is staying in Rajcza, so that she should buy honey from him, which was of the best quality. Mrs. S., believing the honey seller in what he said[?], especially as he described exactly how well her mother was enjoying herself in Rajcza etc., bought a litre of honey from him and did not even haggle over the price.
The next day the man came to Mrs. Z., a sister of Mrs. S., and passed on to her greetings from her husband in Zakopane, who had recommended him to her so that she should buy honey from him.
Mrs. Z., who happened to be at her sister's, the one who had bought the honey 'from Rajcza', realised that the man was a swindler and held him.
The honey seller, seeing that he had fallen into the 'trap', gave Mrs. Z. his passport, promising her that he would give back the money for the honey he had taken from her sister.
But when he had left the woman, he called a policeman, with whose help he took the passport back from Mrs. Z.
Now that is what you call a wily swindler.

10,000 people took part in the funeral of the bestially murdered Jewish merchant.

The funeral of the bestially murdered Jewish merchant Baruch Mangarten, about whom our paper has already reported in detail, turned into a silent, unofficial protest demonstration against those who embitter and shorten Jewish life.

Although no one had officially announced when the funeral would take place, many thousands of people nonetheless began streaming to the synagogue square at about 6 in the evening, and the number grew from minute to minute. At about 8 in the evening, when the wagon carrying the deceased arrived in Kielce escorted by 2 representatives of the Chevra Kadisha, Messrs. M. D. Ajzenberg and H. Goldberg, a crowd of nearly ten thousand people had already gathered on the synagogue square, weeping bitter tears.

Heart-rending scenes took place as the 6 little orphans, who accompanied their horribly murdered father, were seated on the wagon. Young and old lamented, and no one could control himself.

Terrible too was the convulsive weeping while Rabbi Harberg[?] eulogised the slain man in moving words, and when Cantor Gornicki recited the "El male rachamim".

As the funeral procession passed along Duża Street, an indescribable panic suddenly broke out in the great crowd because of 2 Christian youths who accosted several Jews and wanted to provoke a brawl. Thanks to the prompt, energetic intervention of the police, who arrested one hooligan, calm returned and the funeral procession continued on towards the cemetery.

The funeral was arranged at the expense of the kehilla. The tragically murdered Jewish merchant was given a grave of honour among the most respectable of the deceased.

Heart-rending scenes also took place at the cemetery during the tahara and while the 5 little boys said Kaddish.

At about half past 10 at night the funeral ended, and with broken hearts the thousands of people left the cemetery together with the unfortunate widow and 6 orphans.

A sacred duty lies upon the city of Kielce to concern itself with the tragic fate of the widow and the orphans. The 2 youngest children must without fail be taken into the orphanage, and for the widow with the older orphans one must see how to make arrangements.
Prime Minister Składkowski's inspection tour of the Kielce voivodeship.

A few days ago the Prime Minister, Gen. Składkowski, made an inspection tour through a number of towns and villages of the Kielce voivodeship, where Prime Minister Składkowski wished to acquaint himself personally with the want and poverty prevailing in the said voivodeship because of the terrible windstorms, hail and fires that recently destroyed many dozens of villages.

The Prime Minister visited several districts (powiats), among them the districts of Końskie and Opoczno, which suffered most from the terrible storm.

Prime Minister Składkowski travelled on a peasant cart from village to village in order to see the devastated areas for himself.

On Thursday the Prime Minister stayed in Kielce, from where he went out to visit the Kielce district, which also suffered much from hail and fires. In this district the hail destroyed 15 villages over an area of 3410 hectares.

The total damage suffered by the population of the Kielce voivodeship from hail and terrible fires amounts to up to 1 million zł.

After the visit Prime Minister Składkowski assigned a sizeable sum of money as urgent aid for the impoverished population, as well as a large sum for public works, at which the population of the ruined areas will be employed.

On the inspection tour the Prime Minister was accompanied by Messrs.: Vice-Minister Jaszczembski[?], the deputy head of the Presidium of the Council of Ministers Sobolewski, the Kielce voivode Dr. Dziadosz, Deputy Kozłowski and the director of the Chamber of Agriculture Eng. Ślaski[?].
Organisation of a large credit bank.

Since the well-known crashes and bankruptcies of the local banks, our city of Kielce has had no genuine public cooperative credit institution. The merchant and working circles, already oppressed enough as it is by the bitter times, suffer very much from the shortage of money. There is simply nowhere to discount a bill of exchange, even the best one, and when a merchant, small trader or artisan holds the very best bill, he has nowhere to take it. He often has to come to the street usurers, from whom he of course emerges fleeced[?]; they take enormous interest, and sooner or later the interest-payers must become poor people. Not even an interest-free loan (gemilut chesed) is to be had anywhere. And when someone does get one, it costs him dearly.

A number of respected industrialists and merchants have therefore begun to take an interest in this extremely important question, and have decided to found in Kielce a large "Credit and Discount Bank", from which all Jewish merchants, small traders etc. will benefit.

The first organising meeting took place this week. At this meeting the legal and formal side of the credit institution was discussed, and corresponding drafts were worked out.

As we are informed, the new Credit and Discount Bank, at whose head, as is known, will stand the most respected and wealthiest Jews of the town, will receive the proper moral and material support from the "Joint" and the "Foundation".

This news has aroused great satisfaction in the town.

This united bloc comprises some two thousand and several hundred eligible voters.

The united bloc has also joined in technical blocs with several other particular groupings.

The first large election rally of the united Zionist electoral bloc will take place in the next few days.

A Rain in Fine Weather.

[Kielce — State Lottery.] This Monday there prevailed — to speak in the style of the meteorological bulletins — sunny weather with slight cloudiness. Despite this, a rain fell, and quite a big one at that.
But anyone who regarded this phenomenon as unnatural would be mistaken; on the contrary, it recurs regularly every month — there is only a difference in the "rains", because this is no ordinary rain, from which people shelter under a roof or an umbrella. The rain — these are the many prizes that fall in the drawings of the State Lottery, and their number depends on the class of the lottery.
The 20th of this month was the last day of the drawing of the 2nd class of the thirty-sixth lottery. On that day there were drawn not only two main prizes of one hundred thousand zł. and the regular daily prizes, but also the big prizes that still remained in the wheel.
The latest results of the drawing are as follows:
One hundred thousand zł. were won by numbers 97,034 in Łódź and 136,803 in Poznań; the tickets were bought at the local branches of one of the Warsaw lottery agencies (kolektury). Fifteen thousand and twenty-five thousand zł. fell in Kraków on numbers 56 840 and 64,746; in Lwów number 170,678 was finally sold, on which the prize of twenty thousand zł. fell.
As we see, it was truly a "rain" of prizes, a rain that certainly spoiled nobody's mood. Whoever wants a chance of such a rain pouring over him next month should not forget to renew his ticket for the 3rd class, whose drawing begins on the 13th of August of this year.

Which Outworkers Must Be Insured with the Ubezpieczalnia.

[Kielce — labour and social insurance.] The economic organisations have lately been recording very many conflicts because industrialists are being compelled to insure with the Ubezpieczalnia (social-insurance office) the chałupnicy (home outworkers) whom they employ. In practice, outworkers are employed in two ways: 1) either the manufacturer gives the work out to an intermediary or contractor, who employs the outworkers directly, 2) or the firm employs the outworkers directly, just like the workers, with the one exception that they receive the raw material at home to process. Until a short time ago the Ubezpieczalnia imposed the obligation to insure only the outworkers of the second category, i.e. those who work directly for the firm. Lately, however, the Ubezpieczalnia carried out an inspection and issued an order that all outworkers must be registered without any exception.
This order contradicts the order of the [Trade?] Ministry. In the opinion of the circles concerned, the question should be settled by the supervisory authority as quickly as possible.

The Kehilla Board Determines,

[Będzin — kehilla.] That Mr. Landner May Not Be a Member of the Kehilla Council.
A new “victory” of the Agudah majority in Będzin.
On Wednesday the Będzin kehilla board held a meeting at which it dealt with the interpellation of board member (“dozor”) R' Eli Ber Werdiger, in which it is pointed out[?] that the chairman of the council, Mr. N. Landner, may not belong to the council.
The grounds are as follows: after the death of board member Mr. D. Rozin, the first candidate for the board was Mr. Landner, who is at the same time automatically chairman of the council. But since Mr. L. declined to serve as a board member, he has lost “both worlds”: he belongs neither to the board nor to the council.
That is how the Agudah majority understands it, and it adopted a resolution that the board determines that Mr. Landner may not be a member of the council.
The resolution is being sent to the Starostwo (district office), where the matter has to be decided; this did not, however, hold the Agudah majority back from notifying the gmina staff not to carry out the orders of Mr. Landner as chairman of the kehilla council.
Of the National faction only board member Neumark was present at the meeting.

What Is the Present Situation in the Będzin Gemilut Hesed Fund?

In connection with the circulating rumours about the situation in the Będzin interest-free loan fund, we turned to the present head of the fund, Mr. Holenderski, delegate of „CEKABE“, who gave us the following information:
My task is to carry out an audit of the activity so far, to collect the overdue, so-called „frozen“ debts, which amount to a considerable sum, and to bring about a general meeting at which a new board is to be elected, which will restore this important institution to its former level.
— Have there been abuses in the fund? — we asked.
— To that question — says Mr. Holenderski — I will be able to give a clear answer once the audit, which I am already conducting, has been completed.
To the question about the management so far, Mr. Holenderski explains that the management was not as it should have been; nevertheless the fund, although weakened, is still sufficiently viable.
— Is it true that the gmina [municipality] borrowed a certain sum from the free-loan fund?
— How large the loan once was I cannot tell you, but as of today the gmina owes the fund 150 zl.
The rehabilitation of the fund — says Mr. Holenderski — is under way; the debts are being partly repaid according to the means of the borrowers.

Which Apprentices May Sit the Examination and Which Craftsmen May Train Apprentices?

According to Article 158, point 4 of the Industrial Law, a person may be admitted to the master's examination who submits a craftsman's card and a certificate from the starostwo [district office] that he has independently run a workshop in his trade for at least 6 years.
According to the clarification of the Ministry of Trade and Industry, the 6 years also include the time during which the craftsman ran his workshop before he received the craftsman's card, if he received the craftsman's card on the basis of acquired rights.
Craftsmen who employed juveniles or workers before 16 December 1927 have the right to keep apprentices.
To prove that one employed juveniles or qualified workers at that time, one may make use of documents or witnesses.
Apprentices who trained with non-diplomaed masters may be admitted to journeyman's examinations.
All candidates for journeyman who submit an application for admission to journeyman's examinations by 30 June 1937 will be admitted to the examination, regardless of whether they did their apprenticeship with a diplomaed master or with a craftsman who holds only a craftsman's card.
