Tolerating Lawless Schnorring

2. Attempts at reform.
It goes without saying that if one had kept within bounds and known how to distinguish between a penny alms for a professional beggar and a public support for the common good, one would not have given to the former as to the latter with the same indifference, and it would not have amounted [?] to "serving it up just to discharge one's duty," because one cannot wriggle out of the great [burden?] [?]. One would not, at a given moment, have viewed everything from the beggar's standpoint; and if it has indeed reached the sad level of schnorring in the true sense of the word, then to blame are all those among our public workers who with an easy conscience looked on at the terrible lawlessness. When the population was brought to the point of handing out money right and left,
with such lawlessness, with such routine of petty alms, the population came to loathe giving to everything (we mean those who give) and [wished] only to reduce it as far as possible. And here came all sorts of "individuums" who know the art of taking money for themselves, and they sneaked [?] into this line [?]; well, it is no wonder that schnorring, philanthropy and public obligation are understood as one and the same and practised as one and the same.
At every opportunity we have spoken about and shed light on the matters of schnorring and philanthropy. We have pointed out the harmfulness of the professional schnorrers, who multiply from day to day, to our pain and shame, thanks to the bitter situation. And about philanthropy we said that it must not be made an everyday matter; above all we argued that giving to public institutions is permissible only when it benefits the town and is not calculated merely to cover administrative expenses.
The extraction of money from the population, and especially from the middle strata, has thus reached its culminating point. People are exhausted and cannot give to everything; order must therefore be introduced in this field, if one does not want to collapse altogether.
The air must be cleansed radically, starting from aleph. In Zagłębie, as in Upper Silesia and in the large towns and shtetls, professional schnorring must be abolished with no excuses. Somehow people have talked themselves into believing that this is not an easy thing to carry out, whereas that is far from true. True, the plague will not heal by itself, but a remedy is quite easy to find.
All that is needed is an institution, we say: the charitable society, which should take upon itself the responsible mission, and the question can be solved quite easily and definitively.
Of course, this by no means solves [the problem of] philanthropy [?] when it comes to transforming schnorring into a modern philanthropy that will benefit the community. But one must begin, as we said above, from the beginning and then proceed step by step, until the harmful elements are eliminated that have brought so much lawlessness and demoralization into our painful problems, which have been exchanged for petty schnorring.
A strict review must be carried out in this field and, above all, the going from door to door of all sorts of professional and "respectable" schnorrers must be abolished.
If our Jewish kehillot were not frozen, if they did not have to deal with lawsuits and with promoting [?] so-and-sos as presidents, if they did not have to worry about enlarging the staff for ever-new [?] religious needs, they would have to take this mission into their own hands. But since they have more important worries than healing [?] the wound that brings us so much humiliation, we would suggest that the function be taken over by the Jewish charitable (dobroczynność) societies.
Lawless schnorring and all kinds of "charity knockers" in their various forms and nuances must finally disappear from the Jewish street. In their place new forms of decent, modern philanthropy must arise, which will be a deliverance for the poor, the weak and the helpless and for the oppressed sufferers, to whom one must hold out a hand when they are about to fall.
This important work, which demands so many reforms and can benefit the community, we would entrust to our charitable societies, each in its own town.
R. Les.
Małachowskiego Street in Będzin

[Będzin — municipality and streets; feuilleton-style article.]
Indeed[?] yesterday a Jew, covered all over in blood, suddenly burst into the editorial office and, holding his head, kept on shouting: No, what goes on in your town is simply unbearable. What happened, what is the matter with you — we keep questioning the Jew — who did this to you and what happened? Do you still not see what happened, while the blood is running? Yes, but who did this to you, and has the assailant been caught, and who is he?
Give me a chair and let me first of all catch my breath — the Jew answers — and I will tell you that the assailant has not run away at all and there is no need to chase him, because you together with your "city fathers" are to blame for my battered[?] body. And he begins to tell, quite calmly: I am a stranger, not a Będziner, but what does "stranger" mean, when I have been travelling to Będzin for some[?] 50 years and know every alley and lane as well as my five fingers. So I arrive by train, just between day and night, at dusk, but as soon as I leave the railway station terror falls upon me: it is pitch dark, a veritable Egyptian darkness. Night it had indeed already become, but the lamps were in no hurry to light the pavements. Only as well as I can feel my way even in the dark — I walked on, but needless to say, walking in the dark, even when one knows the town, when you barricade yourselves — and I immediately fell onto a mountain of stones. I thought: oh well, if the pavements are made for the stones, then surely the wide street may be for people. And indeed, as best I could, I scrambled[?] out of the mountains of stones and up onto the roadway — but here I met my real defeat: the roadway is all dug up; I put a foot in and could not get it back out, and then I suddenly see the flash of a tram. I went[?] out of my mind and started shouting: Master of the Universe, how does one get out of this danger[?]. That I came away with my life[?] and must recite the "Gomel" blessing — about that there is nothing to say; I have come to show you what you have made of me, and at the same time to get instructions from you on how to reach you without coming to harm?
The Jew would not be persuaded that there is no other way, since the street has to be rebuilt[?], and he insists to me at once that back home, in their little town, there are finer streets; they too are attended to[?] and repaved[?], but the pavements are done in a different fashion, and the main thing — quickly, so that before you know it the work is finished; whereas here with you one cannot get out of it at all, and you pretend not to know and guess who the assailants are and whether they have been caught, when there is no need at all to chase after them.
Oh well, we Będzin residents are used to treading on dug-up streets even in the dark, but here we see what impression the town makes in the eyes of strangers the moment they arrive in town.
It is truly unheard of to make so light[?] of the citizens. One takes the longest and busiest street in town, a street that everyone who arrives or wants to leave must pass through, and simply makes such a street unusable for the inhabitants. What does it mean — the pavements piled with stones? Oh well, we are no specialists and do not know in what manner the work should be carried out so that it disturbs the appearance and the citizens as little as possible, but what is certain is that with such work one certainly ought to have hurried, and in the worst case it can surely be done section by section: as soon as one section is done and definitively finished, the material is brought to a new section, that is completed, and then a new section is taken up, and so on continuously.
But we see that the work is now being done quite differently: stones keep being laid on half the street along its whole length[?], and that is not done quickly but one by one; afterwards they lie and lie, then a long time passes until the street is dug up, and so nobody hurries at all, as if it were a house being finished to which no one has any access until the keys are handed over.
Surely it must be stressed that public works should be carried out swiftly, and not disturb the movement of the population without end.
The representatives of the town must not allow this destruction[?], which harms the town's citizens; they must make every effort to carry out the work as quickly as possible, so that the street is completely cleared and handed over for the use of the inhabitants.
It is high time to hurry up with the work and to finish it.
Selekt.
My This-Year's “Exile Town”...

[Będzin — humorous feuilleton; summer.] I knew it! I foresaw it! As soon as my wife [lit. "my Jewess"] dug in her heels — "nie pojedziem" [Polish: we won't go][?] — that this year we're not going[?] to any letnisko [summer resort], I knew that this not-going would come down on my head.
I pleaded with her as one pleads with a robber:
— Mateshi[?] my crown, my little treasure, my greatness, my bright[?] sugar-doll, what does it mean, not going to any summer resort? [—] a person like you. You barely walk[?], you barely stand on your two stick-thin legs; have you forgotten that you have a meteorological station in your legs that tells you what kind of weather ["pogoda"] it's going to be... The legs say: sun, sand, plaża [beach] — all such things that Będzin doesn't have.
— "Dosyć!... Nie pojedziem!" [Polish: Enough!... We won't go!] — so she shouted. "I am stanowcza" [Polish: firm].
Well, it's hopeless; when you have a "stanowcza" wife nothing helps.
Oh, why did I press my wife so hard to go: after all it's healthier for the pocket when a wife sits at home in the [—], when my wife becomes[?] "komoshe-dne"[?]. It comes down on my head, and that's just how it is. As I insisted, my wife's staying in Będzin will, shuga[?] Zion, bring me into the ground while still young.
To my misfortune, this year such heat waves have set in, and my wife, may it not befall you, is no "sromele"[?] when it comes to heat. Well, in the countryside she manages: she undresses like Eve in the Garden of Eden, in that "costume" she feels lighter[?]... she smears her body with some cream, and that, she says, "okhlushet" [prob. Polish ochładza, cools][?] her...
But what does one do in Będzin? In Będzin she can't very well take off her clothes, and here the sun fries, fire falls from the sky.
So I had fried[?] troubles. All day long I have to be at home and help her... groan ["stenken", Polish stękać]. As soon as she lets out a groan, I have to be ready to help her along[?]. After every "oy" I have to say "oy vey", after every "akh" I have to say "akh-akh".
She says:
— Oy Feitl... I'm dying.
I answer at once:
— Oy, Meitl, I can't stand it.
She says:
— Feitl, I'm melting.
I answer at once:
— Meitl, I'm choking.
All day long I stand beside her with a towel and a fan. I fan her and she fans me. I put a lick of cold lemonade into her mouth and she gives me a gulp of lemonade. I wash her forehead with vinegar and she washes my forehead with vinegar.
And only by day? At night too. In the middle of the night she wakes me:
— Feitl, are you asleep?
— No, Meitl, I'm suffocating ["dushishe", Polish duszę się][?].
— Feitl, it's stuffy ["dushne", Polish duszno] for me...
— Feitl, open the windows!
So I fuss around my wife all night, and in the morning I'm a dead man, I'm dropping off my feet.
Now I have troubles from her walks; she only has complaints against me:
— Feitl, one can't even get through the street, the streets are all dug up, holes and ditches — it's mortal danger!
She puts on a dark dress — she comes home smeared with lime. She puts on a light dress — she comes back smeared with tar, and every time she comes home with dust in her eyes[?], she ruins my Sabbath[?]:
— Feitl, for heaven's sake[?], would you tell me what kind of town your Będzin is? That one can't get through the street? "To jest skandal!" [Polish: It's a scandal!]
This week I took pity on her — what is the poor thing to blame for? She's used to the summer resort. So I began to think how one could "uspokoić" [Polish: calm] her? I thought and thought, until I came up with it.
— Meitele, I have a plan!
— What kind of plan?
— We'll make a summer resort in Będzin.
— How?
— You'll see, just watch[?].
From then on I've made a summer resort in Będzin; I do everything just like a letnik [summer holidaymaker]. In the morning I open the windows, and in front of the window I set up a band of jokers to bellow like cattle, bleat like goats, crow like roosters.
My wife snores with relish and her face smiles. I can tell from her face that it "działa" [Polish: works][?] strongly on her.
Before noon I put a heap of dung in front of the window, and when the "smell" comes into the house, she breathes[?] a bit easier.
— Ah... ah, what a delight[?], a bit of air... a nice bit of powietrze [Polish: air]...
Towards evening I take her for a stroll in the cowshed. She sits for an hour, sniffs to her heart's content, and when she comes out she feels she has gained something...
In the house I've set up a pot of thorn-flowers, next to it a tub of water, and covered the floor with sand. My wife lies stretched out on the hammock, flies bite, and I walk around all day long shouting:
— Staniki! [bras] Jagodniki! [blueberry buns] Zabawki[?] dla dzieci! [toys for children] Wiśnie! [cherries] Lody! [ice cream] Majteczki! [panties] Okulary plażowe! [beach glasses] — a summer resort with all the little climates!
Friday towards evening I come home loaded like a mule, from head to foot with packs, sweat pouring down my face, I look like a locomotive. My wife runs to meet me, unpacks the parcels, I lie down on the hammock and she hands me a little bowl of wild strawberries ["pozhomkes", Polish poziomki] with sour cream — just like at the summer resort.
On the Sabbath we sit by the pot of thorn-flowers, wash in the tub, rub ourselves with the sand — just like at the summer resort...
By the window lies a fresh little mound of dung and "perfumes" the house, just like at the summer resort.
— How am I doing now? Praise the Almighty for it, may it get no worse. My wife is half a letniczka [female holidaymaker] in Będzin, I am a letnik and do everything like a letnik, and in my house it's exactly as at the summer resort...
The Devils' Dance in the Gmina...

[Opinion — Będzin, the kehilla and community politics.] By L. Goldsztajn.
It storms and seethes [?] in our little world; grave accusations fly from both sides, abuse each uglier than the last; the atmosphere is poisoned, the air is heavy, one could [?] suffocate...
— They are storming that house of the dead which calls itself the "gmina" [the Jewish community]...
And this fortress has fortified itself so well, fenced itself in with barbed wire — and it cannot be conquered; the fierce attacks do not help — and wooing [?] does not help either...
Strangely, though, public opinion knows nothing: something is said and something is not said, something is whispered and something is told, and nobody knows where the truth lies. But it would simply be a crime to hush everything up, to choke it all down inside — no! Everything must be said openly and clearly, even if it is unpleasant for the guilty party, for the guilty one must, after all, be ready to bear the consequences. If someone had the courage to commit a public crime, he must also have the courage to bare his breast to the shooting arrows of the public.
And therefore I wish, from this place, to deal with the whole complex of questions that has arisen in this muddle [?].
As said, the situation now created is such that it has reached its peak — it cannot go on like this!.. For must we wait for outside factors to decide? Or are the morbid ambitions of our communal workers so great that they want to bring things to the point where everything collapses, so long as they satisfy their private aspirations?..
Mr. Rubinlicht was put forward entirely by the progressive circles of Będzin, and from them, from them alone, he received his mandate, both as kehilla representative and as president of the kehilla board. But Mr. Rubinlicht must admit that he has betrayed those who gave him his mandate. Mr. Rubinlicht, for incomprehensible reasons, deserted to the Agudah camp, to the very camp by which he was hated and despised, by which he was fought in the ugliest way. What is the reason for this defection? We knew that Mr. Rubinlicht is a man of compromises. But we did not know that Mr. Rubinlicht would, without any reservation, accept the policy of the Agudah flatterers and ruthlessly fight the just demands of the progressive-democratic circles. What motives drove him to it?
Mr. Rubinlicht broke the record of public scandal with his famous "explanation" to the supervisory authority, which he attached to the budget — a matter lying exclusively within the competence of the council. Here Mr. Rubinlicht galloped too far and badly overstepped the mark. If Mr. Rubinlicht wants to be on bad terms with the president of the council, Mr. Langner, and wants to make friends with Mr. Skoczylas [?] — be my guest! But to fight and annul resolutions of the council, to fight and annul the budget — when the council alone has the right to strike out items and insert items — only because the Agudah is a minority on the council, only because Mr. Langner, with whom you have personal quarrels, is president of the council — that is going too far!
By what right did Mr. Rubinlicht write in his "explanation" that the council's striking out of the items was an act of revenge by individuals? So Mr. Rubinlicht alone in the whole town is the voice of the entire public opinion, and the council is only individuals? The council, that is, which by the same majority elected Mr. Rubinlicht president of the kehilla, had legal value then, and today the council is less than nothing... So writes Mr. Rubinlicht in his "wyjaśnienie" [explanation]: that it is merely an act of revenge by individual persons...
How far the flirtation with the Agudah has led Mr. Rubinlicht astray we can see from how he fights like a lion for R' Mendel Lewin, with how much zeal he defends the item for R' Mendel Lewin. This item, which the council struck out by a majority, i.e. entirely lawfully, the president supports with arguments of his own, and sets them out there... in his "explanation".
Here one would like to ask:
— Dear Mr. Rubinlicht! You sat at the council meeting at which the council struck out the item for R' Mendel Lewin; why did you not fight for that item at the meeting, at least as hard as you defended the 300 zł. for painting the gmina premises, or the 200-odd zł. for furniture for the gmina? Why did you not put forward then the arguments that Będzin has only three morei hora'ah [rabbinical decisors] and must have a fourth; why did you not explain this to the members of the council of the Jewish kehilla in Będzin? Only now have you told it, for the first time, in the "grounds" to the supervisory authority.
Or perhaps the supervisory authority will surely be capable of understanding that we lack a fourth moreh hora'ah, while the Jewish members of the kehilla council will not, by no means, be able to grasp it? Or perhaps you lacked a little courage for it at the time?..
And let us not be subjective, and let us admit: Mr. Rubinlicht as vice-president — by all means! Mr. Rubinlicht as ławnik [alderman] in the magistrate — very good; Mr. Rubinlicht in the Chamber of Commerce, in the commercial court — very good; Mr. Rubinlicht [?] in the merchants' association — also good; but Mr. Rubinlicht as head of the community in the Będzin gmina — here we have been bitterly disappointed... Here the threadbare phrase "economic" is not enough; here we want a consistent political line; here we do not want to see merely a little shop that sells burial plots and seats in the synagogue and buys dayanim and beadles along with gravediggers; here currents come in, and each current wants, and fights for, the right to press its seal on the matter called the gmina. Here there are disappointments over which we and the Agudah are waging a struggle, and here lies our disappointment. Mr. Rubinlicht handed us over to the Agudah, to meet their demands a full hundred per cent, ignored our demands; Mr. Rubinlicht declared war on us and we had to take it up; he can have no complaints against us.
And now about the latest revelations: on the merits we do not wish to express ourselves. A commission has been elected; let it first pronounce its verdict, then we will return to the question and consider how far the charges raised are consistent with the honorary office of a president of a kehilla board. But the fact that Mr. Rubinlicht turned for protection to his new "allies", and that they fight desperately for his rehabilitation [printed "rehabilimation"], and that Messrs. Riński [?] and Skoczylas [?] pelted us with a sea of excuses — this in no way calms the tempers; it has exactly the opposite effect, because we know that this is a love dependent on an interest; because we know that it is compensation for the famous "wyjaśnienie"; because the Agudah, which only yesterday fought and smeared him — at the elections to this same gmina, at the election of the president, and at the last town council elections — cannot all at once make him holy and pure; and that is the sad part of it.
Let Mr. Rubinlicht [misprinted "Rublglicht"] remember that his policy will not bring him to his goal. The crafty Agudah politicians will use him for their purposes, then they will abandon him, and then he will remain lonely and forsaken, for — "the Moor has done his work, the Moor can go"... And that will be the reward for his desertion and betrayal of those who sent him into the gmina, entrusted him with a mandate, which he abused.
— The reward will be well deserved!..
How Was the Letter-Box Born? — by Z. Haber, Haifa

[Feuilleton — history of the post.] Until the year 1840 everyone who wrote a letter had to come to the post office and hand the letter over there. The letter was registered — who was sending it and to whom it was going. Nothing was paid for it, because the postage had to be paid by the one who received the letter. If the letter was not accepted, the post brought the letter back to the writer, and if he did not want to pay the fee for there and back, the post had the right to throw the letter away.
When postage stamps began to be introduced in 1840, one of course still had to come to the post office with every letter. One had to pay there, and the receipt for the postage was pasted on by the postmaster himself in person...
Of course this was not very convenient, especially when sending love letters: it was not easy for women to go to the post office and inform the postmaster that So-and-so son of So-and-so is sending a little letter... In those days women, too, carried on love affairs with strange men, and the same the other way round — strange men did not dislike strange women..
The matter was very unpleasant, but nothing could be done about it...
Only in the year 1848, during the Leipzig fair of that time, did the post introduce letter-boxes for the first time.
Everyone could buy stamps at the post office; at home they stuck them on the letters and afterwards dropped them into the boxes that had been set up at the places where the fair was held.
In this way they wanted to spare busy merchants the trouble of having to go to the post office when they wished to send off their letters.
Twice a day someone from the post went round from one box to the next and took the letters out of the boxes.
Naturally, people then heard about the boxes everywhere, and the first city that subsequently introduced letter-boxes was Paris. It is said [?] that it was precisely the postmaster's beautiful wife who was a blazing fire for the letter-boxes, because she did not want her husband to know to whom she was writing letters.
Today there is literally not a single village in the world that does not have letter-boxes everywhere. Looking at it, it seems to us that this cleverest thing in the whole world must surely have existed for thousands of years.
But cultural history records exactly the dates of every new invention, and so we learn that the letter-box is not even a hundred years old yet.
Yechiel Seiner [?]: Comfort Ye...

[Literature — prose poem for Shabbat Nachamu.] By the rivers of Babylon our forefathers hung their fiddles upon the willows. And there the soul of the people glowed in the burning fire of sorrow and hatred, and created the flaming magic song that is stronger than death —
By the rivers of Babylon...
— Arise, poet! Play out your mighty word of comfort, redeem the people's melody, free it from the stifling air [?] that rings with voices of blood and vengeance.
...A shadow of death, leaden air, dry bones in the valley, groaning tones, cries of woe from one end of the world to the other, voices pleading for mercy;
— The voice of my people!
And a folk-melody trudges [?] in captivity, writhes in burning [?] torments [?] at the gates of Rome.
— Who has sensed [?] what song of our present-day wrath; the songs of today's generation; who has dreamed out [?] the flaming magic oath by the rivers of blood of our present-day exile; who has poured together all the bloody groans of our tormented national soul into a single chord —
By the rivers of Babylon our forefathers hung their fiddles upon the willows:
Arise, poet! Free our captive folk-melody!..
Let Us Console Ourselves... — by Ben Amotz

[Zagłębie — satire; kehilla elections.] Let us console ourselves.
In those terrible days when "our daughters and sons were taken into captivity", as the prophet laments: "My young men and my maidens are gone into captivity", when black clouds hid the light of the world from us, when Job's tidings suddenly poured down upon our heads and the curse of the Rebuke was fulfilled: "Without, the sword shall bereave, and terror within", outside the echoes of the exploding petards resounded and inside the blood froze with fright — in such a time of trouble for Jacob we fell into a terrible despair, we gave up on a better tomorrow and looked at the future with mortal terror.
Suddenly a bright ray appeared on our darkened horizon, a voice was suddenly heard in our camp, a voice that awakens the dry bones, brings the dry bones back to life: Arise to battle, brothers! Hear the call of redemption that comes to you, do not despair, Israel is not yet widowed, the Jewish people lives and will live. Gird up your loins, lift up your heads, raise them to heaven and let your voice be heard, for such is "the order of the world": after every calamity comes a deliverance — after the martyrs in the Land of Israel we have, thank God, kehilla elections, which will bring a new stream of life into the Jewish camp.
— Let us console ourselves.
* * *
Let us console ourselves.
In the town there was turmoil; from person to person the news passed that something terrible was brewing, that mobilized forces were preparing to launch an attack on our kehilla; the air (in the kehilla office smelled of gunpowder; any moment now, we thought, everything is rolling downhill and the kehilla will, God forbid, be turned into a house of the dead, a place where demon dances are held, a place where lawlessness and demoralization gain the upper hand, where useless work is carried on, a seat of the scornful where the ugliest demagogic tricks are wrapped in mantles of holiness.
So we thought, and over this we began to lament — but let us raise the cup and say the blessing "Who redeemed us"... let us give praise to those who always bring us redemption, to those who seek nothing ever but the common good, to those who at every step strive to strengthen peace and unity in the Jewish kehilla and whose entire work is aimed solely at strengthening the Jewish religion, for the mission rests upon them, they are after all "great in defence and great in building"..
And indeed, in such a time of trouble they responded, and all as one man set themselves to the holy work, and everything was saved, all the evil spirits were repelled, and the integrity of the kehilla president was restored.
— Let us console ourselves.
* * *
Let us also console ourselves that in the election commissions of Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa the Agudah leaders do not have a majority; for according to reports from various towns and various places where the election commissions consist of an Agudah majority, the names of the "undesirable" voters are being struck off on the basis of paragraph 20.
It is possible that in the Zagłębie towns the Agudah leaders, even if they had the power in their hands, would not have made use of that high-handed paragraph, for in Zagłębie people in general think very little of the ugly deeds, of the informer systems that the small-town strongmen use. But be that as it may, we must be grateful to the heads of the election commissions for not using paragraph 20.
— Let us console ourselves.
* * *
Let us then take comfort in the fact that in the present ... [?] time, when all human progress has gone bankrupt, there are still in Zagłębie Jewish employers with idealistic hearts who, poor things, cannot bear that Jewish workers should be employed in their factories. If you ask them for a donation for hungry unemployed families — "gladly" [?]; but work — "who ever mentioned it?", that is a matter for Esau, not for Jews.
There are [?] indeed Jewish manufacturers in Zagłębie who employ hundreds of Jewish workers, but these manufacturers still belong to the old generation; the new ones, on the other hand, the upstarts, the "cultured" ones, really cannot stand to watch Jewish workers work hard..
— Comfort ye, comfort ye my people..
To the Activists of the Gemilut-Chesed Funds in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — interest-free loan funds and the kehilla elections; opinion piece.]
At the present time, when in all cities and towns we stand before new kehilla elections, we receive from the broad Jewish masses, from all their strata, urgent proposals that we, as people who have worked for years in the gemilut-chesed funds and have much experience in Jewish public work, should put forward our candidates for the kehilla elections, with the aim of taking over responsible offices in the kehillot and conducting the work in such a direction that the kehillot are transformed into true popular institutions and bring the maximum benefit to the Jewish popular masses — and not as until now, when the kehilla was a place of quarrels and party frictions and, at best, dealt only with mikveh and rabbinate matters.
With whatever motives the largest [?] oppressed part of the Jewish population turns to us, for us — who for years have taken upon ourselves the burden of caring and working for our impoverished brethren — the question arises: what are we to do? What position are we to take on this question? Will our participation in the kehillot bring the desired benefit to our voters in general and to the gemilut-chesed funds in particular?
On all these questions I consider myself competent to state my opinion and to give my colleagues a guideline on the matter. In the last term of the kehilla administration, 5 years ago, I made the attempt and was elected in the Wazyersk [?] (probably Zawiercie) kehilla, held the office of chairman of the council, and despite my untiring work in the kehilla I came to the conviction that the futile work is a pity, because in our kehillot there reigns, unfortunately, such rottenness, so much small-minded egoism, that every effort to accomplish positive, useful work there for the Jewish population is useless.
As for the subsidies we receive from the kehillot: because of the permanent shortage of money that reigns there, our participation would only make obtaining the subsidised sums truly difficult; whereas when we stand outside the camp, we often succeed, by exerting a certain pressure, in having the subsidies paid out to us.
We must not be represented in the kehilla for a second reason as well. A present-day "rich man" — as soon as the kehilla has done him a little injustice when drawing up [?] the budget or on some other occasion, he first of all takes his revenge on the gemilut-chesed fund and no longer pays his monthly contribution.
This is not the place to develop plans for how our kehillot should be reformed so that they become popular institutions; but in the state in which they find themselves now, one must note with regret that our participation there can bring us no benefit whatsoever. We only burden our best people with strenuous, useless work, which we need to devote to our gemilut-chesed institutions, which we have created and built up through years of long work and which are the only useful establishments for our grievously suffering people in the present hard time.
Józef Liberman
(Chairman of the Wazyersk [?] Gemilut Chesed Fund and member of the board of "CEKABE").
Ideal Wives (A Summer-Cottage Humoresque) — Shmuel Rubinshtein

[Feuilleton — humoresque.]
Shmuel Rubinshtein.
Ideal Wives.
(A summer-cottage humoresque.)
There are wives — ideal wives — who send their husbands off in summertime to a dacha while they themselves stay in town to look after the business and mind the house; they do not travel together with their husbands, so that the husbands may really have more pleasure there — for what kind of holiday would it be with wife and children along?
"Mendel," one such wife said to her husband, "don't worry at all about me and the children; we'll have quite a nice time in the avenues [?]. You go to Bystra and spend your couple of months' holiday there in good health; you, poor thing, need a little rest — rest up and don't stint yourself; you needn't even write me a letter; forget altogether that you have a wife in the world, live as if you were a bachelor..."
Naturally the husband accepted the proposal. Three days after he had settled in at Frankel's guesthouse, he received from his wife a big parcel — a present. In it were a box of cigarettes (papirosy), a bottle of "Carmel" and a kilo of chocolate bonbons.
"The cigarettes with the Carmel are for you," his little wife wrote him, "and the tasty chocolate bonbons are for the girls you will get to know there; spend time with them like a gentleman; forget that you are a married man."
The husband was so moved by his wife's present that he wanted to send her a letter of thanks at once, but he remembered that he had promised her not to write. Indeed, he thought to himself, for two months I'll forget that I'm a married man; there's no wife, no family; I'm a bachelor, a free bird!
Another little wife went even further. After she had talked her husband into taking a three-month holiday, she went to two pretty girls of her acquaintance who were also due to go to Bystra, and talked them into staying at the same guesthouse where her husband was lodging.
To her husband she wrote that same day: "My dearest, the Zimmermanns and Miss Schwarz [?] are leaving tomorrow for a couple of months; they will stay at the same guesthouse where you are. I have asked them to amuse you. Be a gentleman and go to meet them at the railway station, have a merry time with them, take them to the cinema and the pastry shop; don't forget that they are girls and love to have a good time. Have a good, merry time and don't think about anything. That I should have the slightest suspicion about you? — I am never jealous; it is foolish to be jealous. If you want to visit [?] Klara often — she is very pretty and, it seems, not indifferent to you; she is a very lively one, a brunette full of temperament... Don't take me for a fool: I know everything; I also know that until you married me you had your eye on her... On the contrary, remember your bachelor years...
From me, your ardently beloved wife,
Mary."
A few days later the same husband received from his wife half a dozen neckties with four fine dress shirts. Together with the things he received a letter in which his little wife had written:
"I am sending you ties and shirts. I believe you did not take enough with you to change into. I want you to please everyone — as Klara writes me from Bystra, two pretty Warsaw girls are staying at your guesthouse. Today's girls look at fashion, so I want you to be most fashionable. Klara even wrote it to me with another intention: she wanted to make me jealous so as to detach [?] your interest in the Warsaw girls... But it doesn't bother me that you spend time with them and enjoy yourself. Look, my husband, amuse yourself as best you can; don't mind me. The greatest pleasure would be for me to know that you are spending your time very well, that my husband is enjoying life."
That is how the little wives look after their husbands at the summer lodgings.
— — — — — — — —
Of course all this is a writer's fantasy, but... what a beautiful, splendid [?] world our world would be if such wives really existed...
—o—
New York — San Francisco.
In America a film, "New York — San Francisco," is now being shown. The film's content, its manner of portrayal and its individual episodes are all extremely interesting. The action takes place in a passenger aeroplane as it flies from New York to San Francisco. That in itself is original. The director shows us a whole gallery of various types who have met by chance in the aeroplane. We meet here criminals and "loyal" citizens, secret agents and rich women, merchants and petty bourgeois, proletarians and plain idlers; passions and conflicts are discharged [?] here, world-views and perspectives find expression — real material for a motion picture.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Va'etchanan)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Va'etchanan
—o—
a) "Let me go over, I pray thee, and see the good land" (3:25)
"Rabbi Simlai expounded: Why did Moses long to enter the Land of Israel? ... The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: Do you seek anything but to receive the reward? I account it to you as though you had performed them."
Tractate Sotah, folio 14.
The Seer of Lublin interpreted: "I account it to you as though you had performed them" — a commandment that one wanted to perform but, through circumstances beyond one's control, did not perform — of it is said "I account it to you as though you had performed them": it has an even greater merit than a commandment that one actually does, for it is hard to perform a commandment without an admixture of ulterior motives, of intentions that contain a percentage of self-interest; whereas[?] the commandments that one did not perform, but which Heaven reckons as performed — those are reckoned without ulterior motives.
—o—
b) "Neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the Lord" (4:2)
Reformers once came to Rabbi Hershele [Zvi Hirsch] of Berlin and proposed to him that the prayers be shortened a little and the religion be reformed in general, so that the youth would remain loyal to the faith. With this whole reform — so they wished to show — they were[?] aiming only to strengthen Judaism.
He answered them:
— The Torah already foresaw this, and that is why it says "Neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the Lord": under the pretext of "keeping the commandments of the Lord" you shall not diminish anything from the commandments...
—o—
c) "And make you a graven image, the similitude of any figure" (ibid., 16)
This is aimed[?] — said Rabbi Mendele of Kotzk — at those who cling to the mere form of the commandment, forgetting the essence; that is what is called idolatry...
• • •
— What is the difference between a Misnaged and a Hasid? — asked Rabbi Moshe of Kobrin.
And he answered:
— A Misnaged fears the Shulchan Aruch, and a Hasid fears God...
—o—
d) "When thou shalt beget children, and children's children, and ye shall have remained long in the land, and shall corrupt yourselves"
The fear of corruption begins with the children and the children's children, with the coming generations, with the young folk... Imrei Chen.
—o—
e) "And there ye shall serve gods, the work of men's hands... But if from thence thou shalt seek the Lord thy God" (ibid., 28, 29)
Serving foreign idols — that is always done by the many, the mass; it is always a mass psychosis. "Ye shall seek" — in the plural; but[?] seeking God — that is always done by individuals. "Thou shalt find Him, if thou seek Him with all[?] thy heart" — in the singular... Leket David.
• • •
"U-matzata" ("thou shalt find") sometimes means: enough ("if all[?] the fish[?] of the sea be gathered, will it suffice[?] for them" — u-matza lahem). When seeking God, the seeking itself is enough: "ye shall seek — and thou shalt find"; the very seeking already suffices...
Rabbi Simcha Bunem of Przysucha.
—o—
f) "Keep the Sabbath day to sanctify it" (5:12)
Therefore — said Rabbi Yechezkele of Kuzmir — a Jew has a special soul on the Sabbath, an additional soul (neshama yetera), because the temptation [not] to keep the Sabbath is great: the evil inclination has an argument — livelihood. So the good inclination had to be given another soul to help it, an additional soul, so that the two together would overcome the evil inclination...
—o—
g) "Honour thy father and thy mother, as the Lord thy God hath commanded thee" (5:16)
"As He commanded thee — at Marah." Rashi.
What is being emphasised about honouring father and mother, that it was already commanded at Marah?
Because the natural honouring of father and mother, which even gentiles observe strictly, comes from the awareness that parents raised you, fed you and clothed you. The Jews, however, were commanded to honour father and mother at Marah, when they ate manna and "thy raiment waxed not old upon thee" — the children simply did not need the parents' food and the parents' clothing. The egoistic veneration simply did not exist, and therefore among Jews the commandment of honouring carries a much loftier intention, has a much greater meaning. Ksav Sofer.
• • •
The Torah warns about honouring a father [no fewer than][?] three times, and about honouring a son — not at all; and yet, it seems, people are more careful about the honour of the son than about the honour of the father: parents sacrifice more for their children than the other way round. Leket Amarim.
—o—
h) "And with all thy soul, and with all thy might" (6:5)
"And with all thy soul — even if He takes your soul."
And why does Rashi not expound likewise: "and with all thy might — even if He takes your money"?
Because when someone's money is taken from him, it really[?] is hard for him to serve God... Out of poverty it really[?] is hard to be a lover of God. Rabbi Yisrael of Ruzhin.

(Instead of a report on a consultation at the Sosnowiec Artisans' Association)
Says the president:
"Comrades, craftsmen,
I want to hear your counsel,
tell me at least:
how do we share out the spoils here,
when we have just two little benches [seats]
but would-be sitters — a great many;
so tell me plainly, without twisting:
what does one do here with so many[?].
The men's tailors want to sit,
and the shoemakers want to as well,
the ladies' tailors, great connoisseurs,
and others too, for a sample.
A sage is needed[?] to seat
all these gentlemen;
I shall surely value you
and gladly take your counsel.
A consultation I call at once
of comrades, of the best ones —
let their word be heard
and let them pass strong, firm resolutions.
I myself will not interfere,
I will wait quite patiently —
whoever wants may enjoy it here,
only do not put the blame on me."
—
And Reb Itshe the Black
with his big stick
went off to all the tailor voters
to call them, to rouse them:
"Hurry, comrades, as fast as you can,
over there, to the mandates;
you may all be perfectly sure
that I will not betray you at all."
—
A great crowd came:
presidents, the greatest representatives,
God forbid no dolts —
but truly the cleverest and the best.
The best of the trades
began calling out the candidates
in order to draw up the list
and share out the mandates.
One says Moyshe, one says Zalmen,
Mendl, Yankl, Gershon, Zerach,
a second comrade says Kalmen,
a third says: let it be Borukh.
—
A day went by, a night went by,
and no end was reached;
they pondered and thought on and on,
until the deadline for submission
arrived.

What Do Our Great Ones Say? Our Survey on the Kehilla.

[Będzin — satire; kehilla elections.] The new coming comrade Braunfeld.
What will the coming kehilla look like? — we asked.
First of all the kehilla must be democratized, beginning with the synagogues, which must be reorganized according to the Bundist programme.
That is:
Quite simply: on Shabbes the Torah reader shall, at the end of the weekly portion, also be obliged to read the "Folks-Tsaytung".
On Yom Kippur the whole day-long praying must be abolished, and an 8-hour praying-day must be introduced with a one-and-a-half-hour lunch break.
A cantor may only be engaged through the mediation of the professional class union, because a cantor belongs to the proletariat — for he says: "Hineni he-ani" ["Here I am, the poor one"].
The Eastern Wall must be abolished; at the top our comrades will pray; "shishi" and "maftir" will go to comrade Berkowicz and comrade Langner; King David's hakafa will go to comrade Froim Lazer and comrade Janek; whereas the hakafa "Ozer dalim" ["Helper of the poor"] we leave to Józef Goldberg.
Doctor-candidate Hamburg.
We found the doctor standing in the Shmone Esre prayer facing not the Eastern Wall but the Western Wall (a doctor-revolutionary's practice). After he had bowed at "Modim" and said "May our eyes behold Your return"... (the last word we did not hear clearly; we surmise he wanted to say "to Zion"...) he turned to us and declared that he never intends to enter the new gmina; but if he does enter, he will do it solely in order to split the "dozers"[?].
"In the new gmina I must take up the office of auditor of the bookkeeping, for I understand complicated matters — even in the programme of the P. Ts. [Poale Zion] I find my way.
In the gmina I intend to introduce proletarian reforms: of all religious institutions only the mikveh and the steam bath will remain — that is the only place where the proletariat settles accounts with the capitalists and lashes them.
As a revolutionary I will introduce that the distinguished 'Ma tovu' shall be said after praying, and 'Aleinu le-shabe'ach' shall be begun before praying, so that people start spitting at the outset[?] of the prayers."

"Plażomania" [Beach Mania]

[Humour — poem; summer.]
Everyone, everyone, everyone,
both the groom and the bride,
everyone runs, everyone rushes,
and they must[?] wear bathing costumes.
Where to? — you want [to know], I'd tell you:
— to the... plaża [beach]
to roast oneself,
catch sun and avoid the shade —
from great to small —
though it doesn't always turn out well.
Some on sand and some on grass,
some smooth and some with blisters[?]..
some on brown and some on black,
some the shoulder, some the heart —
[?]. When someone turns quite red
and his skin peels..
night comes, he cannot sleep;
[?] — he knows: the beach's punishments.
And one catches a burn,
whoever wants and whoever can,
whoever has time and whoever is idle,
knows that he too has a... day off[?]...
Poor, rich,
by the river,
big and small,
ugly and pretty —
one shows the other his "mechile" [backside, euphemistically]
and great is the grandeur there,
both with the lad and with the maiden...
In short, along the length and the breadth
people lie spread out,
"burning" hard and smoking heavily[?],
some a little and some more,
and one runs into the water,
some red, some pale,
and one comes out wet,
and afterwards one sweats again,
and one tells beach jokes;
one tells and everyone listens —
it's "progressive" and it's "modern".
In short, in summer life the fashion is big
for soda water and ice cream [lody]
and "jedyne moje zdrowie"[?] [Polish: "my only health"]
also for "plażomania".

In the Tangle of Life (4)

[Serialized novel — Kraków, Zawiercie and New York; installment 4.]
(A novel with dramatic events in Kraków, Zawiercie and New York)

Dovidl was badly frightened, yet he went with the stranger. The man led him into a house where Selma lay in bed; they showed him the baby, a little boy, and he was afraid to touch it.

Finally Selma's brother told him sternly:

"Within eight days you must change your religion and marry Selma; if not, you will regret it bitterly."

Dovidl did not know what was happening to him, and when he left he walked through the streets without a goal, tears pouring from his eyes.

At that time Dovidl, despite all his work, was still quite pious. He did not work or write on the Sabbath. The misfortune made him even more pious; he begged God to strengthen him so that he would not give in to the Christian woman's demand.

But time does not stand still. The day was approaching on which the brother had demanded that he convert; three days were left, and his skin [?] trembled on him.

And just then, one fine morning, as he was coming out of the university, who should come towards him but... Nechama. His head actually began to spin, and he very nearly fainted.

Nechama was just as surprised.

"Nechama!" he cried out.

"Dovidl!"

They seized each other's hands and stood as if welded to one another.

"How is the child?"

"She is well."

"Where is she?"

"Here in Vienna, with me."

"Where are you staying? What are you doing here? How are things with you? Have you perhaps married again already?"

"Calm down, Dovidl!" she said to him with a smile. "You're asking me so many questions at once that I don't know which to answer first. Well then [?]: I am here in Vienna; the child, Etta [?], is with me; she is pretty and healthy and keeps asking about you all the time. I haven't married again. My father wanted to marry me off again, but I told him: 'Father, enough of lording it over me. You already married me off once to whom you wanted, and then forced me to divorce when you wanted that again; but now enough! You can't do with me as you like any more.' It came to a scandal and he insulted me. So I left his house, went to Vienna and enrolled at the university."

"And what will you live on?"

"I have a little money, I'll earn a little and I'll go hungry a little."

"Take me to Etta [?], I want to see the child."

They went to her home, a small room somewhere on the third floor. The child was overjoyed with Dovidl.

"Daddy! Daddy!" she cried. "Where has Daddy been so long?"

When they had calmed down a little from the meeting, Dovidl said to Nechama:

"Listen! We never really divorced; we really still love each other as before."

"As much as before!" she answered.

"You tell me how things have gone with you," Nechama said to him. "You look so thin [?] to me! You seem so worried! What's the matter with you, Dovidl?"

Now Dovidl told Nechama about his entanglement with the Christian woman and why he was so very worried.

Nechama thought it over and then said to Dovidl:

"Listen to me, Dovidl. I believe you that everything you told me happened just so. Don't be afraid! You will go away somewhere with me and the child; let's travel to the Tyrolean mountains and stay there two weeks, and then we'll see what we have to do."

"But you forget, Nechama, that I am not some lawless man; the child really is mine. Run away? I can't!"

"Listen to me, Dovidl," Nechama said to him, "you are not guilty of anything here. She went with you, she gave herself to you, she knew you were a Jew, the whole time she never said a word to you about marriage or about conversion; you also told her in good time that it was better no child should be born, and she didn't listen to you — what does that mean? She wanted to trap you — well, so she trapped herself. She can't force you to marry her, she can't force you to convert; at most she can demand that you support the child, and that you will do — I'll help you. Do as I say: wait a few weeks until tempers calm down, and then I will talk to her."

"You?"

"Yes, me!"

"That's good!" Dovid agreed.

They went away for three weeks.

When they came back to Vienna, Nechama went to Selma, introduced herself to her as Dovid's sister and had a talk with her. Selma was very angry and bitter and spoke in great agitation. When Nechama explained to her that Dovid was willing to pay for raising the child, Selma became so incensed that she threw Nechama out of the house.

On the way home Nechama decided not to tell Dovid about this last scene; on the contrary, she told him that she had settled the whole matter with Selma.

"Really? Nechamale! My treasure! Now we can marry! Now at last we'll go to the wedding canopy in the proper way!"

That very same evening they went to a rabbi and held a wedding.

Fight between the Kehilla Board and the Council — the National faction criticises the kehilla president and the Agudah faction defends him. — An audit commission elected

[Local page; Będzin — kehilla.]
In the heat of the "cucumber season" [the summer silly season] a fight has flared up between the National and the Agudah factions. They are not fighting, God forbid, to conquer [?] any position; the aim is merely to exalt the "hero" of the kehilla.
The fight began at the Thursday meeting of the kehilla board, at which the president, Mr. Rubinlicht, wanted to put before the board the proposal of the National faction that, in connection with the "revelations" [?] uncovered by the council president Mr. Landner, he should lay down his mandate as kehilla president.
Mr. Landner also came to the meeting. Before the agenda was discussed, board member (dozór) Herdiner [?] turned to the chairman, asking him to remove Mr. Landner from the meeting. Mr. Rubinlicht supported the proposal, arguing that although the council president Mr. Landner has the right to be present at board meetings, he was nevertheless in favour of Mr. Landner not being present at this meeting. To this Mr. Landner declared that he would not leave. Mr. Rubinlicht then broke off the meeting and went out with his colleagues to a neighbouring room to hold a consultation.
When Mr. Landner too entered the consultation room, a very sharp exchange of words took place between the two of them, between Rubinlicht and Landner, which led to the meeting being broken off.
The continuation of the meeting took place the next day at 12 noon. After Mr. Rubinlicht's explanations concerning the complaints spread about him, the Agudah majority expressed a vote of confidence in him and declared that the board takes upon itself the penal [?] and moral responsibility for Mr. Rubinlicht's actions as kehilla president.
—
The "rehabilitation" was supposed to be carried out [?] at the council meeting held on Sunday. The result, however, was the opposite. After mutual abuse from both sides, the motion of no confidence in the kehilla president was — adopted.
The meeting takes place [misprinted "kost" for "kumt"] under the chairmanship of the council president, Mr. G. Landner, who makes a 2-hour speech giving a chronological survey of the time when the Zionist councillors elected Rubinlicht president — who later betrayed the Zionists and went over to the "Agudah", which he helps to carry out its plans in general, and in particular to force through R' Mendel Lewin as rabbi of Będzin.
Mr. Landner then presents the report of his audit of the kehilla books, in which there is no trace of the 500 zł. that the gmina owes the gemilut-hesed [interest-free loan] fund, nor of the 1000 zł. that Mr. R. received from Mrs. Haserzweig for a plot of land.
After the report a broad discussion develops, during which the kehilla's "dirty laundry" is washed in front of the "public [?] gallery".
Councillor Riński [?] expresses regret that he has to defend Mr. Rubinlicht, who was elected president by the Zionists, but he does so [misprinted "sut" for "tut"] because "God seeks the pursued" [Eccl. 3:15], especially when the pursued is a righteous man, a man of great merit to Jewish society.
Councillors Piekorski, Klajman and Kisner also speak as defenders; they consider the accusations against Mr. Rubinlicht false and report [?] that the debt to the gemilut-hesed fund has already been paid and that Mrs. Haserzweig gave the 1000 zł. at Mr. Rubinlicht's disposal.
The councillors of the National faction appear as prosecutors and then bring in a motion to express no confidence in the kehilla president and to demand [?] that he lay down his mandate. The motion receives 4 votes for and 4 against and fails. On the other hand, the motion of councillors Klajman and Kornfeld is adopted to elect a commission to carry out an audit of the board's activity.

Craftsmen come out for abolishing the present patent system

[Będzin — craftsmen and taxes.]
At the premises of the Craftsmen's Union a conference of craftsmen took place under the chairmanship of President Goldsztajn. Delegates of the craftsmen's associations of the neighbouring towns also took part in the conference.
On the agenda: 1) the patent [trade-licence] bill, 2) the kehilla elections, 3) credit for Jewish artisans, and other current questions.
On the first bill, the assembled declared that the present patent system for craftsmen should be abolished and that instead a lump sum (ryczałt) should be levied, in which the patent, turnover tax and income tax would be included. The patent categories should be reckoned according to the number of journeymen employed.
On the second point Mr. Landner (Dąbrowa) reported, and it was resolved that the craftsmen may join forces for the kehilla elections only with those groupings that recognise the Central Craftsmen's Union as the sole representative of Jewish craftsmen.
On the question of credits for Jewish craftsmen it was resolved that a delegation should intervene in the matter at the B.G.K. [Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego].
Then Mr. Goldsztajn reported on the new ministerial circular concerning examinations for apprentices and concerning master's examinations.
The most important explanations on this question are given in today's issue on the second page.

An Agudah kehilla president, if need be — only not Rubinlicht; such a proposal came from the National faction

[Będzin — kehilla.]
We are informed that the National faction of the kehilla council has proposed to the "Agudah" that, if the "Agudah" too expresses no confidence in the present kehilla president Mr. Rubinlicht, the National faction will vote for an Agudah president.

A Festive Reception in Honour of Dr. Weinzieher at the Orphanage / The Presidium of “Maccabi” / The Terrible Death of a Mentally Ill Man / On the Election Front / The Post Office Is Already Operating in the New Building / Caught at the Last Minute

[Będzin — Welfare institutions.]
Last Sabbath the children of the “Beit Yetomim” (orphanage) held a reception in honour of the president of the institution, Dr. S. Weinzieher, who had been seriously ill for a long time.
The reception hall was beautifully decorated with greenery and flowers. When Dr. Weinzieher and his wife enter the hall, the children sing “Sto lat” and he is greeted by 2 children of the society's Froebel school, who wish him health and long life.
Dr. Weinzieher replies with a heartfelt speech, in which he wishes the children that they grow up to be proud Jews and loyal citizens, and that they be healthy. Health — says Dr. Weinzieher — is a very precious thing; it is no good to be ill.
Then the children receive fruit and sweets.
The board was represented by Mesdames Ts. Szajn, S. Wajnsztok, K. Cukerman and Messrs. B. Pelc and Wybodzki.
—o—
The Presidium of “Maccabi”.
[Sosnowiec — Sport and societies.]
The new board of “Maccabi” held a meeting, at which the following presidium was elected: Adolf[?] Horowicz (president), H. Szwajcer and Kronenberg (vice-presidents), Asher Klajnberg (treasurer) and L. Binder (secretary).
—o—
The Terrible Death of a Mentally Ill Man.
[Sosnowiec — Accidents and crime.]
In the Balczewski[?] family on Panzadowa[?] Street there was a mentally ill man, who constantly made scenes and beat his mother.
On Monday, during such a scene, a younger brother would not let him beat the mother — whereupon the madman stabbed him to death with a bayonet.
—o—
On the Election Front
[Sosnowiec — Kehilla.]
It is for the time being quite quiet; only negotiations are being conducted about forming technical blocs, for since the idea of peace has burst like a soap bubble, every party or faction wants to save itself within the framework of a technical bloc.
—o—
The Post Office Is Already Operating in the New Building.
[Sosnowiec — Municipal.]
Since yesterday, Thursday, the post office has already been operating in the new building at 3 Maja Street 24.
—o—
Caught at the Last Minute.
[Sosnowiec — Accidents and crime.]
When M. Dasner[?] was about to enter the flat of his son-in-law on Wspólna Street, an unknown “guest” came towards him, gave Dasner a shove and ran away.
Later it turned out that the “guest” had already packed up all the household belongings, but at the last minute he was disturbed by Dasner.
Who Will Head the Lists?

[Sosnowiec — Kehilla.]
As we have already written, there will be a great abundance of lists in the coming kehilla elections, because everyone “makes Sabbath for himself” (goes his own way). The heads of the lists of the political organisations are to be:
From the Zionist organisation — Dr. Melodyst[?].
From the Mizrachi organisation — Yitzhak Sztajnfeld[?].
From the Revisionist organisation — Issachar Gutowski.
From the artisans — S. N. Langer.
From the “Agudat” — Baruch Seczemski[?].
From the small traders' association — Herman Aliner[?].
Right Poale Zion — Yosef Goldberg.
Left Poale Zion — M. Hamburger.
Suicide of a Jewish Shoemaker

[Sosnowiec — Accidents and deaths.]
On Monday Jewish Sosnowiec was shaken by the news that the 39-year-old Leib Bornsztajn, a shoemaker by trade, had committed suicide by hanging himself on a wire in his own flat at Piłsudskiego 42.
Bornsztajn carried out the terrible death when his wife had gone into town. When she came back she saw a horrifying sight: her husband hanging on the door.
All rescue measures were already too late.
Fell or Threw Herself Out of the Window?

[Sosnowiec — Accidents.]
The well-known merchant on Stara Pogońska[?] Street invited to his flat a girl from Kamińsk, to whom he had promised to get a job.
The girl spent a merry time in the flat. Suddenly a scream was heard and the girl fell from the window onto the pavement.
At the groans of the injured girl the neighbours came running and carried her back up into the flat.
An investigation is being conducted as to whether she fell out by accident or threw herself out.
Request to Give Premises to the Interest-Free Loan Fund Refused

[Sosnowiec — Kehilla; Welfare.]
Some time ago, at the general meeting of the Gemilut Chesed (interest-free loan) fund, a resolution was adopted to apply once again to the commissarial kehilla board regarding the allocation of premises for the Gemilut Chesed fund.
The commissarial kehilla refused the request, promising at the same time to give the fund a subsidy if the gmina has money to spare...
An Act of Revenge by a Christian Landlord against a Jewish Tenant

[Sosnowiec — Housing; Kehilla.]
At Kuźnicza 3 the tenant Kopel Salowicz lives with his family in a small room. The owner of the house, wishing to get rid of the tenant, undermined the wall of the flat in which Salowicz lives, and the wall collapsed.
The councillors Wilberszlag and Kajzer took an interest in the family's fate and obtained financial support for them from the magistrate (municipality).
The commissarial kehilla also came forward with help and allotted in favour of the homeless family a whole 5 (read: five) złoty.
It goes without saying that this generous donation from the commissarial kehilla was not accepted.
The “Peace” Conference of the Jewish Gymnasia Did Not Take Place

[Sosnowiec — Education.]
For a long time now Dr. Straskazer[?] of Łódź has been endeavouring to bring about peace between the Jewish gymnasia in Sosnowiec and Będzin, but so far he has not managed to get both sides to meet.
The same fate befell the conference which was to have been held in Szczyrk; at the last minute the conference was again called off.

How the Jewish Population in Kielce Was Frightened Off from Taking Part in the Demonstration about Danzig

[Kielce — Jews and the authorities.]
On Sunday a demonstration on the Danzig question took place in Kielce, organised by the Maritime and Colonial League (Liga Morska i Kolonialna).
Earlier, the Jewish kehilla, the Merchants' Association, the Artisans' Club etc. had received invitations from the Maritime League to take part in the demonstration.
The Jewish institutions gladly accepted the invitation and were preparing a suitable appeal to the Jewish population.
On Saturday a police sergeant ("pshrednik" [?], probably przodownik) came to the chairman of the Jewish kehilla and ordered that guards be posted [?] at the kehilla building, the Jewish gymnasium, the Merchants' Association etc., in order to watch who would throw stones at these buildings and report it to the police. Such guards were indeed posted, but nobody threw any stones.
On Saturday night the authorities summoned the Jewish representatives and gave them to understand, in a polite manner, that the Jews should not take part in the demonstration, and that in general the Jewish population should be quietly told that nobody should hang about in the street, because — as the authorities assured them — they feared outbreaks against Jews by irresponsible elements.
On Sunday the demonstration took place. The Jews, of course, did not come, and Kielce passed the day completely quietly.
Now it is surmised that all these warnings were made only in order to frighten the Jewish population and in this way to be rid of its participation in the demonstration.
Rachele from Ożarków [?] Looks for Her Bridegroom in Kielce

[Kielce — A swindle.]
It happened a few months ago, in springtime. The trees were blossoming, the birds were singing. At that time Rachele from Ożarków [?] got acquainted with a cavalier from Kielce, who introduced himself to her.
"And my name is Pruchińska [?] from Ożarków," she introduced herself to him.
They "saw each other" [?] once and once again. At first he ordered [?] tea with pastries (ciastka), until... until they made "tna'im" (an engagement contract) and agreed on [?] a wedding. As for money, the Kielce bridegroom took a "zadatek" (deposit) of 900 zł. and an engagement ring. After that he left Ożarków, and our Rachele wore her eyes out waiting for her intended.
Seeing that the young man had "dried up" [?] — not a sound, not a sight — she began to write. She writes here, she writes there, and nothing. So Rachele dressed herself up "in vinegar and in honey", and the bride from Ożarków came to Kielce. Here she found out one small detail: that no such person with such a name had ever lived in Kielce.
Well, Rachele went with tears in her eyes to the gmina (municipal office) and told the whole story. Rachele went back to Ożarków ashamed.
The Director of the Kielce Izba Skarbowa — in Zagłębie

[Kielce — Taxes.]
On Tuesday the director of the local Izba Skarbowa (Treasury Chamber), Mr. Hajdas [?], and also the naczelnik (head of department) Mr. Cyrwiński [?], travelled to Zagłębie in order to carry out an inspection (lustracja) of the tax offices in Sosnowiec, Będzin and Dąbrowa.
As we are told, the director was already at the tax office in Sosnowiec [?] at 7.30, in order to establish whether the officials come to work punctually.
The Summer Colony for Poor Jewish Children in Suchedniów

[Kielce — Welfare and education.]
As every year, this year too the Parents' Committee of the poor Jewish children in the public schools, Messrs. Tencer [?], Cytryn, Tenenbaum and Chajt [?], has organised a summer colony for the poor Jewish children in Suchedniów. In the colony, which is arranged in a very fine manner, there are about 90 children.
Since maintaining such a number of children for a period of several weeks involves larger financial means, which the Parents' Committee does not have at its disposal, the Jewish population is asked to take an interest in the colony, thereby giving 90 poor children — who suffer want and hunger all year round and sit in the winter months swollen from cold — the possibility of enjoying the fresh air for at least 4–5 weeks and of being nourished a little.
An Emissary of the Jerusalem Executive in Kielce

[Kielce — Zionism.]
This week the emissary of the Jerusalem (Zionist) Executive, Mr. Post, stayed in Kielce on matters of the shekel campaign.
In his presence a larger meeting of the representatives of all the local Zionist groupings took place, at which Mr. Post reported on the present political situation in Zionism and in Eretz Israel and on the exceptional [?] political and organisational significance of this year's "shekel sale".
It was unanimously resolved to proclaim a shekel week in Kielce. In the course of the week at least three thousand shekels must be sold in Kielce.
The shekel week ends on Sunday, 2 August of this year.

As we are informed, the first big meeting on the forthcoming kehilla elections will take place next Saturday. The election meeting is being organised by the United Zionist Election Committee.

Relief Campaign for the Widow of the Bestially Murdered Jewish Merchant Baruch Mangarten, of Blessed Memory

[Kielce — Relief.]
On the initiative of Mr. B. Harberg [?] a committee has been formed here which concerns itself with the tragic fate of the widow and unfortunate orphans of the bestially murdered Jewish merchant Baruch Mangarten, of blessed memory.
Last week a flower sale took place for this purpose, which brought in an income of 250 zł.

Visit of Deputy Yitzhak Gruenbaum to Kielce

[Kielce — Zionism.]
As is known, the member of the Zionist Executive, Deputy Yitzhak Gruenbaum, is now staying in Poland.
The Zionist groupings in Kielce are making every necessary effort so that the dear and esteemed guest of Polish Jewry should, among other places, also visit the voivodeship capital.
Terrible Storms and Fires in the Kielce Voivodeship

[Kielce Voivodeship — weather; natural disasters.] This week a terrible storm, violent cloudbursts and thunder again passed over a number of towns and townlets, as well as over many villages, damaging part of many settlements. In many places large fires broke out because of the thunder [i.e. lightning]. The hail also destroyed a great many grain fields and fruit trees. The damage amounts to many hundreds of thousands of złoty.
Secondary-School Graduates Wishing to Enter the Warsaw Polytechnic

[Warsaw — higher education; announcement.] Following the pattern of previous years, the administration of the Jewish Academic House in Warsaw is organising a preparatory course for the competitive entrance examination to all faculties of the Warsaw Polytechnic. The aim of the course is to perfect the physical-mathematical sciences of the secondary school and to supplement them in accordance with the requirements set at the competitive examination. The competitive examination begins on 25 September. The teaching staff consists [sic] of all important teaching aids and collections of examination material from previous years; graduates from the provinces enjoy cheap lodging in the Academic House. Information is given and registrations are accepted by the office of the Jewish Academic House, Warsaw, Namiestnikowska 7, every day from 10 to 12 and from 5 to 7, tel. 10-13-92.

At Wednesday's meeting of the kehilla board in Będzin, the letter of parnas Kornfeld was dealt with, in which he demands that the kehilla books be handed over to him for inspection.

Export conference at the Chamber of Commerce.
On the 12th of this month Mr Władysław Raduszycz-Nowski[?], vice-consul at the honorary consulate of the Polish Republic in Casablanca, is coming to Sosnowiec.
Vice-consul Raduszycznowski[?] is coming here with the aim of acquainting himself with the economic structure of the Zagłębie region and with the export possibilities of firms of the Kielce voivodeship to Morocco.

Building disaster in Będzin.
4 workers lightly injured.
Yesterday morning a scaffolding of Pliasz's[?] building on Małachowskiego street in Będzin collapsed. 4 workers were lightly injured.

Attacked his companion.
Israel Balderman and Leibish Lauran[?], both of the „orchei porchei“ [tramps, wayfarers], were walking from Olkusz to Wolbrom. Beyond Rabsztyn Balderman seized his companion by the collar and, beating him, demanded money.
These days Balderman was sentenced by the Sosnowiec district court to 6 months' prison and loss of rights for 2 years.

While threshing grain a son killed his father.
Józef Sabata of Kaushiglea[?] [perhaps Koziegłowy] was busy with his 23-year-old son threshing grain in the barn. At a certain moment the son accidentally struck his father, who fell down and died a few minutes later.
Swindled a poor Jewish fruit-seller out of a few złoty

On Wednesday 2 elegantly dressed young men came to a Jewish fruit-seller on Rybna street in Będzin, bought a kilo of cherries and handed over a 20-złoty banknote. When the Jew gave them change, they regretted the „deal“ and demanded the 20 zł back. Having no choice, the Jew took back the small change and returned the 20 zł. But when they had gone he saw that the young men had given him back 6 złoty less...
—o—
A father raped his 7-year-old girl.
Klekacka[?] Helena of Zawiercie reported at the police station that her husband, a mentally ill man, had raped their little girl of 7 years.
To the public!

(Communiqué of the kehilla board in Będzin)
In connection with the latest campaign of lies and slander against the kehilla president Mr Rubinlicht, we consider it our duty, for the sake of truth, to state that at the board meeting of the 23rd of last month all the accusations levelled against Mr Rubinlicht were considered, and after a precise examination, in which we acquainted ourselves with all the material concerning the alleged sins, we came to the resolution:
a) that all the charges against Mr Rubinlicht are groundless and have no foundation whatsoever.
b) that in the very acts with which he is reproached, Mr Rubinlicht served the kehilla's interests faithfully and honestly, for which thanks and recognition are expressed to him.
c) that the whole campaign of malicious lies is an act of personal revenge by Mr Landner against Mr Rubinlicht, which aims to undermine the authority of the kehilla and to bring it to ruin and destruction, turning it into a place of strife and personal squabbles.
d) that the kehilla board declares its solidarity with Mr Rubinlicht regarding the accusations levelled against him, and takes upon itself the moral and legal responsibility for them.
The kehilla board in Będzin.
478
Statement concerning the „Rubinlicht“ affair

We, the undersigned board members of the Będzin Jewish kehilla, having acquainted ourselves at the kehilla office with the content of the communiqué, declare that the board as a whole has in no way declared solidarity with the conduct of Mr Rubinlicht, nor taken upon itself the responsibility for the acts of which he was accused at the council meeting of 26/7 this year.
At the board meeting mentioned in the communiqué, only his „good friends“ of the Agudah, with whom he now forms a majority after deserting the National-Progressive faction, declared solidarity with Mr Rubinlicht.
At the same time we declare that as long as the investigation commission, headed by the council chairman[?] Mr Landner, is not given the opportunity to investigate the accusations levelled against Mr Rubinlicht, it was altogether premature on the part of the board to pronounce on this matter and to adopt resolutions, and therefore we bear no responsibility whatsoever for them.
Jakob Neumark,
Moshe Manela,
Nachman Tenenberg,
Tsvi Strachlitz.
