Explanations of the Będzin Kehilla Council on the Budget for the Year 1936

[Będzin — kehilla; budget; rabbinate.] In the name of the kehilla council the chairman, Mr. Landauer[?], handed the starosta's office the following explanations on the budget.
Having acquainted itself with the administration's explanations regarding the budget, the council does not consider it sufficient and necessary to present its own arguments to justify the individual items of the budget.
1) As regards the income items, there is no difference whatsoever between the budget as projected by the council and by the administration.
2) The reduction to the extent of 10 per cent in the item "rabbinate" is justified[?] by the fact that the members of the rabbinate have, besides their fixed salaries, also side income, such as from weddings, divorces and the like, so that the side income amounts almost to as much as the salary.
3) As regards the striking out of the item for the son of Rabbi Lewin of blessed memory, the council, whose majority consists of representatives of progressive groups of Jewish society, has established that there was on its part no act of revenge whatsoever, as the administration insinuates, but that it was guided exclusively by public opinion. The council holds that a member of the rabbinate must be able, by his authority, to influence the broad masses as well as the youth, and must possess the necessary qualifications, religious as well as secular; and the son of Rabbi Lewin of blessed memory possesses no qualifications whatsoever — he does not even know the Polish language, which is necessary for carrying out the official duties of a member of the rabbinate; he therefore lacks the ability to represent the kehilla before the authorities.
Therefore the council could by no means agree with the position of the Agudah minority, which in this case was guided not by the good of Jewish society but by the hardened[?] policy of the Ger court, Ger — as is known — wishing to take over the Jewish communities by filling the rabbinical posts with its own people.
As an illustration of the bitterness that the engagement, under duress[?], of the son of Rabbi Lewin of blessed memory aroused in progressive Jewish society, the following fact may serve: on the day of the Rabbi's funeral the representatives of the Agudah demanded ultimatively that Mr. M. Lewin be engaged as a member of the rabbinate, threatening that in case of refusal they would not carry out the burial of the Rabbi of blessed memory. Because of the unpleasant situation thus created, the administration temporarily engaged Mr. M. Lewin.
Such conduct[?] aroused sharp agitation in society, and it delegated such respected citizens as Mr. Chaim Szajn, Mr. Szymon Fürstenberg, Mr. Mordechai Szajn and Mr. Rubinlicht, as president of the administration, at their head, to the Starosta to express a protest. The Starosta expressed his wish that, in order to calm tempers, Mr. M. Lewin should be a member of the rabbinate until the end of 1935. The administration, wishing to comply with the Starosta's wish, insisted on this, and the salary for Mr. Lewin was entered into the budget for the year 1935.
But when the council again set about drawing up the budget for the year 1936, it again took its earlier standpoint and, for the reasons already mentioned above, considered it right to strike out completely the item for Mr. M. Lewin.
As regards the administration's argument that the other members of the rabbinate are already people of advanced years and cannot properly carry out their functions, then, understandably, logically and consistently, one would have had to transfer them to emeritus status and engage young forces in their places, who would be better able to adapt to the demands of the present time. The administration does not proceed so because, as we have already mentioned, it takes no account at all of the actual state of affairs, but wants to continue an outdated system that still prevails in many communities.
To illustrate the council's objectivity, the following fact may serve: item 15 in section 9, for the support of Jewish emigrants from Poland, which is indisputably very important, was also reduced by the council, acting within its far-reaching economies, to 2,000 zł instead of the 5,000 zł projected by the administration.
Taking into account all the above-mentioned remarks, the council has the honour to request that the budget be approved according to the council's project, remarking that the introduction of any changes whatsoever in the budget might[?] infringe the rights of the council and undermine its authority vis-à-vis the administration.
We are sure that the supervisory authority will take the above-mentioned remarks into consideration and approve the budget according to the council's project.

In the Katowice Magistrate "Pure Aryans" Were "Manufactured"

[Katowice — court; forged "Aryan" papers.] These days an interesting trial concerning Jewish [?] racial purity took place at the Katowice district court.
In the dock sat: Stanisław Kwaśny, an official of the Katowice magistrate (city hall); Józef Kucz, owner of the film bureau "United Europe Film"; his wife Jadwiga; the clerk Walenta Słomiak; and the former magistrate official Wiktor Gawęda.
The story is as follows: in 1934 the German Jew Adolf Rosenblum of Berlin wanted to obtain there a concession for a company importing Polish films into Germany. But since only a racially pure Aryan can obtain such a concession, Rosenblum got in touch with Józef Kucz, who promised to supply him with an "authentic" document about his (Rosenblum's) pure-Aryan descent for the price of 6 thousand marks. Rosenblum agreed. Kucz then turned to the magistrate official Kwaśny to issue such a document for Rosenblum, and for this he promised him 1000 marks. Kwaśny issued a document in which it is officially confirmed that Rosenblum is a bricklayer by profession, of the Evangelical faith, and that in 1902 he married a woman, also an Aryan of the Evangelical faith.
Kwaśny sent this document to Kucz in a sealed envelope through the magistrate employee Gawęda. Kucz's wife Jadwiga took the document and gave the messenger in return a sealed envelope with 300 marks, instead of a thousand as had been agreed.
Rosenblum in Berlin, however, was not satisfied with the documents; he made a series of inquiries and then sent everything back to Katowice so that another document would be issued to him. He sent the letter to Kwaśny. Kwaśny then gave Kucz two blank forms to fill in, and Kwaśny was to add the signatures and seals. The forms were filled in by the clerk of "United Europe Film", Słomiak, with Gawęda dictating to her. Soon, however, the affair was discovered and all participants were charged in court.
After the speeches of the parties the verdict was pronounced, according to which Kwaśny was sentenced to 3 years' imprisonment and loss of rights for 10 years; Kucz and his wife — to 1 year's imprisonment, suspended for 5 years; Gawęda — to a year and a half's imprisonment with loss of rights for 10 years; Słomiak was acquitted.

Israel Silberschatz, of Blessed Memory

[Obituary — Dąbrowa and Katowice.] Untimely death has untimely carried off Israel Silberschatz, a Zionist and general Jewish communal worker, who had lived for many years in Dąbrowa and lately in Katowice.
The deceased belonged to the few maskilim — a conscious Zionist, a modern Jewish intellectual; he was active for our reconstruction fund, the "Keren Hayesod", for which he also subscribed fairly large sums.
Rabbi Chameides eulogised the esteemed deceased in warm words, praising his virtues and mentioning, among other things, his former devotion to Torah study before he began his struggle for a livelihood.
Jews of Dąbrowa and Zagłębie came in large numbers to accompany the deceased to his eternal rest.
Honour to his memory. May his soul be bound up in the bond of life.

Kehilla Hodgepodge.

[Zagłębie — kehilla elections; commentary.] The Będzin kehilla board has become "capable of work". — How Zagłębie is preparing for the new kehillas.

At a time when in almost all of Poland the kehillas have, as it were, come back to life, there is a bustle of preparations for the elections and every day brings other surprises, new "little flowers" — the town of Będzin, "a city and mother in Israel", the "luckiest" one, whose term of office has not yet ended, will have the opportunity to watch from afar how the new kehilla boards take shape and are born. Upon my life, it is a delight to sit off to one side and observe it all from behind the curtain.

Upon my life, it is a fine thing if one can stay passive [printed "pasiḥ"] towards the whole kehilla complex and play the role of a free listener, as if it were not us that is meant here. But if one regards the matter as ours, as our own property, which we must tend and spare, knowing that no blemish should come upon it — then we do not know what is better: the kehillas that have come back to life, or those that are still "static" [?], such as Będzin, for example.

And here we see how intensively [printed "intensiḥ"] the council and the board work. When it is a question of a more or less important matter, it is examined from all sides and "conscientiously", and only after a "thorough" understanding [?] do they begin to look at one another. It is therefore no wonder [?] that all the council sessions are so eagerly attended by the public and arouse so much interest in town, so much curiosity, that in town this is the topic of the day.

So at least naive people could think; people who do not know the town's circumstances would have believed, on attending a session, that our kehilla representatives are devoted body and soul to the community and are with all their heart set on the welfare of the Jewish members.

Yes, unfortunately, that is how it is from the left side; but when one tries to turn the page over to the right side, it becomes plainly evident that flattery and lies, intrigues and unheard-of frivolity play first fiddle here, and it is with these "logical arguments" that they operate and want to push everything through in this way.

And when a council session takes place, the gallery is full because one can have a very [?] good time there, and cheaply. A trifle — how well the public is entertained when one hears how one tells the other off [?], and, upon my life, one can curse there no worse than the "yurenes" [?, apparently market women] at the fish market. Connoisseurs even say that in the kehilla building people curse each other more sincerely and much more successfully, more aptly...

We in Zagłębie were afraid of the new kehilla elections; we knew what that bit of "work" smells of; we trembled at the thought of people tripping one another up and in the end washing their dirty linen in public, and soon — so we imagined — the antisemitic press would come and serve its readers the delicacies in little bits, on compote saucers, a little every day: see what light heads the "Zhidkes" [Polish slur for Jews] have, and so it is no wonder what they busy themselves with.

A heat simply came over us when we thought about what means people would want to use to get into the kehillas, and then the thoughts came: who knows whether we will not get even worse levies, whether they, the new representatives, will not bring us even more shame?

Now, as we watch what is going on in Będzin, it becomes easier for us, truly easier, because we see that there is nothing left to lose, that it cannot be worse than it is. Representatives — they are ours, and they do not understand how low they have fallen; we sent them as our emissaries into the kehillas and set them at the proper height, which they have degraded in an ugly way, and they have fallen down the mountain, and so they keep on desecrating Jewish honour and stop at nothing [?]; and if they say that they want to save Jewish honour, it is a lie — do not believe them, for had they wanted [?] it when it was time to act, they would not have lost themselves like this and dragged along with them, without mercy and without any sense of honour, everything that is called Jewish honour and pride, Jewish decency and modesty.

On all sides they operate from an egoistic standpoint, and small-minded partisanship decides. Let them at least not take the words honour and prestige into their mouths.

* * *

And in the other towns of Zagłębie they are already preparing for the elections; meetings and consultations take place, people make countless wholly and half watery speeches from which nothing comes out.

Thus in Sosnowiec they could not arrive at any unification, although there were various conceptions. Had each party only not wanted to stand higher than it is in reality, one could have found a modus that could have satisfied the parties, and one would not have got a profusion of lists, which will bring no honour, fame or integrity at all to Jewish Sosnowiec.

Quite certainly various plans and arrangements [?] will still come up, thanks to which the situation will have to be changed. Be that as it may, one should remember Jewish honour on every occasion; let it serve as a pillar of fire for the Jewish population of the town.

In Zawiercie they wanted [?] to manage to create unity, but the Aguda [Agudat Israel] realised that this was not so favourable for it, so efforts were made for the bloc to fall apart [?], so that in that place no more than 7 lists were obtained. It goes without saying that for such a moribund town as Zawiercie, the fragmentation will bring no great benefit to the Jewish population, and the quarrels and rifts that, God willing, will arise later will certainly bring no honour to Jewish honour either.

And Dąbrowa, the little town that supplies us at all times with the most bizarre sensations, did not lag behind in the kehilla elections either. Here it too prepared an astonishing surprise for us: it set about in earnest applying paragraph 20, and in this way it disqualified permanent residents. Is this not a newly invented piece of news, which only Dąbrowa could think up? Is this not an ugly stain of shame, which is simply outrageous [?]? And most interesting of all: the person in charge of the paragraph is none other than Mr. Bernard Rechnitz!

Yes, what Dąbrowa can still give us!

In Kielce, too, election fever has already begun, and here and there voices and opinions are heard about the future kehilla representation, towards which people are beginning to relate with attention and reverence.

It is gratifying to record that all the national groupings have united and are going to the forthcoming elections with a single list. Amid today's fragmentation and lawlessness this is a great plus, and the Jews of Kielce have thereby shown their maturity in the political and social field.

Diverse, then, will be the birth of the coming kehilla representations.

Selekt.
Once Again: Quick Aid for Zagłębie

[Będzin — municipality and health; article.] About a "pogotowie" [emergency ambulance service], quick rescue for Zagłębie, we have written more than once and pointed out how urgently it is needed. We have stressed [?] that Zagłębie is not some provincial little town where an accident happens once in a blue moon. This is a pulsating industrial region, where everything rushes and moves ever faster, and one thing chases the next without pause. We have victims from heavy industry, from small-scale manufacturing, from tram traffic, etc., so that very often the victims pay with their lives, because there is no quick rescue: one does not get the doctor, the medicine and the ambulance at the very minute.
But it is not enough that no progress is made in this field, that the question is lightly scoffed at — in the Zagłębie working district things are even going backwards.
Thus in the Będzin municipal bathhouse, which is administered by the Magistrat, there is no telephone. And when a woman fainted, she could easily have paid with her life, because it took too long until she was provided with medical help.
And it will be interesting when we add that the bathhouse used to be connected by telephone, and they went and economized and removed the telephone, by which a total of a few złoty a month is saved. It goes without saying that these few guilders play no role in the city's budget of millions — so what is being saved here? And on top of that people's lives are put at risk.
A bathhouse is, after all, an institution for the public, and it must absolutely be connected by telephone, and in this case the few złoty a telephone costs can play no role.
On the contrary, one must strive to speed up rescue in case of an accident, and not look to save a few złoty that are of the smallest significance in the municipal budget.
R. Les.
Melancholy (Leaves from a Friend's Diary)

[Literature — sketch; diary leaves.] By P. Blumenkranz (Częstochowa).
(Leaves from a friend's diary.)

Evening at home. A twilight like all the others — the kind that bore simple people and are sung [?] by poets.
I stand at the window and stare at the bloody ball of the sky opposite. I look, not knowing at what or why. One thing only I feel with all my limbs: that I am strangely melancholy and oddly heavy at heart.
I feel as if everything in me wanted to burst into lament, as if everything in me wanted to howl, like a stray dog late at night.
I don't know what to do with myself. I begin to circle the room — once, twice, three times, ten — until I grow tired and stop, as if lost, in the middle of the room; my gaze wanders over the [dusty?] walls and halts at something crawling that has come down from a crack in the wall and is strolling up toward the beam. It seems to me as if I had just squashed this little creature with my fingers, and a strange smell reaches me — the bedbug stench comes from me myself, from my whole existence.
I approach the window again: a crowd of children are playing noisily, with laughter and crying; romping, falling, scuffling [?], weeping, and then at once beginning to laugh through their tears. They twist their little mouths to cry and immediately burst out laughing, childishly, heartily, without any "why".
And a thought — perhaps a clever one, perhaps a foolish one — pecks its way out of this picture and demands: you fool, son of Pikwalk [?], what are you gnawing yourself for? Who told you a tale that in everything one must find a meaning? Who talked you into the business of mending the world? Play hide-and-seek for grown-ups too, and it will go well with you!
But the melancholy does not heed the advice [?]; it makes itself comfortable and lies down on my heart. I find it hard to breathe, like an asthmatic; at this moment I want to hide, to bend my head down somewhere and lie, think nothing, do nothing, only lie long, long, and never get up again...
So I think — and do the opposite: I run quickly out into the street. I want to look at the thousands of smiling faces of the young people, at the shine of their laughing eyes, and become "infected" by it all. "Perhaps — I think — their carefreeness will influence me, cheer me up."
But once in the street I feel lonely and forsaken. The noise oppresses me. I try to avoid the laughing glances, I "lean" against the wall and "ponder":
— And perhaps my present feeling is a consequence of my isolated life? Surely I am going down a bad road, for by turning away from people you lose every pleasure [?] in life.
Therefore:
— The best way — so I persuade myself [?] — is public work; attaining honour, you forget your broodings and are swept along by the stream of life. And how? Simply: clown around with everybody, spin along with them and swindle along with them.
And now it seems to me that I have found a means of forgetting, but my refined grandfathers, who would not go to sleep as long as the last grosz had not been distributed among the poor, do not let me throw myself into this [—] character, and my cursed conscience, also an inheritance from those same world-mending grandfathers, cries out in me:
— If it's forgetting yourself, if it's relief you want — far better brandy, better women, and not some [self-important?] pseudo-public-spiritedness: through the first you may perhaps even be purified, but through the second you will creep off to the place of which it is said "none that go unto her return" [Prov. 2:19].
But the lust for life rebels further and argues:
— Life is hard, heavy and tormenting. One must push one's way through with one's elbows, crookedly, and the "article" [?] conscience is already outdated; and on the other hand: who needs an inherited conscience? Should one not crown with a lofty name everything that makes it more comfortable and easier for us to push through the few years in this little world, created once out of boredom?
So the thoughts tangle themselves into a ball inside me as I drag myself along the city walls.
— Idzie pan do kina? ["Are you going to the cinema, sir?" — in Polish]
So asks a girl who has noticed me after all. A girl of my age, also unmarried. Both of us, by the way, wander about without "a corner of our own" for "almost" the same reasons: I because I did not look, and she because she looked too much.
Now she wants to go to the cinema, and specifically with a man, because her girlfriend may also be there with her fiancé.
I say:
— Unfortunately I'm not going.
She asks:
— Why? It's a beautiful picture, after all.
— I have no time.
— How so [?], you're out strolling!
— One can stroll and be busy.
With a discreet grimace she purses her too heavily painted lips, throws me a contemptuous look, as if to say: invite a scab-head to a minyan... — and tosses at me:
— Well, do widzenia! [goodbye]
— Do widzenia...
And I am alone with myself again, hurry home so as not to meet a second girl, and my contrarian head goes on interpreting:
— The small, seemingly insignificant episode with the girl shows that because of your "over-cleverness" you have missed out on life. When she invited you, you should have gone; and when she talked about Gable's sweetness, you should have added that she, the old maid, surpasses F. Gaal [Franciska Gaal] in charm, even if it would have been somewhat exaggerated.
You will be worn down by your seriousness. You were always pondering how to live, until old age began to dwell in your heart.
* * *
I am lying at home again. Pitch dark. From the street lamp a patch of light falls on the table and thereby enlarges the surrounding darkness. The melancholy gnaws, bites, torments. Perhaps I should take to writing and so possibly [?] relieve the tormenting sorrow?
I take the pen in hand. But precisely at this minute I feel how spiritually drained [?] I am. My whole self laments into the mute darkness, laments without words, like a mute who wants to bring forth a few sounds and cannot. I drop my exhausted head onto my hands, like a Jew at his supplications, and from within comes a cry without lips, the cry of an abandoned child:
— Mama!...
On the Road to the New Kehilla

[Sosnowiec — kehilla; kehilla elections; opinion piece.]
In the present article we intend to deal with the question of why the so-called professional intelligentsia of Sosnowiec has given up on the kehilla.
— What for, to what end, and with whom?
So an old communal worker, who devoted long years to the work of the kehilla, asks us:
— What do you think about "the new kehilla elections"?
— I don't think about the kehilla at all... the work there is a waste. I have more important places to apply my energy.
And a young activist of a popular Jewish organisation answers us:
— My organisation wants to take part in the elections, and it demands my candidacy in first place. But I have no desire to sit in the kehilla...
It is possible that this organisation, because of the attitude of its chairman, will not put up a list at all.
The more prominent communal figures in Sosnowiec are all but offended if one talks about their candidacies for the kehilla.
— What, do you think I've gone mad?!...
That, more or less, is how the situation looks when one speaks of popular individuals, in whom no town is rich.
———
How does it look among the parties?
There too every more prominent activist would like the kehilla mandate to be taken by his... comrade; he himself forgoes the pleasure. For the time being, however, things have not yet reached the candidates, only the question: who with whom?
Zionists? That has already become too general a notion. Which Zionists? "Al ha-Mishmar", "Et Livnot", "Mizrachi", Revisionists, the League for Labour Palestine. The fool [?] may react to this with a smile, yet it is a fact that the Zionist family has become enormously [?] differentiated, and each group is more concerned that its opponent [?] from the same family should not survive than with the interests of the kehilla. At the meetings of these separate groups you will hear talk about this and that, but not about the need truly to care for the authority and the content of the kehilla.
The "Agudah"?
The Orthodox of old used to knock on the doors of people who amounted to something, understood something and knew something; they called them into the kehilla even though they were without beards, without sidelocks and even a little bit Sabbath-breakers..
The "Agudah", however, has thrown out a slogan of the sort "stai da stega pa staie" [?], and so a kapote and a hat have become enough to become a dozor [kehilla board member] in Israel.
Right Poale Zion and Left P.Z. — these are parties that tremble for their own house; what they have in mind is to save their mandate, and they cannot think about the kehilla.
———
So an open and free field has been left, and whoever feels like it can play at kehilla elections.
Already now 10–12 lists have been announced.
It would also be worth taking a stroll through the Hasidic shtiblekh; for lack of space we put it off to another time.
To some it may seem that we exaggerate; we assure you that reality is far sadder.
A frightful, terrible and destructive invasion of the kehilla is in preparation!
———
We asked a very experienced party activist:
— What do you intend to do to check this invasion?
— We will make combined (bloc) lists..
— With whom?
— With these very wild lists.
No party can count on a larger number of mandates. And joining up with opposing parties is, after all, not possible.
Instead, one can exploit the clause in the electoral regulations that allows combined lists: grab half a dozen [?] with lists and attach them to oneself; one may sometimes be lucky and win their "remainders", and if somebody from among them does slip into the kehilla, one can later use him in certain votes — for a rabbi, for a shochet, for this or that subsidy.
Did the last kehilla council not give us examples enough?
———
The kehilla must on no account become a refuge for all sorts of fools, troublemakers [?], good-for-nothings, coarse ruffians, lawless people and seekers of a roll with fish!
Let us not smear our own faces with soot with our own hands!
The kehilla is the central institution of Jewish life, the only Jewish institution in Poland under public law, the representation of all Polish Jewry.
Even the "Bund" has finally decided to re-enter the kehilla. No Jewish institution can boast that all strata and groups of the Jewish population are actually represented in it. The kehillot in Poland should serve as a model for Jewish communities in other centres all over the world. We cannot know at all what role our kehillot will be called upon to play in our present living conditions, in today's political reality.
The healthiest, the best and the most active elements of the Jewish street must be concentrated in the kehilla.
All the unqualified persons and cliques who bring with them corruption, venality, lawlessness, boorishness and ugliness must find the doors of the kehilla shut!
How can this be done?
The Jewish street is not so sick, the Jewish masses are not so lawless and benighted — they will find the way.
For our part, we shall not fail to light the way.
Y. N-baum.
A Little Feuilleton — Dachas

"I" and "She".
I know, the reader hates old topics...
I knew a Jew, an Orthodox one at that, who once told me that apart from old wine he has no use for anything old.
I take, of course, a great responsibility upon myself when I write about dachas [summer cottages]...
Who has not yet written about the dachas of the Diaspora? The immortal Sholem Aleichem, the mortal Der Tunkeler [Yosef Tunkel] — may he live long (with us, after all, one usually becomes immortal only after death) — and even I, a simple living man — what have I to do with mortality and immortality? — have also written many times about dachas and their attributes. And yet I am writing once more about this threadbare topic, for a simple reason.
One night, at a dacha in Olkusz, I held a conversation with a creature whose name I shall tell you later; for now I shall simply call her "She".
The conversation turned on various topics.
I: Who are you, that you dare to rob me of my sleep?
She: I am a great lover of people, I adore the human body. On the other hand I hate everything that smells of spirit...
I: Fine, but what do you want of me?
She: First of all I ask you to conduct your conversation with me in the dark. I have no use for any light. In the light everything becomes too real, and I love a person when he is sunk in sleep, when he moves over into the world of dreams.
I: What do you demand of me?
She: I do not want your soul, God forbid... I lay no claim to your heart. I am not one of those who love to conquer foreign bodies by storm; no, I go about slowly and almost always reach my goal. True, people often disturb my pleasures, but I make do with little... a couple of minutes are enough for me. Afterwards they may curse me, revile me, drag me through the mud — it bothers me very little.
I: (suddenly feeling a bite, I start up from sleep and see a... bedbug) What, it was with you that I talked in my sleep?
She: Yes! But I am not one of the ordinary bedbugs... I belong only to those bedbugs about which Sholem Aleichem, of blessed memory, once wrote...
Rebus.
Our Panorama.

[Zagłębie — kehilla elections; weekly satirical feuilleton.] (The world goes on its way. — Nothing has changed. — Boaz of the Book of Ruth and Boaz of Strzemieszyce. — Paragraph 20 has come back to life. — Police escort a gabbai from the shtibl. — The "Kiddush Hashem" in the Dąbrowa synagogue — not allowed to speak. — Building materials instead of money. — A "shishi" for packs of roofing felt.)

The Jewish street — so we thought — is so sick, so broken by the blows we[?] receive from all sides, that interest in the coming kehilla elections would be like interest in last year's snow. It turns out, however, that we were greatly mistaken: the world goes on its way, the same chase after mandates as before. The same fight, and above all — lawlessness and demoralisation march at the head of the contending sides...

The first "victory", which in our opinion deserves to be immortalised in the "History of Paragraph 20", was won in the holy community of Strzemieszyce.

The "hero" of the story is a well-known personality and bears the same name as the main figure of the Book of Ruth... The only difference is that once the same man said "Go not to glean in another field" — you shall not go gathering in a strange field — whereas the Strzemieszyce man does the opposite: he drinks wine from other people's gardens and makes use of other people's paragraphs...

And when the kehilla elections approached, this same man and his friends studied section 20 of the election regulations, "and found it written" — they found written there that every voter is like clay in the potter's hand, whether he has the right to vote or not. If so, why should those who are not loyal to the rabbi and to the free-loan fund have the right to vote — how can that be? And indeed the election commission ruled that "the Zagderisn[?] shall not enter the congregation" and took away the vote from some 120 kehilla-tax payers ("etat-payers").

When the "living dead" learned of the verdict, "popular wrath" awoke in them and they went out to fight.

"The people" wanted to make the first "attack" on the "superior-man"[?] hero as he would be walking home from the shtibl on Shabbat, but it did not succeed, because his wife, having received secret information that an attempt on her husband's life was being prepared, reported it to the police station, from where 2 guards were sent, who escorted the fine Jew home from the shtibl.

—

In Dąbrowa "Paragraph 20" did not hold such great sway, because, firstly, the chairman of the election commission in Dąbrowa is no Ger Hasid... and secondly, in Dąbrowa "culture" is in general more developed than in Strzemieszyce.

The proof of this is the "Kiddush Hashem" that took place last Shabbat in the Dąbrowa synagogue.

And this is how it happened: among the patrons of the synagogue in the town of Dąbrowa the idea was born that the synagogue as such should come out in the coming kehilla elections with a list of its own. To tell the truth, this is a very "logical" idea: why should all the little societies and party kloyzn go with separate lists and the synagogue worshippers not? Especially since, after all, the gmina (kehilla) is nothing more than a religious institution — so who is the closer in-law, the synagogue or, l'havdil, the "Bund"?..

So the shammes announced and proclaimed to the synagogue worshippers that at 4 o'clock in the afternoon the public should come into the synagogue, where they would be taught a chapter on elections.

But woe to the ears that hear such things, woe to the ears that do not want to listen to such matters. Something that has a broad[?] effect on both body and soul — and they began to make a racket and a din until the speakers left the bimah...

Evil tongues even say that this "piece of work" stems from the united "shtreimel guild"... But be that as it may, thanks to the kehilla elections it came to a "Kiddush Hashem" in the synagogue in the town of Dąbrowa.

—

In the Sochaczew shtibl (number 2) in Będzin the gabbaim have introduced a system that will undoubtedly arouse tremendous interest in the Jewish world. Namely, the hitherto personal system of pledging money when called up to the Torah has been abolished. The gabbaim, being very practical people, proceed from the standpoint that money is in general a superfluous thing in the world and "sakvitirt"[?] only to lead mankind astray from the straight path... and they have introduced pledges in kind: for example, instead of one złoty the person called to the Torah shall pledge a towel, a bucket, and for larger sums other things that can be useful for the "shtibl".

Apart from that, exceptions are made for aliyot, since one cannot compare the value of a "revi'i" with a "shlishi" or a "shishi"; so the gabbaim indeed gave the "fat" aliyot to those who declared they would give "bigger" things. Among them there was also a craftsman, a tinsmith, who for the "shishi" for the whole year promised to cover the shtibl roof with roofing felt.

The transaction was made, but when the concessionaire had snatched a few "shishis", he said: Stop! "I forgo the shishis and I'm not covering the roof"...

As we are informed, the gabbaim are not at all discouraged by the tinsmith having returned the "package"; on the contrary, they are sure that "the great world" will welcome their economic plan with open arms...

Ben Amotz.
Our Youth at the Summer Colonies.

[Zagłębie — youth; summer colonies.]
The train pulls away from dusty, smoke-blackened Zagłębie, and in the course of a few hours it brings itself into the beautiful Beskidy region.
Seeing the beautifully overgrown mountains, one is reminded of the mountains of the Land of Israel, which once also looked finer, being covered with vineyards and olive trees, and today strike one with dread by their nakedness and desolation... And the pain is greater still when one remembers how the Arabs are still today destroying thousands of trees which our brothers planted and tended with so much effort, hoping [?] thereby to erase step by step the traces of the two-thousand-year-old destruction...
At the Jeleśnia station we are surrounded by local inhabitants who beg us to rent lodgings from them on the best terms. They wonder where the former crowds of guests from Zagłębie are, who used to be gladly exploited by them; and now it is already almost the end of summer and one sees only single individuals, who look as if they had lost their way in the region...
— Has there been an antisemitic incident in your village yet? — we ask our landlord.
— No — he answers — and especially now certainly not, because the village head [wójt] called the whole village together a few weeks ago and said that he demands that peace and order reign, as always, and that nobody dare insult anyone, because it is not nice for our face to be blackened in the newspapers, as happened in other villages; and besides, we would also suffer materially, because nobody would want to come sniffing around here — so the wójt said — and he immediately ordered notices to be posted throughout the village to the same effect.
In the evening we hear singing of familiar motifs [?] that carries over the whole village.
— That is from the colonies — our host explains — there are many Jewish young people here in the colonies and they feel very good, and it is homely with them; they dance and sing for whole days...
The next morning we paid a visit to the "colonists". Already from afar one sees three blue-and-white flags fluttering on high, a sign that three colonies are located here together.
Our first visit is to the colony of "Chashomer Chadati" [sic, for "HaShomer HaDati"], which occupies several large buildings and in which there are up to 150 members, boys and girls, from Zagłębie, Kraków, Katowice and other places.
The "begringer" [?] members of the leadership take me around the rooms, show me their "inventory" and arrangements, and gladly inform me about the life and situation of the colony, from which one can see that the young people truly feel good and at home here, although they do not have all the comforts and have to do the "black" kitchen work themselves.
Besides this they are also busy with cultural work, such as talks on literature, Zionism, etc.
— What are the relations like between your colony and the other, neighbouring colonies of "HaNoar HaTsiyoni"? — I ask them.
— Until now the relations have been very friendly, but in the last few days they have become somewhat strained because of a flag which we managed to take from them; and in a scout organization that counts as a defeat, especially when it came to them from "Chashomer Chadati", which "HaNoar HaTsiyoni" regarded as idlers in the laws of scouting, and here suddenly they display such "heroism" as to "rob" a flag...
— But I did see a flag hanging at "HaNoar"? How did that happen? — we ask the leaders.
— They did that illegally, because according to the rules of scouting they must redeem the "captured flag", and indeed they turned to us with an inquiry about redeeming their flag, but after we demanded twenty złoty from them for the "Keren Kayemet", they gave up and hung out a new flag... Since that incident we have to reinforce the guards every night, because "HaNoar" no longer leaves us in peace and organizes frequent night raids on our colony — but without success..
— one of them exclaims in triumph...
Afterwards we go to the colony of "HaNoar". The colony was divided into two parts, in which there are only young people from Zagłębie.
During the conversation the dispute over the seized flag immediately surfaces, and complaints are heard that the seizure was not legal, and they promptly show me their "vak-reib" [?], which they seized from "Chashomer Chadati" during a night raid...
One thing is worth noting: on the Sabbath complete peace reigned between the camps, and "HaNoar" came to pray in the "Shomer HaDati" colony, and all the points of dispute were forgotten!... Such is the power of the Sabbath angels of peace!..
At the third Sabbath meal (shalosh seudos) very fine "Oneg Shabbat" talks and singing were held in all the "colonies".
The colony of the Katowice community.
Here there is also a charitable colony of the Katowice kehilla, in a green, splendid building, which has been divided into three turnuses (shifts) of one month each; and the children, boys and girls, of needy Katowice parents enjoy every good thing here and are under good, tender supervision in all respects, both in the religious sense and in the hygienic sense.
From time to time the children are visited by representatives of the Katowice kehilla, who spend time with them very merrily and leave them fine gifts.
"Plug" [?], the Katowice kehilla distinguishes itself very well in this respect — would that the same were said of the Będzin kehilla!
The instructors' colony of "HaShomer HaDati".
In the last few days a new colony has opened here for instructors (madrichim) of the "HaShomer HaDati" movement, in which the older youth from all of Poland are gathered, numbering 130 members, boys and girls.
Our Zagłębie is also nicely represented here by a large number of conscious young people of both sexes.
I attended some of their talks and lectures here, and I must add that they stand at a very high level, and it is worth watching with what interest the lectures on psychology, pedagogy, Zionism, literature, scouting and history are listened to and discussed [?]. After each lecture a broad discussion develops in the Hebrew, Yiddish and Polish languages, from which one can observe a joyful phenomenon: that the Jewish religious youth has entered a renaissance epoch and that it will accomplish much for the Land of Israel and the Jewish people, and therefore they deserve that Jewish society should take more interest in them and pay them greater attention.
Elchanan Zyder.
Since When Have Paper and the Eraser Been in Use?

[Science and culture — history of paper and the eraser.] By Z. Haber, Vienna.

In very ancient times people wrote on papyrus leaves; these are large leaves that last a long time, on which one would scratch with a stylus everything one wished to say. Later, parchment was used. Our holy scriptures are written to this day on parchment, which never spoils and never tears.

When did people begin to write on paper? That is not known exactly. Chinese cultural researchers maintain that 1,900 years ago paper-making from bamboo was already known in China. Whether the Chinese really were already making paper then, there is no document whatsoever. Only from the year 1751 do we know that the Arabs took over from the Chinese the secret of making paper, but we do not know this either — whether the Arabs really began making paper at that time.

Only in the year 1228 did Emperor Frederick begin to write on paper. A document of his has been preserved and is in the Paris Louvre. It appears, however, that paper was very expensive and could not be introduced into daily use. For years people still wrote on parchment, and paper was used only in royal palaces for various documents or for letters between kingdom and kingdom.

Only at the beginning of the 15th century did people begin trading in paper at the Leipzig fair. At first, however, business did not go well, for only around 1480 did larger quantities of paper begin to be sold, and only then did it begin to become an article of common use.

Since when do we know of the eraser? Until 170 years ago it was customary to write again on paper that was no longer needed. Paper was expensive, so people would scrape old written papers with a sharp little knife, smear white paint over them and then write on them again.

In the year 1720 people tried to rub out written paper with soft bread.

Only in the year 1760 did the English chemist Priestley begin to make rubber from caoutchouc, but it did not occur to him to introduce rubber into trade and to let it be used to erase written things. In the year 1770 his pupil Magellan ("Megeles") of Portugal began to introduce Priestley's eraser into trade and passed it off as his own invention. In the year 1775 erasers were brought for the first time to the Leipzig fair, and they were to be sold under the name "black skin".

The prices, however, were so high that in the first years not a single piece could be sold.

Only much later, already in the 19th century, did people begin to make erasers more cheaply, until they became an article of common use without which one cannot manage at all today.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Ekev)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Ekev

a) "And He afflicted you, and let you hunger, and fed you with manna" (8:3)
"From here [we learn] the lighting of candles on the Sabbath." — Midrash Peli'a.
A witty interpretation:
The verse seems strange: what sort of affliction and hunger is it to eat manna? But the Gemara says in Yoma: "One who has a meal should eat it only by daylight." For seeing what one eats satisfies in a certain sense, and therefore the manna did not satisfy, since one only felt in it the taste of food but did not see it; and since the verse calls this an affliction, the lighting of candles necessarily follows: that when eating there must be light, that one must see what one eats... — Kometz ha-Minha.

b) "Your garment did not wear out upon you" (Deut. 4 [sic])
The Gemara says in tractate Shabbat: "Why are the Torah scholars of Babylonia distinguished [in dress]? Because they are not men of Torah." In Berakhot, folio 6, it is said: "The clothes of the rabbis that wear out — it is from the demons' rubbing": the demons rub against the clothes of the Torah scholars out of envy of their Torah, and therefore their clothes become rotten[?] and torn. That is why the Gemara asks: why are the Torah scholars of Babylonia distinguished — why do the Torah scholars of Babylonia dress so splendidly and elegantly? And the answer is "because they are not men of Torah": since they cannot study, the demons do not envy them and do not tear their clothes... — R' Tzvi Hirsch Weliger[?].

• • •

When the Rebbe R' Shmelke of Nikolsburg [Mikulov] was in Berlin, the maskilim conducted a debate with him about the Polish Jews and wanted to prove that two things clearly set the German Jew apart from the Polish one: the former dresses cleanly, decently, and tells no lies, whereas the latter goes about ragged and slovenly and is, on top of that, a liar and a thief.
Said Rebbe R' Shmelke to him[?]:
The two things are especially bound up with each other, for R' Pinchas ben Yair enumerates (Sotah, folio 49b) ten things that come from cleanliness: cleanliness leads to purity, leads to abstinence, and so on, up to the holy spirit. So cleanliness, purity, leads to all those great things.
Therefore the evil inclination does not let the Polish Jew get to cleanliness, to purity, at all, fearing that it will bring him to those great levels, up to the holy spirit. The Polish Jew may promise the evil inclination that he will go no further than cleanliness — it does not believe him; after all, he is a liar...
Whereas[?] the German Jews, who are such[?] truthful people — the evil inclination does not stop them from holding to the first level of cleanliness, knowing that they are honest people, and once they have given it, the evil inclination, their hand, they will not do otherwise and will keep to it...

c) "As a man chastens his son" (Deut. 8)
The Rabbi of Ostrowiec was once asked: where does it come from that even the worst father has a warm attitude toward a child, while there are children who are cruel toward their parents?
He answered:
— As is known, all human feelings are inherited from the previous generations, all the way back to Adam. Now, Adam had children and had toward them, as a father, a fatherly feeling; but he had no father, and the feeling toward a father remained alien to him. Hence among people the feeling toward a son is more developed than toward a father...

d) "And your silver and gold is multiplied, and all that you have is multiplied" (ibid., 13)
Pride always comes to a person from satiety, from being full: "His belly is full — [he does] all kinds of evil." But with money a person is never full: "No man dies with even half his desire in his hand." So where does pride over wealth come from?
The thing is that every rich man, although he always lacks more than he needs, is nevertheless sure, so sure, that he will attain what he lacks... "They that trust in their wealth and boast in the multitude of their riches." Although every magnate actually possesses only half... he trusts that he will attain the rest: "and your silver and gold is multiplied, and all that you have is multiplied" — he is sure of it, and therefore: "then your heart be lifted up, and you forget." — Panim Yafot.

e) "And takes no bribe" (10:17)
"To appease Him with money." — Rashi.
That is: God cannot be bought off with charity; that is a bribe, and God takes no bribe... — Leket Amarim.

f) "And to serve Him with all your heart" (11:13)
"What is service of the heart? — That is prayer." — Rashi.
The Hatam Sofer used to pray at length. One of his disciples asked him: Rabbi, wouldn't it be more fitting to shorten the prayer and in that time rather study Gemara with Tosafot?
The Hatam Sofer answered him:
The Gemara says: "Whoever prolongs his prayer, his days and years are prolonged." So, by praying longer I will live longer and manage to make up the few delayed pages of Gemara with Tosafot.
Don't Worry, Brother!

"Der Kokh-Lefl" (The Ladle) — Humour and Satire — compiled by Amutzli.

Don't worry, brother,
don't be a fool,
for worries
bring sorrow.

True indeed,
you have no money,
and what you need
you lack.

Your wife keeps
demanding of you —
chic, a little dress
on her body.

Daughters ripe
for the market,
they lie heavy
on your neck.

Grown sons
with diplomas —
neither here
nor there.

Your heart is
deeply wounded,
you're already signing up
for "Aid".

You wait
for an answer —
they tell you
you have a house.

Ah, the tenants
don't pay:
the house is threatened
with a deficit.

You'd sell
the property,
but there's no such fool[?]
nowadays[?].

Yet worrying can
do no good,
except to make
your heart weak.
