Chatzkele Kalbonik on the Danzig Affair

I heard something[?] ... I got[?] ... I've become so hoarse. You know from what? From shouting "Precz!" [Down with!]
Oy, what can I tell you, that day[?] I shouted "Precz" and "Precz" again. "Precz z hakenkreuzers" [Down with the swastika men] — that's what I shouted.
Right after noon I went to the Ratusz [town hall], took my stand among the ...[?], and when I heard the first "Precz", I stuck my hands in my trouser pockets and let out a yell:
— Precz, cholera, psiakrew! [Polish curse]
How they thought they'd ...[?] smoothly; the Germans thought they'd snatch Danzig for nothing — not with me around! If need be I'll put on[?] hobnailed boots, and I'll tell the eldest of the heroes[?] ... [?].
How they go to take away my sea — may a misfortune come upon them!
When I heard the speeches at the Ratusz, I badly wanted to get up on the platform and tell the Germans the honest truth, but they wouldn't let me, because they said I was too hot-headed[?], that they were afraid of my tongue. Had it happened at our place on the "Zhimne"[?], I'd have [given it to them] properly, like to the Kaiser[?]; and since it happened at the Ratusz, I bit my lips and kept quiet[?]; but when they shouted "Precz", I too shouted with all my might, though I had no[?] access to the Germans.
I still wanted to say something very important, but I'm hoarse, and ...[?] with the paper.
I wish you a good Shabbos, and stay healthy.
The Importance of Eating Fattened Geese... In Place of a Speech by a Kehilla Commissioner, Copied Word for Word.

Gentlemen! Since my rule is coming to its end (unless, so to speak, things[?] happen beyond the course of nature, dina de-malkhuta dina [the law of the land is the law]...), I have come — I have come to hand over to you, and you shall tell it to your children and children's children, what I achieved during my rule as Commissioner, may his glory be exalted.
That I saw to it that you should eat kosher calves' feet — that you already know from my sermons and written articles. But do you also know that for the fat goose legs you have been relishing you have me to thank as well? On the contrary, show me a single kehilla president in Zagłębie who would set up a goose-fattening farm so that the gourmands[?] could enjoy fat fattened geese?... And not only fattened, but the geese also carry a great hekhsher [kashrut certificate] — even my friends of "Zerushanr"[?], who are punctilious about the slightest crumb of hametz, eat the geese too...
Unfortunately the public does not appreciate my good deeds; they are obstinate, disloyal[?] and don't want to pay the levy [etat]. Therefore I turn to you for the last time — "Cast us not off in old age" — don't let me fall, bring the "mastnik"[?] into every[!] kehilla, and by this merit I may perhaps yet be elected to the new kehilla administration, amen.
Serenade of a Straw Widower

Come, my dear, into my arms,
let me kiss your throat and nape;
have no fear of my shrew [wife],
she surely won't catch us...
She, my plague, is far from here,
she too is "having fun" [bawi się] very[?] nicely,
let's not waste[?] the time —
every minute is a pity..
K—r.
From the Election Fair.

"Der Kokh-Lefl" has managed to intercept the correspondence of a certain political organization. We print the little letters verbatim:
1. To the Zionist Organization.
On behalf of the executive of our party, we propose that you take us into your bloc.
Of the 14 mandates we demand only about ten places; the remaining mandates you may keep for yourselves.
We hope that with us you will get through easily; the programme is a side matter.
With Zionist greetings, for our party,
Berl Benkel.
2. To the "Agudah".
Being unable to come to terms[?] with the Zionists, who are heretics and suspect in religion[?], I turn to you with a proposal to unite[?] for the elections. If you demand it, I can stand on the religious standpoint, on the foundation of the Torah and tradition.
With the blessing of the Torah, for our party,
Berl Benkel.
3. To the Left Poale Zion.
Honoured comrades!
Not wishing to unite with the Jewish bourgeoisie, I turn to you concerning a united electoral bloc of the Left Poale Zion with our organization.
If you demand it, I can stand on the standpoint of merciless[?] class struggle.
With revolutionary greetings, for our party,
Berl Benkel.
Note by "Kokh-Lefl":
The remaining letters, to the Right Poale Zion and to the porters, as well as the name of the said party, we cannot publish for reasons beyond our control.
The Election Campaign — In Place of a Leading Article.

For corns one gets an ointment; better to soak them and cut them out.
For toothache it is good to apply a fig with pepper; the most radical remedy is — the dentist's pliers.
"Meridn" [haemorrhoids] is a disease just like all other diseases. Whoever suffers from this ailment must turn to a doctor, but not to a doctor of philosophy.
To the reader:
Here there was actually meant to be an election article about this and that, but as soon as he dipped his pen the author remembered that elections are coming — and began to talk about... haemorrhoids.
—o—
Love and Dinner!
Wife (to her husband): Apart from love there is nothing in the world.
Husband: You're right, my little wife, but what's new regarding a bit of dinner?
Return of a Lost Article.

In the premises of the Jewish kehilla in Będzin (3 Maja Square 4) the Zionist declaration of the kehilla president has been lost.
Honest finders are asked to hand it in, against a good reward, to the vice-president of the kehilla council.
In the Tangle of Life

[Serialized novel — Vienna, Bern, Kraków; installment 5.]
(A novel of dramatic events in Kraków, Zawiercie and New York) 5)

Nechama now cautiously explained to Dodl that it was not right for them to stay in Vienna. They could no longer study here at the same university, because it could lead to unpleasantness. She therefore persuaded him that they should go away to Switzerland, where they would be able to go on studying undisturbed; there they would both begin to study medicine and later work together.
Dodl liked this, and they went off to Switzerland and settled in Bern; there they at once enrolled at the university.
In Bern Dodl tried to get lessons in Hebrew; Nechama, for her part, knew how to make lace, so she took on work stitching lace and earned a little by it. They studied together, struggled together, worked, and went hungry too.
So a stretch of time went by.
The students here also had a students' fund, and Nechama became the official [?] with whom money for the students' fund is deposited.
The president of the fund was a student whom everyone called by his first name, "Bernard".
He was tall, dark-haired and very likeable. He had rich parents in Kyiv, who sent him a lot of money; his father had been willing to spend a great deal of money so that he could study at Kyiv University, where in Tsarist times there were restrictions on Jews, but for all his efforts he did not succeed, and so he sent Bernard off to Switzerland.
Bernard often gave handsome sums to the students' fund, and he also worked energetically to get other students to give for this purpose. Since Nechama took a great interest in the fund, the two of them were therefore often seen together. Every time some student event was being prepared, both of them were very active and were always seen together.
This even vexed Dodl a little; several times he even asked her about it in a mild tone, but Nechama made fun of it; she never gave him a direct answer, she only said:
"Trust me and don't ask me!"
Once she went off to a students' ball. Dodl wanted to go too, but he was very tired. So she went alone, and came home very late, around 4 o'clock before dawn, a little tipsy. She said something then about how they had kissed. The next morning he questioned her about what she had meant by the words "he kissed her and she him", and she said that it was nothing; she had been a little drunk and so had talked nonsense.
But later this is what happened:
Dodl came home in the evening, and his little daughter Etta [?] was very glad to see him and said to him:
"Papa, Uncle Bernard was here, he brought me chocolate, he kissed me, and Mama too! He is so nice."
Dodl stood rooted to the spot, as if he had been hit on the head with a stone.
"What is going on here?" he asked Nechama.
"I don't have to give you any explanation at all," she answered proudly.
"You can do whatever you like?"
"Yes," she answered.
"And I too?" he asked.
"Certainly."
"If so, I want a divorce [get]."
"You can have it!"
"When?"
"Whenever you want."
"Tomorrow?"
"Let it be tomorrow!"
They said nothing more. In the morning Dodl went to the rabbi and told him that he wanted to divorce his wife; she was sent for, and within an hour they were divorced [printed "again"?].
When Nechama now came home, Bernard was already waiting for her; he knew nothing of all this. She walked past him and went into her room. Soon a desperate groaning was heard from there; he ran in. An empty little bottle of iodine lay beside her [?], and her lips were black as coal. He raised an alarm and she was revived; afterwards she lay seriously ill. For two weeks Bernard did not leave her bedside; he showered money, called in the best doctors, and she was put back on her feet. But she had taken too large a dose, and her health as well as her looks were no longer what they had been before.
Dodl now conceived the idea of going to America. Right after the divorce he got on the train and went off to Vienna; he was drawn to see Selma and the child before he left.
When he arrived in Vienna he let Selma know about it and asked her whether she wanted to see him. She was very glad and answered him at once that she did.
He went to see her.
Selma justified herself to him for what she had done; she explained to him that she was a socialist and a freethinker and did not hold with the old ways. Only under the influence of her fanatical brother and her mother had she then, when she was in a nervous state, acted hysterically; but that was over now, and she begged his forgiveness. At the same time she told him that she was already married; her husband was an educated man, his name was Artur Sengert [?]. He loved the child, whose name was Michael, and had registered him under his own name.
Dodl saw the child and spent a little time with him. Then he told her that he was going to America and would send [support] for the child as much as he possibly could.
He took leave of Selma and the child and went away.
Now he decided also to take leave of his parents, and for that purpose he travelled to Kraków.
(To be continued).
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Strike of the Seasonal Workers

What's new in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 19 Av 5696 — piątek 7 sierpnia 1936 [Friday, 7 August 1936].)
Będzin
Strike of the seasonal workers.
At the beginning of this week the workers on the public works went on strike. The strikers demand work 6 days a week and a raise of the daily wage from 1.60[?] to 4 zł. The strike is proceeding calmly. On Tuesday the building workers showed their solidarity with a one-day strike.
— The workers of the tile (stove-tile) factory have gone on strike. The strikers have occupied the factory. On Monday the factory director gave a speech in which he appealed to the strikers not to make the situation harder, so that the factory could go on running; to this the workers declared that they stand by their demands and that until they are met the strike will continue.
Workers deny the complaints that they molested Jewish passers-by.

A delegation of the striking sewerage workers in Będzin came to the editorial office, in the persons of: Szlomo Grigcajner[?] (Kołłątaja 48), Wacław Adamczyk (Akszei[?] 43) and Nigul[?] Szwarcfuser[?] (Podzamcze 61), who ask us to declare to the public that the complaints that someone among the strikers molested Jewish passers-by are invented.
The hooligan who on Tuesday evening molested a Jewish passer-by on Sienkiewicza Street — the workers wanted to catch him, but they did not succeed.
A revolver bullet explodes and wounds a Jewish boy.

Six-year-old Matek Grune found a revolver bullet in the street. With this "find" he quickly ran home and showed it to his older brother. The latter went out into the yard with the bullet and began to hit it with a stone. At that moment the bullet exploded and gave the older brother a deep wound in the neck.
It is characteristic to add that the wounded boy, who ran to the local hospital, did not receive help there because the doctors were busy. Only after waiting about an hour did he go to Dr. Teichner.
Merchants' Association in defence of President Rubinlicht.

At the board meeting of the Merchants' Association, which took place last Sunday, Mr. M. Unger submitted a proposal that the board should react to the public attacks against the president, Mr. Rubinlicht. A discussion developed over the proposal, after which it was decided to deal with the matter at the next meeting of the board.
Popular train to Krynica. A return ticket for only 13.80.

As we have already written, the Jewish Society for Knowledge of the Land in Będzin is organising a popular train to Krynica for 3 days, i.e. from the 14th to the 16th of August. The price of return tickets is 13 zł 80 gr. Departure from Katowice on Thursday the 13th at 23.46. Arrival in Krynica on Friday the 14th at 7.50 a.m. (the train stops at Szapieniec[?]). Departure from Krynica on the 16th at 23.02, arrival in Katowice on the 17th at 4.25 a.m.
Tickets are available at the "Orbis" [offices] in Katowice, Sosnowiec, Będzin and Chorzów.
Participants living more than 20 kilometres from Katowice, such as Dąbrowa, Strzemieszyce, Sławków, Olkusz, Zawiercie and Częstochowa, receive a 50 per cent discount to Katowice and back.
Those who wish to take part must provide themselves with tickets in good time.
He made 'order'...

The owner of a grocery shop in Gzichów, a well-known Endek, while in a drunken state, made "order" in his shop: he scattered the goods, demolished the fittings and afterwards treated his family to blows.
Only the police, who were called, calmed him down.
Almost a tram disaster.

On Wednesday at midday a young Christian woman, wanting to run across Małachowskiego Street, fell onto the tram line; at that moment a tram arrived, which was stopped instantly, thanks to which the Christian woman was saved from certain death.
At the critical minute...

Thieves got into the flat of Mr. Zygiel (Sączewska[?] Street) and began packing up the household goods. At that moment Mr. Z. arrived and disturbed the "work".
The thieves got out through the window.
Travel News

[Będzin — travel.]
The local “Orbis” [travel bureau] announces: 1) groups (of no fewer than 10 persons) making an excursion to Kraków on the “Sachiniek”[?] will receive free tickets for the return journey. 2) Those travelling to Karlsbad may take 1200 zł. with them. All formalities are handled by “Orbis”; and 3) the price of a ship ticket to Eretz Israel is only 11 pounds.
—o—
Delegate to the World Congress.
Mr. Chaim Szajn has gone as delegate from Będzin to the Jewish World Congress, which opens this Saturday night [motzei Shabbat] in Geneva.
The Second Instalment of the Lump-Sum Tax

[Będzin — taxes.]
We draw attention to the fact that 15 August is the last date for paying the second instalment of the ryczałt [lump-sum] tax on turnover[?]. After this date the tax office may already carry out distraints and impose costs.
Searches

[Będzin — police.]
On Monday evening secret police came to Szpigelman's bookshop, where a search was carried out, after which 4 pamphlets from the latest numbers of the “Groszowa” Library [penny library] were confiscated.
Searches were also made in the “Kultur” and “Hazomir” libraries.
What Is Heard on the Election Front?

[Sosnowiec — kehilla elections.]
Small traders' sections declare for a list of their own. — Hard[?] to create a union of religious Jews. — Brit Hatzohar or Brit Hachayal.
On the election front it is still calm; despite the fact that the deadline for submitting the candidate lists already begins next Monday[?], all is nevertheless hush-quiet. Consultations of each group are still going on, and quiet wrangling around the question “who is to head the list?”.
The question of creating a bloc of religious Jews is also meeting certain obstacles, because the “shtiblech”, which have “strength”, demand mandates for themselves and do not want to be wholly dependent on the “Aguda”. Because of this it is quite possible that several Orthodox lists will appear.
The situation is no better in the national camp, where everyone goes his own way. Even in the ranks of the Revisionists and “Brit Hachayal” a dispute has arisen over the resolution adopted at the last meeting that the list will appear under the name of Brit Hatzohar and not of “Brit Hachayal”, although the latter possesses a larger contingent of voters.
In the artisans' ranks there is no unity either. The “Chaitn” [tailors'] society, to which the artisans' association turned[?] about a union, came out against the proposal. The tailors' guild too, which claimed the first place on the candidate list, is somewhat offended, and its members have been given a “free hand”...
Full of energy, the small traders' association goes to the elections. Because of the differences of opinion on the question, the board called a conference of all the sections, which were to state their position on whether the small traders' association should put up a separate list.
After the matter had been explained by Messrs. Oliner, Glajtman and Kajzer[?], almost all the sections (14) declared that non-party parnassim must be elected to the new kehilla, who will defend the interests of the community at large and not meddle in any politics whatsoever.
The Jewish Patrons at the “Palais de Danse”

[Sosnowiec — violence.]
Had, poor souls, a spoiled Friday night...
On Friday night a bloody brawl took place at the “Palais de Danse”, into which the Jewish patrons were also drawn.
The incident began under the following circumstances: at 11 o'clock three persons, two men and a woman, entered the premises and took a table. When the guests were tipsy, one of them began wandering[?] about the hall and disturbing the guests.
At a certain moment the man went up to a small table at which a young Jewish man was sitting with a young lady, and invited her to dance. When the young man told the drunkard to calm down, he fell upon him and beat him badly. The impudent act stirred up the other Jewish guests who were spending Friday night in the restaurant, and a general fight broke out between the two sides, during which chairs, bottles and several lethal implements flew through the air.
At the alarm raised by the owners of the restaurant, police arrived and put an end to the brawl. The chief “hero” had several teeth knocked out.
Jewish Boy Saved from Death

[Sosnowiec — accident.]
On Saturday afternoon Mr. Cwajgenhaft[?] was sitting with his 3-year-old boy on the balcony of his flat on Szernama[?] Street.
When the boy leaned against the balcony, the whole front side fell down onto the pavement. By a miracle Mr. Cwajgenhaft snatched the child and thanks to this saved him from death.
Old 5-Złoty Coins Not Valid from 30 September

[General — currency.]
Bank Polski announces that on 30 September of this year the period for exchanging the old large 5-złoty coins of the years 1929 and 1930 expires. After this date these silver coins will lose their value and will no longer be exchanged by Bank Polski and its branches.
The Financial Crisis in the Kehilla Treasury

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.]
Shochtim threatened a strike if they do not receive their salaries.
As we have already written, the “honeymoon months” in the gmina [kehilla] are already over, and the klei kodesh [religious functionaries] have not been receiving their salaries for several months now.
In connection with this the shochtim intervened with the vice-president Dr. Wercman[?] on the question of paying them their salaries. Because Dr. Wercman did not receive the shochtim's delegation properly, the latter decided to go on strike and notified the gmina office of the decision.
The threat naturally frightened the commissarial rulers of the kehilla, who began negotiating with the shochtim that they should withdraw the strike decision.
The shochtim agreed to this after the promise that they would receive 50 per cent of the slaughter revenue.
Kożek [?] has finally got his comeuppance...

On the streets of Sosnowiec a certain Kożek [?] was well known; he is not normal, but when it came to beating children he was “fully conscious” — and he beat Jewish children in particular, threw stones at them, and so on.
Thanks to the intervention of the town councillors Pliner and Kiwer, Kożek has been taken away to the barracks for the insane.
For abandoning a child.

In the fields of the Pekin colony workers found a 9-month-old child.
The police, who began investigating [?], established that the child's mother is the 26-year-old Michalak.
These days the “devoted” mother stood before the local district court and was sentenced to 6 months in prison.
Suicide of a Jewish woman

Last Friday Mrs. Gerszenowicz poisoned herself. The suicide died.
—o—
Collision of a tram with a motor vehicle.
At the corner of Mandoszewska [?] and Prez. Mościckiego streets a tram collided with a lorry. Several of the tram's windows were smashed, and the front part of the tram was also damaged.
—o—
A bloody wedding in Mrzygłód.
In the flat of a certain Bartoszek in Mrzygłód a wedding took place. When the guests were already thoroughly drunk, a bloody brawl broke out among them, during which one of the guests had his belly slit open [?].
Large Meeting at the Kielce Rabbi's on Creating a United Jewish Bloc for the Kehilla Elections

[Kielce — kehilla; elections.] On the initiative of several dozors (kehilla board members) and parnasim of the outgoing kehilla, the Rabbi of Kielce, Rabbi Rapaport, convened on Wednesday night at his residence a large meeting of the representatives of all local political parties and economic organisations, as well as non-party people, concerning the creation of a united Jewish bloc for the forthcoming kehilla elections.
The session was attended by representatives of: the Zionist Organisation, Mizrachi, the Revisionists, Agudah, Poale Zion (Right), the merchants, the small traders' and craftsmen's association, as well as delegates of the Chmielnik and Chęciny Hasidim.
The meeting was opened by Rabbi Rapaport, who gave a short introductory address on the purpose of the meeting and on the urgent need to create a unity list of all Jewish organisations and associations.
Dozor Leichter, one of the initiators of the united Jewish bloc, supplemented Rabbi Rapaport's speech and appealed to those assembled to make every effort to create the united Jewish bloc, which in the present time of trouble for the Jews is simply a vital necessity.
A lengthy discussion then developed on the manner and form of creating the unity list. Many speakers asked that the sharpest legal measures be applied against the "rogatka" [?] and all sorts of [?] lists of private seat-grabbers, in case such a united Jewish bloc is created.
Then the representatives of the Zionist Organisation, Messrs. A. Finkelsztajn and Editor Wielani [?], made declarations that the Zionist Organisation will go to the most far-reaching compromises in order to bring about a united Jewish bloc.
A similar declaration was also made in the name of Mizrachi by Mr. Chaim Lezi [?], in the name of the Revisionists by Editor Radal, in the name of the small traders by Mr. Żanszkowski [?], Agudah and others.
It was then decided to elect a political committee of 11 persons, one representative of each group, with the participation of Rabbi Rapaport as an objective and disinterested mediator between the parties.
This commission held its first session last night, at which the manner of distributing the mandates in the council and in the board was discussed. The session lasted until late at night.
The news of the possibility of creating a united Jewish bloc aroused great satisfaction among the greater part of the Jewish population of Kielce.
On the other hand, this news caused an understandable panic among certain outside [?] seat-grabbers, who will thus be unable to realise their careerist aims and private ambitions.
We, for our part, welcome the formation of a united Jewish bloc and wish it success and prosperity.
The Yahrzeit Candle Restored Domestic Peace

[Kielce — Human interest; true story.] A few years ago the Kielce young lady G., quite by chance, was staying with relatives in Krynica, who used to take her along to all the dancings and other spa entertainments. Miss G.'s parents were [?] not rich at all, and so she was modestly dressed and therefore felt a little uncomfortable against the background of the [?] splendidly dressed spa ladies, who outdid one another in expensive gowns.
But it was not only her modesty that made her stand out among the fair sex of the spa guests. She also stood out for her innocent beauty, true Jewish charm and slender, elegant figure.
That is why she indeed had great success.
Among the many "dancing partners" one stood out: a young man from Łódź, K., the son of very well-to-do parents, who fell in love with the Kielce young lady from the first moment.
And once, during a dance, when he, happy, was looking into her eyes, he suddenly said to her ardently:
— You are my destined one! Without you life loses all value for me.
The young man from Łódź was young, impulsive, rich and, above all, deeply in love. He did not put his plans on the "long bench", and without consulting his parents he married the young lady, who felt happy, overjoyed: she loved the young man and, besides, was freed from poverty [?], easing the lot of her parents as well.
There was, however, one more "party in the matter" [?] — the young man's parents, who remained very displeased with the match.
"The 'Snek' [?] (the boy) has, with his rash step, as they put it, completely wrecked their plans, but it is not too late yet. It can still be saved" — and the in-laws on the young man's side began to strive consistently for the couple to separate and divorce. They were not held back by the fact that their daughter-in-law had given birth to a grandchild. They pursued their goal consistently by every means — and achieved it.
The young couple's happy life was broken.
The young wife returned to her parents with a small child in her arms, and some time later received a get (divorce) from her husband. He was very unhappy, he wept, but could not go against the will of his parents, on whom he was materially dependent. Yet he still loved her and greatly longed for her and the child.
Now it happened that not long ago old S. had a yahrzeit. He went to the synagogue and asked the shammes to set up a yahrzeit candle by the prayer stand.
And here a strange thing happened. The thick yahrzeit candle went out for no reason at all; he asked the shammes to fix the candle. A while later it went out again. The same thing repeated itself a third time.
— What can this mean? — he asked the shammes in fright.
The shammes shook his head meaningfully and said:
— Ask the rabbi a she'eila (ritual question).
The superstitious K. [sic] went to the rabbi — the same one who had arranged the couple's divorce. The rabbi, having heard the story, declared that in his opinion it was a bad sign, and that it would be desirable for him to restore the young couple's happy life.
K. was deeply shaken by this story. That very day he telegraphed his former daughter-in-law in Kielce that she should come at once to Łódź and bring the child with her.
And here comes the happy end.
In these days the couple was to be married again.
Tax Office Seizes the Kehilla Budget

[Kielce — Kehilla; taxes.] This week the Kielce tax office placed a seizure (attachment) on the kehilla's budget (etat — the communal tax) for the year 1936. The tax office is claiming from the kehilla a sum of some thirty-odd thousand zł. for state taxes and for the Ubezpieczalnia (social-insurance fund). The communal taxpayers are receiving demands to pay the communal tax at the tax office.
It is characteristic that the tax office demanded payment of the communal tax before the taxpayers had received payment orders ("nakazy") from the kehilla.
In connection with this there was a very great commotion in the kehilla this week among the communal taxpayers, who asked for various explanations and at the same time took out receipts for the communal-tax sums they had already paid months ago.
"Ya'amod!" — The Informers Are Back!

[Kielce — Informers; commentary.] The town of Kielce has not yet calmed down from the vile deed [?] committed in his time by the "High-Holiday musaf cantor" who utterly ruined the head of the [?] merchants' association — about which we already wrote in our paper at the time — and already one has heard of a fresh, base villainy.
New informers and scoundrels have denounced the head of the small-traders' association, who was detained this week at the investigation office, and thereby caused a man [?] needless heartbreak and moral suffering.
Fortunately, this time the denunciation did not succeed; the summoned [?] witnesses rejected all suspicions against the detainee, who was indeed soon released.
The plague of informing is starting to rage again in Kielce, and who knows to what misfortunes these scoundrels will lead. It was a little quiet — and "Ya'amod!", the informers are back!
Graves and Tombstones Desecrated in the Kielce Cemetery

[Kielce — Cemetery; kehilla.] This week unknown hooligans again broke through a section of the cemetery wall and desecrated a row of graves and tombstones.
It is therefore the duty of the kehilla to take an energetic interest in the matter and adopt all kinds of measures so that such outrages are not repeated. The kehilla must also intervene with the authorities and demand that they order a strict investigation of this.
Verdict in the Big Trial of the Municipal Officials Who Embezzled 24,286 zł.

[Kielce — Court; municipal embezzlement.] This Wednesday the Kielce District Court pronounced its verdict against the former municipal (magistrate) officials of the enforcement (execution) department who from 1930 to 1933 embezzled a sum of 24,286 zł.
The head of the enforcement department, Edmund Kowalski, the official Wojciech Stanisławczyk, and the bailiffs (executors) Ignacy Lewandowski and Wacław Miniewski [?] were sentenced to 2 years' imprisonment, and the bailiff Józef Kowalski — to 8 months' imprisonment. The convicted also lose their civic rights for 5 years.

The Election Fair in Sosnowiec Has Already Begun

[Sosnowiec — elections.]
For a whole week all the organizations and groupings were busy putting together the candidate lists, which must be submitted by today, Friday. Only after that did the election fair really begin.
In the course of yesterday 7 lists were submitted, but presumably there are[?] fictitious lists among that number; the true face will become clear only on Saturday night.
— Among the Revisionists a stormy meeting took place on Sunday over the question „who heads [the list]?“. After a passionate discussion the majority was in favour of Mr. Jasna [Yasna] figuring first.
In the Hasidic circles a „sensation“ was caused by the bloc of: the Koziegłowy faction together with the Aleksander, Żarki[?] and Chęciny[?] Hasidim; at the head of the list figures Mr. Avraham Gasner[?].
— It's going to be merry in the town...

[Będzin — welfare; followed by seven short news items: Będzin, Zagłębie, Katowice, Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa.]
A few weeks ago the magistrate (municipality) of Będzin set aside a certain sum for the half-colony (day summer camp) for poor schoolchildren.
Of the sum set aside, 900 zł. was allotted for 100 Jewish children, i.e. 30 groszy a day for each child.
The half-colony for the Christian children was already in operation, whereas for the Jewish children — not necessarily. After all, it's not a matter that has anything to do with local politics...
But as the saying goes: „better late than never“ — on Wednesday a meeting took place in the kehilla premises with the participation of the school guardians (opiekunowie), before whom Mr. Rubinlicht declared that after great effort he had obtained the 900 zł. from the magistrate for the half-colony, which must start operating as soon as possible.
After the discussion of the matter it was decided that, since the colony can operate no more than 2 weeks, the children will receive better meals 3 times a day.
In all 100 children will benefit: 90 from the 3 public (folk) schools and 10 from the Talmud Torah.
The half-colony will already be operating next Sunday in the garden of the public schools on Kościuszki Street.

Starosta Halts Peasants' Agitation Against a Jewish Shopkeeper

[Włoszczowa district — antisemitism.]
In the village of Bichawa [?], Włoszczowa county, the Jew Yehoshua Drewner [? first occurrence printed "Yrewner"] has lived for 50 years, making his living from a small shop and also from a field.
Recently a Christian shop opened in the same village, and from then on severe torments began for the only Jewish family in the village. The local inhabitants, who had been on the best of terms with Drewner, began to boycott him [?] and stopped buying from him [?]. But that was still too little, and the peasants actually wanted to force the Jew to leave with his family. To this end the doors and windows of his shop and of his flat were smashed, in order to make the Jewish family's life miserable.
And it came to pass that Drewner went to Włoszczowa, went in to the starosta and told him of the troubles and harassment from the peasant population against him.
The starosta at once sent for the chief agitators and fined them 25 zł.
When the agitation did not stop, Drewner intervened once more with the starosta, who ordered 20 men to be arrested.
After their release the starosta came out to the village in person, assembled all the peasants and warned them that if anything bad happened to the Jewish family, 10 peasants would have to guard the Jew and his family every day, and whoever refused would be fined 100 zł.
Since this strict order the village has been quiet, and relations between the peasants and Drewner are friendly again.
What Does the Penal Code Say About Paying the Deduction for the 'Ubezpieczalnia' Withheld from Workers?

[Law — penal code and social insurance.]
Article 58 of the Penal Code states that whoever runs an establishment employing labour (a factory, workshop, business) and deducts from the pay of the workers and employees the due contribution for the "Ubezpieczalnia" [Social Insurance Institution] and does not pay the money in to these institutions, is liable to a penalty of arrest of up to three months or a fine of up to three thousand zł.
As one sees from this article, many merchants and manufacturers can be prosecuted for not paying in the money that must be paid to the "Ubezpieczalnia". Anyone who merely owes money to these institutions is thereby already liable to the penalty.
It goes without saying that the penalty applies only to persons who owe the "Ubezpieczalnia" the sum deducted from the pay of workers or employees. But one is not punished with arrest when one owes the institutions money for the part of the contribution that the employer himself is obliged to pay. Yet it is always the case that anyone who owes the "Ubezpieczalnia" also owes it the sum deducted from wages.
There are also many cases where employers pay the whole contribution themselves and do not deduct it from the workers' pay. In such cases one can indeed [?] defend oneself against the charge under Article 58; one must add, however, that for the law there exists no such requirement [?] that the employer pays the whole contribution. It is officially assumed that in the contribution the employer pays in there is a part that is counted as deducted from the worker's pay.
Sudden Death at the Starostwo

[Zawiercie — kehilla.]
On Tuesday morning, in the penal department of the Zawiercie starostwo [district office], the 62-year-old house-owner Michał Lewensztajn of Kromołów died suddenly.
Lewensztajn had come to the starostwo for the trial against him; he was accused of not having allowed the licensed chimney sweep to sweep the chimneys of his house.
At a certain moment Lewensztajn declared that he did not feel well and fell to the ground. The district [?] doctor, who came at once, established that Lewensztajn had died of a heart attack.
When the kehilla learned of this, the Chevra Kadisha sent the hearse and delegated several mitaskim [burial attendants]. When the latter arrived on the spot they no longer found anyone, because the family had hastily taken the deceased to Kromołów, so as not to have to deal with the kehilla, since the deceased had been a rich man. Because of this the secretary Mr. Lewkowicz [?] immediately drove out to Kromołów, where everything was already prepared for the burial. After consulting with the starosta, the latter issued a decision that the deceased must not be buried without the consent of the Zawiercie kehilla.

After 22 Years. (The "benefits" Jews have from the World War.)

[Leading article — 22 years since the outbreak of the World War.]
Every morning, when one picks up a Jewish newspaper, one is afraid to open it; the hands tremble with fright and dread: who knows in what places anger has suddenly poured out over the handful of Jews, and what new inventions have been devised to fight the Jew, who everywhere and at all times is the eternal scapegoat, the perpetually restless soul that falls apart at every rustle of a page. Somehow we have acquired nerves of steel, since we have grown indifferent to everything, so that often one gets the impression that we have resigned from our eternal existence, which is at the same time so rich and so varied.
In one place — so we hear — we are not wanted, despite our having brought the country and its citizens so much benefit; "elsewhere" we are simply dangerous, regardless of the fact that we bring in drive and revival, wealth and initiative; that they have set upon us and look only for our faults — it is not even worth talking about. We are, after all, a people that remains responsible for every individual, and as soon as there is a single outcast, our whole community remains the guilty party before the entire world. We are the cause of everything bad, and whatever resounds in the world is that the Jew, with his cunning, wants to grab the whole world.
Yes, "we want to rule the whole world" — and this happens at a time when we have no place of rest in any country at all. Is it not comical and tragic at once, something only we, as a stiff-necked people, can grasp? Could other peoples in the world have existed, and on top of that been active, under such terrible, inhuman conditions? Can normal peoples, accustomed to leading a human life, compare themselves to our abnormal conditions?
The Jewish people, living in every corner of the globe, has after all been well trained by the rulers of the world, which has remained an incomparably excellent lesson for us; and at all times we have borne the most inhuman persecutions and torments on our laden shoulders, and we have always withstood the most terrible examination.
Which people in the world could presume to endure this endless path of thorns? A people hunted and tormented, living in the worst conditions. Our history is rich — blood and tears, struggles and persecutions under the most inhuman conditions occupy the top place in our epochs. Other peoples would in such a case not have kept a human appearance; with us, by contrast, it is a kind of charm, a kind of remedy to heal the wounds and purify the conscience.
But we are already far, very far away from that epoch. We are no longer in [?] the Middle Ages with the Crusades, when Jews were ceremonially burned in the lime-kilns with the Shema Yisrael [on their lips].
Today we stand, somehow, at the 22nd anniversary of the world slaughter, which gave mankind so many novelties. A trifle — how far the world has progressed, what gigantic inventions have come into being. When one tries to compare, when one wants to draw a parallel between before and now, the enormous progress is truly beyond recognition.
The order of the world had to be halted: one chapter ends in the year 1914, with the outbreak of the World War, and a second begins after the "outbreak" [?] of the world slaughter. True, the war has been stopped; officially no wars are being waged. But how much blood is being spilled in all countries under the existing "peaceful" conditions? Who nowadays is not bloodthirsty?
In recent years the world has been enriched with colossal new inventions, which are truly a pride for mankind and civilization — but are these fine deeds not drenched in blood? Is there not a "peaceful" battle going on in almost every country? And since the world cannot get back onto the straight line, since the blood still cannot stop flowing, one must, after all, look for the causes — and then the first scapegoat [lit. kapparah-chicken] is the Jew. The Jew is guilty of the world crisis; he is the one "who wants to turn the whole world upside down."
Be that as it may, the Jew is everywhere and at all times the scapegoat. In Europe there is no room for him, he must be driven out quickly — so he ran off to Palestine. There the petrified and frozen earth cried out: come here, work us, drain us, breathe a spirit of life into us — and it did not take long until wastelands were turned into blossoming settlements and petrified earth was turned into splendid colonies and vineyards. A new life began [?] to pulse there, which the world admired; but this too "civilized" Europe could not tolerate, and efforts were made to kindle a fire among half-wild creatures, who became a blind tool in the hands of dealers [?] and consider it a sacred thing to do what they are ordered. And so devoted, idealistic, useful work is turned back into ruins, and meanwhile blood is spilled and victims fall, who are killed for the sanctification of the Name.
That is what we Jews have gained from the great World War, after which countries and peoples were liberated from their oppressors.
To the Arabs!

[Poetry — Land of Israel.]
Not with a storm of swords dipped in blood,
not with the fire of weapons do we come here,
but with the pure faith, young and sunny;
peace and labour are our weapon.

There wait for us the withered branches
of almonds, of olives, of pomegranates, of grapes;
we hear the language of the desert's silence:
come to your land, raise it from the dust!

Come back to the land where you once were.
Here soil and garden and tree await you,
the fruits of your own toil you shall eat,
back in the land of your own home.

See: where only scorpions [?] and snakes built nests,
where jackals sobbed themselves out in the desert's wailing,
our kvutzot already bloom, hora songs
ring out from houses built by our hands.

We brought drink to petrified fields,
to flames, to grasses, to rocky earth.
The desert's wrath we quench with forests.
Have you, our neighbours, not heard of this?

Not heard that we sow grain upon stones?
That we carry new life to field and sand?
That together we stand in wrath, as one,
like an iron wall against the enemies of the land?

May your hatred be extinguished, from brother to brother,
may peace bloom in our young land!
With peace we come, we say it again,
we stretch out to you a brotherly hand.

Understand, I adjure you! The time has come,
our destiny now records our great hour
of ploughing, sowing, of building and digging the well,
to water [?] fields and create here an oasis [?].

Not with a storm of swords dipped in blood,
O brotherly people, do we come here,
but with will and with deeds courageous and sunny,
with peace and labour — understand us, I adjure!
The Beach Is to Blame!..

[Sosnowiec — humorous feuilleton.] By J. Oberżanek.

Monologue of a Sosnowiec Jew who in his old age took a fancy to a young wife.

Listen, men: if you are already past[?] the first half-hundred, that is, after fifty — lay down your tools and say a Rabbanan-Kaddish; if there appear on your head, in your beard, "cemetery flowers" — the hearse horses[?] begin to limp towards you!.. When a matchmaker comes to you to propose a match, you should open the door wide, take him by the collar and send him to all the black years [to the devil].

And needless to say if you have, God forbid, been left a widower — once is enough[?]! Marrying a second time means eating reheated krupnik [barley soup]. If, heaven forbid, you have been left a widower, or your wife has gone away[?] from you (such luck happens sometimes too!...) — raise your hands to heaven and say:

— Master of the Universe, thanks[?] and praise to You for what I have had until now, and from now on leave me in peace.

Against whom do I say this? Against myself. In my old age I let a matchmaker draw me in[?]; I shouted:

— Reb Nete, why have you set upon[?] me? What use is a maiden to me in my old years? What will I do with such a "salamane"[?] doll [lalka]?

He talked me into it:

— Reb Hersh Ber, you will see how your years will pass[?]. You will look like an "Adonis"[?], you will start a new life; you are still, no evil eye, "żwawy" [Polish: brisk, lively] enough; you will see, Reb Hersh Ber, that you will yet, God willing...

— Perhaps make a bris? — I burst out laughing.

— Yes, yes, indeed make a bris, why not? You can laugh at all of today's young men, the football players and dancers — may I not sin with my words — you are, after all, still a man[?] "gam pletsu"[?].

Well, I let myself be talked into it by the evil inclination and married a painted "striga" [witch, Polish strzyga], skin and bones. By day, when she still primps herself up a bit[?], paints her lips, plucks her eyebrows and pulls a black dress with a frill[?] onto her bag of bones, it's only half the trouble; but at night, when all the "drodakes"[?] [trappings] are gone, you feel cold in your bones.

What grieves you even more is that this bag of bones thinks herself a "Moyshe Groys" [a big shot]. "Ani dostępu" [Polish: unapproachable], she rattles away[?] "po polskiemu" [in Polish], she is "strasznie inteligentna" [Polish: terribly intelligent] and seeks[?] nothing less than "męskie towarzystwo" [male company]; women, she says, she has no use for, because women are "mutlerins"[?] [gossips?] and men don't care for talk...

And what is she like as a housewife? Heaven forbid she has a clue. Just as my first one[?] — may she have a bright paradise — was a fiery housewife: her cooking, her baking, her darning[?] a sock, her sewing a button onto the underpants — what's past is past[?] — exactly so is this one the opposite. Ah, and woe to what I have lived to see!

When she goes to wash out a pot or rinse a glass, she puts on her leather gloves, so as not to spoil the manicure of her nails; when she goes to make the beds[?], she puts on my smock, so that, heaven forbid, not a single feather should land on her.

But I would have put up with all that — I've truly earned[?] it all; as you say: the dog deserves the stick — I would have put up with all that, if only she at least wanted to stay at home.

In wintertime, right after the midday meal, she takes up her "chemical industry": at the ...[?] of the "yegoyshek"[?] [moustache?] of her upper lip she sits a good two or three hours, now around the eyes and in the eyes, the little nose and the little mouth, now the figure — until she gets the bag of bones in order.

I ask her:

— Felunia (out of my Hendl has come a "Felunce"), why are you dressing yourself up [stroić] like this on an ordinary Wednesday?

— "Na fajf" [Polish: to a five-o'clock tea] — she answers.

— "Na fajf"? Then why do you need to go to strangers' houses to whistle [Yiddish pfeifen — pun on "fajf"]? Better whistle here, at home; maybe it will whistle better for you here than among strangers?

She laughs at me:

— Hee... hee... hee... ha... ha... ha... "ty stary kaszcz"[?] [Polish: you old ...], "wiesz?" [you know?] A fajf is "rozkosz" [delight]... "walc angielski" [English waltz]... tango... "orkiestra gra" [the orchestra plays]. "O-s-t-a-t-n-i-a n-i-e-dz-i-e-l-a" [To ostatnia niedziela — "The Last Sunday", the famous Polish tango]... What do you know, you old koyletsh [braided challah], what life is, what a fajf is... what a dancing is; you know only three things: to study, to eat and to sleep, and I too know three things: to dance, to drink and to flirt.

That's winter. And is summer better? Summer is even worse. In summer she is a guest at home. She has no use for any summer resorts [letniska] and spas; she does in Sosnowiec the same as other women do in Krynica, Ciechocinek or Truskawiec. Sosnowiec, she says, is also a fine town.

So she spends the whole summer in Sosnowiec, comes and goes: comes from a "poranek" [morning show] and goes to the "fajf", comes from the fajf and goes to the dancing. Sometimes she has a "zabawa" [party], sometimes a première at the cinema; everywhere she has "wolne wejście" [free admission], with all the directors she is hand in glove ["button by button"] — and lives it up.

And needless to say, when the heat waves come — then the real season begins for her: at dawn she jumps up, puts on a pair of "majteczki" [panties] the size of a ...[?] [negits], plants herself in front of the mirror and turns, turns this way and turns that way, looks how she will look swimming in the water, how she will look sitting on the sand.

Thus she stands at the mirror for hours on end and keeps turning.

I ask her:

— Feluniu, Felochna, where are you going so early?

— "Jadę do Katowic, na plażę" [Polish: I'm going to Katowice, to the beach] — she answers.

— Well, and you'll show yourself like that among people?

— "A jakże" [Polish: but of course!] — she answered, and with that gave me to understand that a beach is exactly like, to make the distinction, a mikveh; the only difference is that the "mikveh" is set up on "democratic foundations"...

That pleased me very much: a wife goes to immerse — why not, on the contrary, a Jewish daughter must go to immerse.

Only one thing surprised me: yes, immersion, but why every single day? Isn't once a week enough?

So I made up my mind: I must go to the "mikveh" once — "plaża" in the vernacular — and take a look at what goes on there.

Gentlemen, help, Jews, what my eyes saw there! Males with females together... all together in one water. On the water you see nothing but bare heads: the head of a shaven male leaning on the head of a female. He is teaching her to swim — that's a lesson — may my eyes never see such again. After the bath they come out of the water and "nurzać się"[?] [wallow] in the sand.

When I saw my Felunia with her naked bag of bones in the water, on both sides of her two "tickers"[?], two young sunburnt lads [junacy] with muscles and broad chests, with black forelocks [czupryny] — they were my Felunia's "under-tickers"[?] — they taught her to do a "nurek" [dive] in the water, then they led my Felunia out and the three of them wallowed[?] together in the sand.

Now, gentlemen, I already know who is to blame for all the troubles in the world, why we Jews suffer so many troubles, so many evil decrees, so many misfortunes, catastrophes, revolutions, epidemics and other misfortunes — to blame for all of it is — the beach!..
On the Way to the New Kehilla. — What Must Be Done?

[Sosnowiec — kehilla and elections; article.] What must one know on the eve of the new elections to the kehilla?
Whoever has open eyes and a straight mind must understand that the kehilla cannot become a place for individuals who have no record ("stazh") whatsoever of public activity, but only know the trick of how to wangle themselves a mandate. Such specialists hang around the batei midrash, the Hasidic shtiblekh, the suburbs and even some of the societies.
The mandate-taker is without responsibility, and the mandate-givers bear even less responsibility.
Whoever looks now at the pre-election fair, at the candidates' exchange, sees darkness before his eyes when he notices who is not rolling up his sleeves for a kehilla mandate!
Not only fools, coarse louts, not only those who think to win themselves votes with a few litres of "jeszcze raz" [Polish "once more", i.e. another round of drink] or to let it cost them in some other way, but also such whose hands are far[?] from clean. Yes, such types too are scrambling to become head of the community in Sosnowiec and in Dąbrowa.
Well, are we really ownerless?
What, can really every uncalled-for aspirant become guardian[?] of the towns[?] of Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa? Shall we really let such "roll-with-fish" seekers into the kehilla?
———
Those who are truly, seriously and sincerely concerned with the authority of the kehilla must be the first in the fight for a respectful attitude towards the institution that is to be the formal representation of the Jewish population. Not only the electing of such candidates, but even the very putting forward of such lists must become an impossibility!
All honest forces must be mobilised to repel the invasion of all sorts of suspect persons who stretch out their little hands for kehilla mandates. We have such people, unfortunately, in various circles, and that is precisely why the danger is very great.
———
The first fruits of our first article are already here. With satisfaction we can state that during the past week the situation on the election front has changed considerably for the better.
We can already predict that the turnout for the kehilla election will this time be a very large one. The voters will no longer stay sitting at home and leave the kehilla mandates up for grabs.
In the responsible public circles, too, people have finally set about putting the kehilla question, or at any rate the pre-election situation, on a very serious footing.
Certainly days are swallowed up[?] by all sorts of personal questions, but on the other hand everyone already realises that an end must be made to the possibility which by itself creates[?] room for all kinds of wild lists, for all kinds of mandate-draggers.
A consolidation of forces has taken place, or at any rate serious efforts have been made to bring about such a consolidation.
There is no talk of taking all Jews under one tallit. Such a kind of unity would be neither possible nor necessary, and indeed harmful. But there must come a consolidation of the forces that are ideologically close to one another, and instead of a scramble for mandates one must bring about a dispute, a wrestling and a struggle of ideologies.
The Jewish street in Sosnowiec must regain its moral face. The only way to this is — to rally under the banners of definite parties and definite ideas.
A few years ago there was no need to explain such elementary notions. The Jewish street always asked the question: what are you, and only then — who are you?
It is not for this that pious Jews say "Ani ma'amin" 13 times every day — in order to entrust their soul to persons without any creed. It is not for this that Jewish parties have been waging such a bitter ideological struggle for decades — so that at the decisive moment the simple Jew should cling precisely to some worthless[?] empty idler[?].
This must be taken into account first of all by the responsible party leaders: they must see and assess the danger if they themselves do not want to drown in a sea of lawlessness; but at the same time they must also put forward from among themselves the best, the most capable people, with intellect and intelligence and with a sincere will to serve faithfully the interests of the population.
One must come forward with people of weight[?], so that the role of the public worker may shine again, and so that in future people will not have to recoil so when the kehilla is talked about.
———
It would, however, not be right for us to think that only the leaderships of the Jewish parties and responsible organisations can decide here.
The last word will, after all, belong to the voters.
And to them one must say:
Thousands of Sosnowiec Jews have been entered in the voters' register; it is true that no Endek danger threatens us, and someone may think: in any case only Jews will be elected — so why should I trouble myself to go to the ballot box?
If we have many such wise men, the kehilla is lost.
The only salvation for the kehilla at the present moment is a mass, a hundred-percent participation in the kehilla elections. If several hundred votes are needed for a mandate, then the wild seat-grabbers are lost. But if a hundred votes will still be enough to become a "dozór in Israel" [member of the kehilla board] — then the devil will laugh.
The only way, therefore — all voters get ready for the ballot box and all vote only for such lists as are put forward by parties and organisations that have an ideological face and a public past in the Jewish street.
Y. N—boym.
Food for Children.

[Health — children's nutrition; medical talk.] A medical talk. — By a doctor.

Over the course of the last few decades a very great deal has been written about scientific and healthily nourishing diets for adults in general and for children in particular.
And when we meet poorly nourished children, it is very possible that their mothers cannot afford to buy the better foods, and a great number of children suffer real hunger.
It is, however, also worth noting that many children who have enough to eat also suffer hunger, so to speak. This comes from the fact that their food does not contain enough of the healthily nourishing elements needed for the development of the young, growing body. There is certainly no question that the mother would [not] want to neglect the child's health. But there are many mothers, and among them many intelligent women, who show no sign of knowing how to combine suitable foods.
Every mother must remember and take note that unsuitable meals and too much exertion can have a bad effect on the child's delicate digestion and nervous system, because a child's health can easily be undermined; nature, too, has its caprices. As long as the human body is not treated properly, it begins to react, and in children the signs are the following: loss of appetite, quick agitation, nervousness, restless sleep, a pale appearance, catarrh of the nose and throat, constipation or a loose stomach; these are also the causes of colds, which lead to many children's diseases.
Many mothers complain that their children are capricious and will not eat everything they are given. The mother should know that this comes from the child's appetite having already been spoiled by the unsuitable meals the mother gave it from infancy on.
Many mothers are of the opinion that their young children must eat meat, in order to accustom them to this dish, and perhaps it will also make them healthier. But the newest discoveries of science show exactly the opposite. Many children's specialists and scientific scholars have found that a well-balanced diet must contain the most important elements and the vitamins A, B, C, D and G, and also the element calcium, which is found in large measure in milk. Calcium is important for growing children, to strengthen their bones and teeth. The element iron is also necessary; it strengthens the blood. Iron is found in the yolks of raw eggs, in all kinds of vegetables, berries and fruit, and especially in spinach.
Eggs, cheese, nuts, beans and peas are among the foods that take the place of meat and fish.
Sugar is an important food, especially in cold winters; it gives the child energy. But it should be eaten in its natural form, such as honey, sugar, figs, raisins of the dark[?] kind, plums and dates. Sweet foods should be given to the child after the meal.
Children must be accustomed to healthily nourishing foods. With a little knowledge and patience every mother can achieve this. Many children, for example, do not like spinach or other vegetables, or milk and eggs. Then these foods should be mixed with the dishes the child does like. To spinach one can add potatoes, rice, brown kasha [buckwheat] and other vegetables, as well as peas, beans, eggs, cheese and nuts. From this one can make a salad, a roast dish, bake latkes or a pudding, and add raw vegetables, so that it suits the child's taste. Milk can be mixed with soup, puddings, mashed bananas, egg yolks, cocoa and chocolate. Sour milk and buttermilk are also nourishing. The foods the child does not like should be given first, when it is very hungry; then it will feel the taste and really enjoy them. The other dishes, which children like, should be given to them at the end of the meal. In this way they will not overeat on the unimportant foods.
Letters from Home.

[Zagłębie — feuilleton in letters; kehilla, Palestine.] By Ben Amotz.
B"H, [week of] the portion "Choose life"...
To my friend Mr. Shlomo, may his light shine.
I have received your letter, and I am fulfilling at once your request to write an answer to your questions.
First of all: your heavy question, "And Korah, who was clever, what made him commit this folly?" — how does it come about that the kehilla president, who devoted [?] dozens of years to public work, a man who occupies the head of the table in almost all modern institutions, should one fine morning (or perhaps one fine moonlit night...) go over to the camp of the "Agudah" [Agudat Israel] — and not only go over, but become their cantor, and at every call of the "Agudah" take his stand at their prayer-stand and say:
— Here I am!..
So you ask, Reb Shlomo. But you should know that already [?] — the same question is asked by everyone, but none of the askers can give the right answer, and it remains: a draw (teyku).
There are, however, some who have a craving to philosophize, and they toil to find an answer to the above-mentioned question. Some say it is a love that depends on a thing, and some answer the question with Rashi's answer, in its plain sense: "his eye misled him"... The leaders of Agudah politics showed him such things as deceived his eyes, and to this day, whenever any kehilla question is discussed at a board meeting, "the thing" rises before his eyes, and he sees nothing more than the front on the right, of the Agudah...
But then come the tellers of parables and say otherwise. It cannot be otherwise — they say — than that "the Agudah" has captured his body, and he must willy-nilly do their will. There is — they say — a kind of beast whose whole power to master a man exists only when the man lets it come near him; then the victim must follow the beast into its nest, where it sucks the marrow out of his head.
When the kehilla president — they say — was an open opponent of the "Agudah", they were powerless; but no sooner had he granted them a smile than the "Agudah" gained control over him, and they do not stop squeezing his brain...
— What's new on the election front? That question could actually be dismissed with the well-known answer: "All quiet on the Western Front", because battles are taking place and there are also "casualties", but "the street" need not know about it, because it could do harm if "the street" found out what goes on behind the scenes...
The present kehilla elections in Sosnowiec look like a rich wedding in a small shtetl. It is seething and bustling on both sides, on the groom's side, on the bride's side; both in-laws puff [?] and blow themselves up like fattened turkeys before Passover. When people go to the wedding canopy the whole shtetl runs after them, everybody rejoices that rich folks' children are getting married. But after the canopy everyone goes back home, and only the real in-laws remain, who sit down at the tables laden with every good thing...
That is exactly what the struggle for the kehilla elections looks like. In the premises where the "wedding in-laws" are, it boils as in a cauldron; each side gathers its family so as to come to the "wedding" with a large crowd, which will come in very handy later on, when they start talking about heads [of the kehilla].. For everybody knows that the whole struggle revolves around the role of the two in-laws, who in the end must at some point come to an agreement...
The "broad masses" are not sitting with folded hands either, but their role is no greater than that of those small-town hangers-on running after the wedding canopy..
— As for the situation in Palestine? We cannot give you a clear answer for the time being, because one has to wait for the result of the Royal Commission. But according to the latest news we have received, the situation there has "improved" a little. The "improvement" consists first of all in the fact that it has at last become clear who the real masters of the new Yishuv are. Until now we lived in "error": all the achievements of the Yishuv, such as the flourishing colonies, orchards, moshavim and the like — we ascribed to the Jewish workers, or, as they call it, to the "Histadrut". They are supposedly the ones who drained the swamps; but suddenly the "truth" was discovered: done with the Histadrut and done with the privileged. Do you at least know, Reb Shlomo, who the new masters are? — the young Agudah fellows, and perhaps even our very own "9-ers"?! Can one question a fact?
The discovery was made at the small Agudah Knessia that was recently held in Vienna. At the assembly a rebbe gave it to be understood that "when Eretz Israel had to be built, nobody was particular about who the workers were, but now that the house is already finished, the owners must take care who the tenants are"... If so, there is no doubt that the tenants must be exclusively of our own people...
It is possible that the Arab murderers aim with their attacks at making the Jewish workers leave the country, so that the new pious tenants should come in, who would be more "loyal" to them; but that is already a matter for political circles. For us it is merely a bit of "consolation" that it has at last become clear who the real masters of the Yishuv in Eretz Israel are...
Have a good Sabbath, wishes you your friend
Ben Amotz.
The main thing I forgot! If you happen to meet anywhere in your parts our Reb Szapsel Rotholc, give him regards from the editorial offices of "Chwila" and "Nowy Dziennik". Both these Zionist papers are filled with descriptions of the Olympiad in Nazi-land...
The above.

Ciechocinek

[Ciechocinek — spas and resorts; travel sketch.] By P. Blumenkranc (Częstochowa).
(A miniature reportage).

I.
Flowers and Children.
A flat piece of earth, flat and partly sandy. But this earth possesses healing virtues that cure pains, "put" people back on their feet and straighten crooked backs (happy is the believer...).
So people travel there, the pilgrims, and with awe and love they breathe in the salty air and dip themselves in the mud.
But salty air is not yet the proper attraction. One has to make them forget the hardships[?] of their heavy yoke; during the weeks of rest one has to awaken festive feelings in a person, to create for him at least an illusion of elevation.
So the spas are beautified. An acquaintance tells us that the plan to beautify Ciechocinek was to cost 80 thousand złoty.
And Ciechocinek really is beautiful! True, it lacks the splendid villas of Krynica and the natural beauties of legendary[?] Zakopane, but on the other hand Ciechocinek has more flowers than the places mentioned — simply a delight to look at! The whole town is immersed in flowers. We Jews have no special relationship to flowers. With us, as Sienkiewicz[?] says somewhere, all flowers are called roses; but in Ciechocinek one comes to love flowers. How many there are, in such abundance[?] and so masterfully arranged that they catch the eye.
Toward evening, when the flowers begin to spread their scents in salty Ciechocinek, you feel a sweetness enveloping you. They too begin to live along with the surrounding night life. Together with the [—] crowd the flowers begin to show their tricks, and you come to love them, and they become — to you, who once recognised a gentile home by the flowerpots[?] in the window — close and dear...
* * *
Ciechocinek also has another pleasant thing in abundance: children. In the street, in the bar[?], on the beach, in the parks — everywhere you see children, dancing, singing[?], smiling. Thousands of children are gathered by Ciechocinek in the season. They come from the four corners of Poland. Some suffer from poor metabolism, raised temperature, defects of the throat organs; others again, as it seems to the young mothers, are not in good health; but all of them smile, all of them raise a racket, all of them romp about.
Among such a crowd one becomes younger, livelier, one forgets the old age lurking behind one's shoulders. Black-eyed, sun-tanned, almost naked, they jump about everywhere. Together with the flowers they remind one of life, of sprouting life, which does not brood, does not complain, but rejoices without reckoning, rejoices together with the whole life-hungry surroundings...
* * *
But (what "but" — it doesn't fit there) this pleasant crowd is accompanied by mothers, and they, the mothers (may they forgive us), bring into the whole "business" much that is unpleasant and disagreeable.
Today's mothers have just about adopted the system of fattening-house[?] owners: children are not allowed to eat, they are stuffed, fed by force, like geese being fattened.
It is often pitiful to watch how a little Jaś wants to get out into the yard and the mother torments him cruelly, without pity.
"Iola ([—] name among Jews), you didn't finish the tomato, you didn't finish drinking the sour cream, you left some of the cocoa!" And she begins to bargain with her little Iola: to let him off some of the cocoa and add to the sour cream. She bargains with him, and the little one, getting into his ambition, does just the opposite, lets himself be pampered, paid homage[?]; when the mother scolds him, he makes himself throw up, and at every "feast" the destruction of Jerusalem takes place.
And here a few words:
We do not occupy ourselves with pedagogical and educational matters. But we consider today's mothers, with their system of upbringing and especially with their "town celebration," illogical, hysterical and educationally harmful.
Quite apart from the [?] phenomenon of running after eight- and nine-year-old children through the yard, street and forest with a plate or a glass and pushing it into their mouths, the matter is absolutely harmful from a social point of view.
We hold that in today's bitter, hard times, when we, especially as Jews, have to push our way through life with our elbows, the young generation must be hardened from the earliest age.
We must, early and late, in the most varied forms, make it understand and even feel that life is hard, harsh and cruel for us.
True, we need not behave according to the old [—] of our grandfathers, who did not permit a child's smile on our lips and made us, at the age of 7, Jews bearing the yoke of the commandments, and reminded us, after a whole day of cheder, of the exile of the Shekhinah.
Our grandfathers saw fit to uproot from us every childish joy, bade us wait to rejoice with a [—][?] until Lag BaOmer. Everything joyful, merry and smelling of life was hidden from us.
But toward the present generation, too, the educators commit a wrong of the opposite kind: by hiding entirely the horrors of our life.
Of course, one need not tell a child about "excesses" [anti-Jewish riots], about our incessant suffering; by no means should one block up the childish springs of joy; but the child's upbringing must be steered in such a direction that, taking its first steps in life, it should not feel the cruelty of our existence; therefore the child must be accustomed so that the blow it will receive later from life should not be so unexpected and strong...
But these gloomy thoughts soon go away. The mothers finally get away[?] with the little ones, an agreement is reached, and again the cries ring out, carefree, childish. They hop about in flowery Ciechocinek and remind one of life, which grows, which seethes.
The tortures of eating are over. They scatter again, and joyful and fired up they fill with their noise the place of forest, mud — and... flowers.
Since When Have We Had Newspapers?

(By Z. Haber, Vienna–Paris.)
There is not a single country in the world that does not have papers of its own, better or worse edited, but a press of its own, which is the expression of the people's will, which is meant to be the public opinion of the country concerned.
Since when have newspapers appeared? Today this is not known exactly. It is known only that the ancient Romans already published newspapers, which were written and were hung up on the square of the government in Rome. Anyone could read and copy them. There were [?] also "colporteurs", who used to copy the sheets and carry them further, or sent them into the provinces; for this they already took payment.
These newspapers recorded everything that happened in Rome, and besides that all events in the provinces.
Of these newspapers a single copy exists in the British Museum in London. The museum, however, has added a remark that it is not quite certain the newspaper is genuine..
Years ago there was an exhibition of newspapers at the Leipzig fair, and among them one saw a paper that appeared in America in 1850. — This paper measured 2 and a half metres in height and 1.80 in width. In this paper the editors announced that the paper had been coming out since the year 1650 and appears once in a hundred years. It discussed everything that had happened from 1750 to 1850. — The two sheets which, as the editors assured, appeared in 1650 and 1750 have not been found to this day.
As far as is known, the first newspaper appeared in 1688 in Breslau; it appeared in a small format, printed on two pages. The paper appeared once a month and had a circulation of ninety sheets, of which only fifty were actually sold.
The first daily newspaper appeared in England in 1702; in Paris the first daily appeared only in 1777; in New York the first daily newspaper appeared only in 1784; in other countries people began to publish newspapers only in 1779.
The first newspapers had very few readers, since at that time people took no interest in current affairs; the papers appeared weekly [?] with four pages, mostly only two pages, and had a circulation of a few hundred copies a day — whereas today, for example, the "Daily Express" has two million copies and the "Saturday Evening Post" more than three million copies with 272 pages.
Newspapers everywhere stood under state censorship; in England and in America censorship was abolished only in 1830, and in most countries it still exists to this day.
The Paris "Figaro" at first appeared with advertisements only; on the title page one could read: "In this paper every line has been paid for"... Today, too, the paper has the most and best advertisements and is therefore very widely read throughout the world.
